weeks: Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman describes brief episodes, several times a week, in which she suddenly smells burning rubber that no one else can detect, followed by a minute of staring and lip-smacking that she does not remember. She has no delusions and functions well at work. Which diagnosis best explains the hallucinations?
options: Complex partial seizures of the temporal lobe
questions.explain: Why: hallucination modality is a discriminator across causes of psychosis, and olfactory hallucinations with automatisms and amnesia point to a temporal lobe (complex partial) seizure focus. Not the others: schizophrenia's typical hallucination is auditory, human voices in a meaningful language; delirium produces visual hallucinations with fluctuating attention; hallucinogens produce visual distortions and illusions.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who is angry about being referred to psychiatry says he has been "hearing noises" since a concert two nights ago, when he stood beside the speakers. The noise is a constant high-pitched tone in both ears. Why is this not a hallucination?
options: It has a physical cause in the ear and is not a perception in the absence of a stimulus
Hallucinations must be accompanied by a delusion
He has insight, and insight excludes psychosis
questions.explain: Why: a hallucination is a sensory perception in the absence of a stimulus; tinnitus after acoustic trauma has a physical cause, and the test is whether any instrument could detect the stimulus. Not the others: hallucinations occur in any modality; they do not require a delusion; insight is a separate MSE domain and does not define a hallucination.

guide.s: sensory perception in the absence of a stimulus

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with three weeks of low mood, early waking and weight loss now insists that her intestines have rotted away and that she is being punished for a crime she committed decades ago. She has never been psychotic before. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
questions.explain: Why: the delusions are mood-congruent: hyper-negative, self-referential content (rotting, guilt, punishment) that tracks a depressive episode. Delusional content that fits the mood points to a mood disorder with psychotic features. Not the others: schizophrenia's delusions are orthogonal to mood and the picture lacks its duration and course; delusional disorder is a nonbizarre delusion without a mood syndrome; schizoaffective disorder needs delusions for two weeks without prominent mood symptoms.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is convinced that the evening news anchor is inserting coded phrases into the broadcast that only he can decode and that refer to his life. He does not believe anyone intends him harm. Which type of delusion is this?
questions.explain: Why: believing that media of any type contains hidden messages meant for oneself that others cannot see is a delusion of reference, one of the subtypes under the older umbrella term "paranoid delusions." Not the others: persecution requires a belief that someone is trying to harm him; external control is the belief that thoughts or body are being operated from outside; grandiosity is an inflated belief about one's own powers or importance and is more typical of mania.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old accountant has believed for two years that a television presenter is secretly in love with him and communicates through her choice of clothing. He works full time, his speech is organised, and he denies hearing voices. Which feature most strongly favours delusional disorder over schizophrenia?
options: The romantic theme of the belief
questions.explain: Why: delusional disorder is delusions without hallucinations, and erotomanic delusions are the classic example of a delusion seen in isolation; the absence of hallucinations, disorganization and negative symptoms with preserved functioning is what separates it from schizophrenia. Not the others: duration beyond six months is compatible with both; an erotomanic theme can occur in either; onset in the fifties is unusual for schizophrenia but is not the defining discriminator.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old described since childhood as odd, solitary and given to eccentric beliefs is diagnosed with schizotypal personality disorder. At 22 he develops persistent auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions and is diagnosed with schizophrenia. Which statement best describes the relationship between the two diagnoses?
options: The early picture was schizophrenia before its age of onset; the developmental phase made the illness visible rather than one disorder turning into another
Schizotypal personality disorder caused the schizophrenia through chronic social isolation
The first diagnosis was an error; Cluster A disorders and schizophrenia are genetically unrelated
Schizophrenia can only be diagnosed if the personality disorder is first ruled out
questions.explain: Why: Cluster A personality disorders are a less severe phenotype of the same illness, sharing a genetic propensity with schizophrenia; a child who is not yet walking at eight months is not noticed to have muscular dystrophy until two years, and the same logic applies here. Not the others: isolation is a manifestation, not a cause; the two are genetically related, not unrelated; there is no such exclusion rule.

guide.s: schizophrenia before its age of onset

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is certain her joint pain flares whenever the barometric pressure falls, and she keeps a diary to prove it. A prospective study of 18 patients over 15 months, matching pain scores to weather, found a mean correlation of 0.016. Which cognitive process best explains her conviction?
options: Perceiving patterns and causal links where none exist, the same tendency that underlies delusion formation
A somatic delusion requiring antipsychotic treatment
Accurate perception of a real but small physiological effect
Malingering to obtain time off work
questions.explain: Why: humans rely on heuristics for probability that fail outside natural settings; the arthritis-and-weather study and the birthday problem both show illusory correlation and base-rate failure, and delusions are the extreme of this normal thought pattern. Not the others: a false belief about one's symptoms held by most patients with arthritis is not a delusion and needs no antipsychotic; the correlation was effectively zero across nine time lags; nothing suggests secondary gain.

questions.stem: During an interview a 28-year-old man denies hearing voices. Twice he stops mid-sentence, turns to the empty corner of the room, and quietly says "not now." How should the perceptual-disturbance component of the mental status examination be recorded?
options: Probable auditory hallucinations inferred from responding to internal stimuli, despite denial
No perceptual disturbances, because the patient denies hallucinations
Visual hallucinations, because he looked at the corner
Thought blocking, a disorder of thought process
questions.explain: Why: patients often deny hallucinations; the examiner may conclude they are present when the patient is responding to internal stimuli as if someone were speaking to him. Not the others: denial does not exclude the finding; looking toward a voice does not make it visual; thought blocking is a sudden interruption of the train of thought, not a reply to an unseen speaker.

questions.stem: A patient's relative says schizophrenia means "split personality." Which historical fact explains where that misunderstanding came from?
options: Kraepelin described dementia praecox as a destruction of the internal connections of the psychic personality, and an amateur translation turned this into a split of the personality
Bleuler described patients alternating between two personalities
Schneider listed multiple personality among the first-rank symptoms
Hippocrates described the illness as a division of the soul
questions.explain: Why: the phrase in Kraepelin's 1919 description, a peculiar destruction of the internal connections of the psychic personality, is the origin of the confusion with multiple personality, via a loose translation from German. Not the others: Bleuler named schizophrenia but did not describe alternating personalities; Schneider's first-rank symptoms are not part of this teaching and do not include multiple personality; schizophrenia is absent from Hippocrates, who described epilepsy and depression but not psychosis.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old university student is brought in at 3 a.m. after a party, terrified that the people around him are shape-shifting and plotting to kill him. Eight hours later the beliefs have gone and he is embarrassed. Which interpretation of the delusions is most consistent with the mental status examination teaching?
options: Acute delusions of this kind are more consistent with alcohol or drug intoxication than with schizophrenia
Bizarre delusions of any duration establish schizophrenia
The rapid resolution proves the beliefs were never delusions
Persecutory content is diagnostic of a primary psychotic disorder
questions.explain: Why: bizarre delusions that persist over time suggest schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, whereas acute delusions are more consistent with intoxication; the time course is the discriminator. Not the others: a bizarre delusion alone no longer satisfies DSM-5 Criterion A, and duration matters; a fixed false belief held during intoxication is still a delusion while it lasts; persecutory content occurs in intoxication, mood disorders and schizophrenia alike.

guide.s: acute delusions are more consistent with alcohol or drug intoxication

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has had seven months of marked social withdrawal, flat affect, near-mute speech and, for the past six weeks, prolonged episodes of holding odd postures with waxy flexibility. Careful assessment finds no delusions, no hallucinations and no disorganized speech. Under current criteria, which statement is correct?
options: Criterion A is not met, because at least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech is required
Schizophrenia is diagnosed, because two Criterion A symptoms are present for more than a month
Schizophreniform disorder is diagnosed, because the catatonia has lasted less than six months
questions.explain: Why: DSM-5 requires two Criterion A symptoms of which at least one is (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations or (3) disorganized speech; negative symptoms plus catatonic behaviour alone no longer qualify. Not the others: the two-symptom count is necessary but not sufficient; schizophreniform and brief psychotic disorder share the same symptom requirement and differ only in duration.

guide.s: At least one must be (1), (2) or (3)

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman developed persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations five months ago, with a marked decline in her university performance. There is no mood episode and no substance use. Which diagnosis fits today?
questions.explain: Why: the same picture as schizophrenia lasting at least one month but less than six months is schizophreniform disorder. Not the others: schizophrenia needs six months of continuous signs; brief psychotic disorder resolves within one month; delusional disorder excludes hallucinations.

guide.s: at least one month but less than six months

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has had auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions for a year. He has also had two three-month depressive episodes during that time, and between them, for several weeks at a stretch, the psychosis persisted while his mood was normal. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this course?
options: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
questions.explain: Why: schizoaffective disorder requires a mood episode concurrent with active psychosis, mood symptoms for a substantial portion of the illness, and delusions or hallucinations for at least two weeks without prominent mood symptoms; this course satisfies all three. Not the others: in a mood disorder with psychotic features the psychosis occurs exclusively during mood episodes; in schizophrenia mood episodes must be brief relative to the illness; nothing suggests hypomania.

guide.s: two weeks without prominent mood symptoms

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with newly diagnosed lymphoma began high-dose dexamethasone with her first chemotherapy cycle eight days ago. Her partner reports she has not slept in three nights, talks rapidly about grand plans and now hears a voice narrating her actions. She has no psychiatric history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder from the corticosteroid
Bipolar I disorder, first manic episode
questions.explain: Why: a psychosis that begins within days of starting a high-dose corticosteroid, with the manic flavour steroids typically produce, is medication-induced until proven otherwise; Criterion E excludes a primary diagnosis while a physiological cause explains the picture. Not the others: schizophreniform and bipolar disorder both require that a substance or medical cause be excluded; paraneoplastic encephalitis is possible but far less likely than the drug started eight days ago and would show other neurological features.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old develops paranoid delusions and disorganized behaviour over two months. On examination he has a coarse tremor, slurred speech, mild jaundice and greenish-brown rings at the edge of each cornea. Which investigation would confirm the cause of his psychosis?
options: Serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper, with MRI showing basal ganglia lesions
questions.explain: Why: ataxia, dysarthria, hepatic signs, hyperreflexia and Kayser-Fleischer rings in a young psychotic patient are Wilson disease; the work-up shows basal ganglia lesions on MRI, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia and elevated liver enzymes, and copper studies confirm it. Not the others: ANA points to lupus (rash, ulcers, serositis); urine cortisol to Cushing syndrome (striae, moon face); porphobilinogen to porphyria (weakness, tachycardia, hyponatraemia).

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with vascular dementia is brought by her son because for four days she has been talking to people who are not there, mostly after dark, and today she is drowsy and cannot keep track of his questions. Which action is least appropriate at this visit?
options: Start an antipsychotic and reassess in four weeks
Examine her chest, abdomen and nervous system
Send urinalysis, a blood count and electrolytes
Arrange urgent assessment in the emergency department if a cause is not quickly found
questions.explain: Why: acute visual hallucinations with evening worsening, somnolence and inattention in a person with dementia is delirium until proven otherwise, a medical emergency needing a cause; sedating and waiting a month misses it, and antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for mortality in dementia-related psychosis. Not the others: examination, basic investigations and, if needed, emergency assessment are all appropriate first steps.

questions.stem: Which feature is the principal difference between delusional disorder and schizophrenia?
options: Delusional disorder does not include hallucinations
Delusional disorder is preceded by a prodromal functional decline
Delusional disorder is treated with psychotherapy alone while schizophrenia requires medication
questions.explain: Why: delusional disorder is nonbizarre delusions without hallucinations, disorganization or negative symptoms, with functioning largely preserved. Not the others: there is no prodromal decline; the course is chronic rather than self-limiting; antipsychotics remain the pharmacological treatment for both.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man in the emergency department is pacing, shouting that staff are conspiring against him, and refuses to sit. Verbal de-escalation has failed. Which pharmacological approach reflects standard emergency practice?
options: An antipsychotic combined with a benzodiazepine, such as haloperidol with lorazepam, by mouth or injection
A benzodiazepine alone, because antipsychotics worsen agitation
Clozapine, because it is the most effective antipsychotic
An anticholinergic to prevent dystonia, then observation without an antipsychotic
questions.explain: Why: for agitation with psychosis the emergency combinations are an antipsychotic plus a benzodiazepine: loxapine with lorazepam or haloperidol with lorazepam, oral or injected. Not the others: a benzodiazepine alone does not address the psychosis; clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance and needs monitoring; an anticholinergic treats parkinsonism, it is not an agitation strategy.

guide.t: 4 · Referral, admission and the first steps

questions.stem: Two patients are described. The first has lifelong flat affect, prefers solitude and reports no unusual perceptions or beliefs. The second has odd magical beliefs and often sees fleeting shadows at the edge of vision, which he is not sure are real; he has never had a fixed delusion or a true voice. Which pair of diagnoses fits?
options: First: schizoid personality disorder; second: schizotypal personality disorder
First: schizotypal personality disorder; second: schizoid personality disorder
First: delusional disorder; second: brief psychotic disorder
questions.explain: Why: schizoid personality disorder has no positive symptoms, only the affective flattening and negative-type features; schizotypal has sub-threshold positive features, unusual beliefs and illusions rather than full delusions or hallucinations. Not the others: the assignment is reversed; schizophrenia requires full delusions and hallucinations in a constellation; neither patient has a fixed delusion or a psychotic episode.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman whose identical twin sister has schizophrenia asks about her own lifetime risk. She is well. What figure should she be given?
options: The same as the population, 0.5%, because she has passed the peak age of onset
questions.explain: Why: the lifetime risk for a monozygotic co-twin, or for a child of two affected parents, is 40 to 50%; these are absolute lifetime risks against a 0.5% baseline, and inheritance is non-Mendelian. Not the others: 10 to 15% is the first-degree relative figure; 3% is second-degree; a well co-twin at 30 has not exhausted her risk, since 20% of cases begin after 30 and the female onset distribution runs into the forties.

questions.stem: An expectant mother who has read that prenatal influenza raises the risk of schizophrenia sevenfold asks whether her child, born after a first-trimester flu, should be screened for the illness in childhood. What is the most accurate reply?
options: The risk increase is real but non-specific, raising autism, learning disability and ADHD as well, and no screening test follows from it
Yes, a childhood neurological examination can identify the children who will develop schizophrenia
The risk applies only to third-trimester infection
questions.explain: Why: maternal influenza in the first trimester carries a relative risk of about 7, but the exposure is non-specific across neurodevelopmental outcomes, and a large relative risk on a non-specific exposure does not yield a screening test; the same applies to soft neurological signs in childhood. Not the others: soft signs are non-specific and co-inherited with learning disability; the effect is first-trimester; the archived-serum study is one of the strongest designs in the field.

questions.stem: Which statement about the age and sex distribution of schizophrenia is correct?
options: Onset peaks in the early twenties in men, with a later and broader distribution in women that includes a second rise after 40
Onset peaks after 50 in both sexes
Women are affected twice as often as men
Fewer than half of cases begin before age 30
questions.explain: Why: the male peak is in the early twenties (23), women peak later and more diffusely with a second rise after 40, once called paraphrenia and probably menopause-related; 80% of cases begin before 30. Not the others: late-life onset is the exception; men are affected more (2:1, or a slight predominance depending on the source); most cases begin before 30.

questions.stem: A patient with schizophrenia asks whether his newborn son should have genome sequencing to predict the illness. Which response reflects the current genetic architecture?
options: Common risk variants each carry relative risks of about 1.05 to 1.1 and tell you almost nothing about an individual, and the rare large-effect variants such as 22q11 deletion are too uncommon to be useful in general practice
Sequencing would give a definitive yes or no because heritability is 80%
A polygenic score can now diagnose schizophrenia before symptoms
The 22q11 deletion is found in most cases and should be tested for routinely
questions.explain: Why: heritability of 80% is a population statistic; the risk is spread across common variants of tiny effect and rare variants of large effect (22q11 deletion, relative risk about 20, but very rare), which is why there is no clinically useful genetic test. Not the others: heritability does not translate into individual prediction; polygenic scores are not diagnostic; 22q11 deletion accounts for a small minority of cases.

questions.stem: Genome-wide SNP data show the genetic correlation between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder to be about 0.70, the strongest among psychiatric diagnoses. Which interpretation follows?
options: The two diagnoses may reflect one disease process expressed in different circuits, and diagnosis is not tightly linked to biology
The two disorders are genetically unrelated and the correlation is an artefact
Bipolar disorder is a mild form of schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is inherited from the mother and bipolar disorder from the father
questions.explain: Why: the strong genetic correlation is consistent with the clinical overlap and suggests that the same process could cause more mood symptoms in one person and more psychosis in another, as one disease in different parts of the nervous system, which is why diagnosis is not tightly linked to biology. Not the others: a 0.70 correlation is the opposite of unrelated; neither is a milder version of the other; parental origin has nothing to do with it.

questions.stem: Four patients with schizophrenia are seen in one clinic. Which presentation carries the highest risk of violence?
options: A man convinced that his downstairs neighbour is pumping gas into his flat to kill him, who has started to talk about defending himself
A woman with prominent negative symptoms and no delusions
A man with grandiose delusions of being a famous inventor
A woman with stable ideas of reference about television broadcasts
questions.explain: Why: paranoia associated with a specific threat, a persecutory delusion focused on a particular person that the patient may feel bound to retaliate against, is the most dangerous scenario (psychotic self-defence), especially in an acute exacerbation. Not the others: negative symptoms, grandiosity and non-persecutory ideas of reference do not carry the same focused threat; random violence toward strangers is rare.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia of 25 years' duration, never previously violent, kills his elderly mother during a relapse. Into which forensic trajectory does he fall, and what proportion of forensic patients does it represent?
questions.explain: Why: late-late starters (about 15%) become violent after years of illness, are often treatment-resistant, and typically commit a single severe symptom-related act, often an intra-familial homicide. Not the others: early starters (about 40%) are violent before the illness with conduct disorder and drugs; late starters (about 40%) become violent at or soon after onset; 85% is the proportion of forensic patients with a psychotic illness, not a trajectory.

questions.stem: Which statement about violence in first-episode psychosis is correct?
options: About 40% could have faced criminal charges at first presentation, and one third of homicides by people with a primary psychotic illness occur in the first episode
Violence is rare in first-episode psychosis and becomes common only after years of illness
Homicide by psychotic patients almost never occurs before diagnosis
Criminal charges at first presentation occur in fewer than 5%
questions.explain: Why: violence is common in first-episode psychosis: about 40% could have had charges at first presentation and one third of homicides by people with a primary psychotic illness occur in the first episode, when the diagnosis first becomes apparent; peak onset in young men, the peak group for violence generally, is a confound. Not the others: each understates the first-episode risk.

questions.stem: A hospital proposes screening every emergency department attender for psychosis-related violence risk with a questionnaire validated in forensic units. Which objection follows from the argument about prior probability?
options: Applied to a low-prior population, the test will produce more false positives than true positives and cause more harm than it prevents
Questionnaires cannot measure violence risk in any population
Forensic patients are less violent than the general population
Screening is only useful if it is universal
questions.explain: Why: the probability that a positive is a true positive depends on the Bayesian prior of the population tested; a test that performs well among forensic patients, 85% of whom are psychotic, will mostly flag false positives in a general emergency population. Not the others: the objection is about the population, not the instrument; forensic and general-population statistics must not be conflated in either direction; universality is exactly the problem.

questions.stem: Which set of figures correctly describes suicide and mortality in schizophrenia?
options: Suicide risk about 13 times the general population with a lifetime risk near 5%; overall mortality two to three times, mostly cardiovascular and respiratory disease
Suicide risk twice the general population; overall mortality unchanged
Lifetime suicide risk 25%; deaths mainly from suicide
Suicide risk 13 times; overall mortality reduced by antipsychotic treatment to population levels
questions.explain: Why: suicide is 13 times more likely, lifetime risk about 5%, higher with auditory hallucinations, delusions, substance abuse and prior attempts; overall mortality is two to three times the general public and most deaths are cardiovascular, respiratory, stroke, cancer and thromboembolic. Not the others: each misstates either the suicide multiplier, the lifetime figure or the cause of excess deaths.

questions.stem: Schizophrenia affects one in 200 people yet ranks fifth among causes of disability in established market economies, close behind conditions ten times more common. Which explanation is correct?
options: Early onset means decades lived with disability, so disability-adjusted life years accumulate far more than in diseases of old age
The illness is uniformly fatal within a decade
Antipsychotics are the most expensive drugs in medicine
Most patients require lifelong inpatient care
questions.explain: Why: costs and disability exceed prevalence because of early onset, lifetime disability and high medical burden; cancer and Alzheimer's strike the old, schizophrenia strikes the young, so its DALY count is high, as is unipolar depression's. Not the others: the excess mortality is two to three fold, not uniform early death; drug cost is not the driver; most patients live in the community.

questions.stem: Coronal MRI scans of a pair of 35-year-old identical twins, one with schizophrenia and one well, show larger lateral ventricles and a smaller hippocampus in the affected twin. What is the principal inference from this design?
options: The structural difference cannot be attributed to genotype alone, since the twins share their genome
Ventricular enlargement is inherited as a Mendelian trait
The well twin will develop schizophrenia within five years
Hippocampal volume loss is specific to schizophrenia
questions.explain: Why: twins discordant for the illness are genetically identical, so a structural difference between them, bigger ventricles and smaller cortex and hippocampus in the affected twin, cannot be explained by genes alone. Not the others: inheritance is non-Mendelian; the well co-twin's risk is 40 to 50%, not a certainty; hippocampal atrophy also occurs in depression and bipolar disorder.

questions.stem: A student proposes that a small hippocampus on MRI could serve as a diagnostic marker for schizophrenia. Which fact defeats the proposal?
options: The hippocampus is also smaller in depression and bipolar disorder, so the finding is a psychiatric-illness finding rather than a schizophrenia finding
The hippocampus is not affected in schizophrenia
Hippocampal volume cannot be measured on MRI
questions.explain: Why: hippocampal volume is reduced in schizophrenia but the reduction is not specific: it is seen across psychiatric illness, including depression and bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia has no objective test. Not the others: the hippocampus is affected, it is measurable, and it shrinks rather than grows.

questions.stem: During cortical development a population of neurons is born on the last day of neurogenesis and must climb a radial glial scaffold past all earlier-born neurons to reach its destination. Which statement about these cells is correct?
options: They are excitatory pyramidal neurons destined for the most superficial cortical layers, reflecting inside-out lamination
They are GABAergic interneurons arriving tangentially from the ganglionic eminences
They will occupy the deepest cortical layer because they are born last
They migrate outside-in, as in all vertebrates
questions.explain: Why: the mammalian cortex is laminated inside-out: late-born pyramidal neurons migrate radially farthest, to the superficial layers, while the earliest-born stay deep. Not the others: interneurons arrive tangentially from the ganglionic eminences; the last-born are the most superficial, not the deepest; outside-in lamination is the pattern below the teleosts, which is why their brains cannot enlarge.

questions.stem: Paediatric neurologists blind to outcome rated childhood home movies and found poorer coordination and impaired left-right dominance in the children who later developed schizophrenia. A public health official proposes using such signs to screen schoolchildren. Why is this unsound?
options: Soft neurological signs are non-specific and co-inherited with learning disability, so a large relative risk does not translate into a useful screening test
The home-movie study has been retracted
Soft signs appear only after the first psychotic episode
The signs predict autism rather than schizophrenia
questions.explain: Why: the signs precede psychosis by ten to fifteen years but are non-specific, the same reason maternal influenza's sevenfold risk does not screen: a big relative risk on a non-specific exposure yields mostly false positives. Not the others: the study stands; the signs precede onset; they are associated with several neurodevelopmental outcomes, not one.

questions.stem: In a SPECT study, striatal D2 receptor availability at baseline did not differ between patients with schizophrenia and controls, but after an amphetamine challenge the reduction in radiotracer binding was 13.8% in patients and 7.1% in controls. What does this imply about the dopamine abnormality in schizophrenia?
options: The abnormality lies in dopamine release rather than in receptor number or the transmitter molecule
Patients have more D2 receptors than controls
Amphetamine has no effect on dopamine in schizophrenia
The D2 receptor is not the antipsychotic target
questions.explain: Why: equal baseline availability with roughly double the amphetamine-induced release means the problem is in the pattern of release, not the receptors or the molecule. Not the others: baseline binding was the same; amphetamine released more dopamine in patients, not less; D2 blockade remains the mechanism of every antipsychotic.

questions.stem: Which triad of observations forms the pharmacological foundation of the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia?
options: Excess dopamine can cause psychosis; stimulants increase synaptic dopamine; antipsychotics block dopamine receptors
Serotonin excess causes psychosis; LSD is serotonergic; antipsychotics block serotonin
NMDA hypofunction causes psychosis; ketamine blocks NMDA; antipsychotics enhance NMDA
Dopamine deficiency causes psychosis; levodopa treats it; antipsychotics restore dopamine
questions.explain: Why: the hypothesis rests on three facts: too much dopamine can cause psychotic symptoms, amphetamine and other stimulants increase synaptic dopamine, and antipsychotics reduce psychosis by blocking dopamine receptors. Not the others: LSD and ketamine are hallucinogens with other mechanisms and no antipsychotic works through them; levodopa can provoke psychosis, the opposite of the last option.

guide.s: Too much dopamine can cause psychotic symptoms

questions.stem: Four intoxicated patients present with psychotic symptoms after taking, respectively, methamphetamine, LSD, ketamine and cannabis. Which pairing of drug and primary target is correct?
options: Methamphetamine: dopamine transporter and VMAT2; LSD: serotonin receptors; ketamine: NMDA channel
Methamphetamine: NMDA channel; LSD: dopamine transporter; ketamine: serotonin receptors
Methamphetamine: GABA-A; LSD: NMDA channel; ketamine: dopamine transporter
All three act primarily on the dopamine D2 receptor
questions.explain: Why: stimulants act on the dopamine transporter, methamphetamine additionally on VMAT2, raising synaptic dopamine; LSD and psilocybin are serotonergic; PCP and ketamine are NMDA channel blockers; cannabinoids cause psychosis less acutely. Not the others: each scrambles the targets; none of these drugs is a direct D2 agonist.

questions.stem: A patient with early psychosis notices three red cars on his way to work and concludes he is being followed. Which neurobiological concept links this experience to the dopamine hypothesis?
options: Aberrant dopamine release assigns importance to spurious events, producing abnormal salience and false causal inference
GABA loss produces the fear response
questions.explain: Why: dopamine carries meta-information about what matters and encodes reward expectancy; released aberrantly it produces abnormal salience, the incorrect assignment of importance to coincidental events, which is the neurochemical face of the cognitive biases behind delusions. Not the others: the observation is not perceptual; serotonergic drugs produce visual distortions, not this; GABA is not the mechanism described.

questions.stem: Glutamate and GABA account for more than 99% of the brain's neurotransmitters, yet a tiny quantity of dopamine can reorganise behaviour. Which statement explains the disproportion?
options: Catecholamines carry meta-information about when, where and how much, rather than the content of the message itself
Dopamine is far more potent per molecule at the postsynaptic membrane
Dopamine is stored in every synapse in the cortex
Glutamate and GABA are inhibitory only
questions.explain: Why: the monoamines arise from midbrain nuclei projecting to the forebrain and signal a change in state, highlight salient information and encode the magnitude of an input: when, where and how much, not what to do, which is why a pinch of transmitter suffices. Not the others: potency per molecule is not the point; dopamine is confined to specific tracts; glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter.

questions.stem: Which receptor instructs long-term potentiation, and through which change is the synapse strengthened?
options: The NMDA receptor instructs it; the synapse is strengthened by recruitment of AMPA receptors
The AMPA receptor instructs it; NMDA receptors are internalised
The D2 receptor instructs it; dopamine is released in bulk
The GABA-A receptor instructs it; chloride conductance rises
questions.explain: Why: the NMDA receptor is the signal for learning: strong pre- to postsynaptic excitation makes later signals more likely to depolarise the cell through AMPA receptor recruitment, with dopamine modulating the process. Not the others: AMPA internalisation is long-term depression; D2 and GABA-A are not the plasticity instructors.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman started on an antipsychotic three weeks ago develops a resting tremor, rigidity and slowed movement. Blockade of which dopamine pathway explains these symptoms?
questions.explain: Why: D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal tract (substantia nigra to striatum) produces parkinsonism, the extrapyramidal side effect. Not the others: mesolimbic blockade produces feeling bad and low motivation; mesocortical blockade carries the antipsychotic and cognitive effects; tuberoinfundibular blockade raises prolactin.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman on risperidone 6 mg daily reports that her periods have stopped and that she has noticed milk from her breasts. Which mechanism explains the finding?
options: Loss of dopamine's tonic inhibition of prolactin release from D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway
Direct stimulation of prolactin secretion by serotonin blockade
Histamine H1 blockade in the hypothalamus
questions.explain: Why: dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits prolactin release; a high-affinity D2 antagonist in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes the brake, and hyperprolactinaemia produces galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Not the others: serotonin, histamine and oestrogen are not the mechanism of antipsychotic-induced prolactin elevation.

questions.stem: Quetiapine at low doses is widely used, off label, to help patients sleep. Which property of the drug best explains its sedative effect?
options: Significant affinity for histamine receptors, an off-target effect of a low-potency, high-dose drug
Stronger dopamine D2 blockade than haloperidol
Selective blockade of the mesocortical pathway at low doses
questions.explain: Why: quetiapine is a three-digit-dose, low D2 affinity drug; the excess drug binds other receptors of the same GPCR family, and histamine H1 blockade produces sedation. Not the others: its D2 affinity is far lower than haloperidol's, which is why hundreds of milligrams are needed; muscarinic blockade causes dry mouth and constipation, not sleep; there is no selective low-dose mesocortical effect.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man treated for a first psychotic episode cannot recall the name of his new medication. He now cannot sit still, has painful muscle spasms, tremor, stiffness and involuntary facial movements. Prescribed in its usual daily dose range, which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explain: Why: the picture is the extrapyramidal family, akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism and dyskinesia, and by the dose-digit rule the single-digit, highest-affinity drug produces the most of it. Not the others: loxapine and olanzapine are two-digit intermediate drugs; clozapine is a three-digit, low-affinity drug whose antimuscarinic activity gives it essentially no EPS.

questions.stem: Chlorpromazine at 600 mg daily and haloperidol at 5 mg daily achieve comparable D2 occupancy, yet the chlorpromazine patient has far less parkinsonism. What accounts for the difference?
options: Chlorpromazine's intrinsic antimuscarinic activity counteracts the parkinsonism its D2 blockade would produce, as if benztropine were built in
Chlorpromazine does not block D2 receptors
Haloperidol is metabolised to a dystonia-producing metabolite
questions.explain: Why: low-affinity drugs must be given in hundreds of milligrams, and the excess binds muscarinic receptors; that anticholinergic action self-treats the EPS, a built-in side-effect pill. Not the others: chlorpromazine does block D2 (that is its antipsychotic action); there is no dystonia-producing metabolite; alpha blockade causes hypotension, not striatal protection.

questions.stem: A patient with schizophrenia and antipsychotic-induced tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia asks whether he has developed Parkinson's disease. Which reply is correct?
options: He has parkinsonism from D2 blockade, not Parkinson's disease, though the symptoms are identical because the net effect on the striatum is the same
He has Parkinson's disease, since the antipsychotic has killed his dopaminergic neurons
He cannot have parkinsonism because he is under 60
questions.explain: Why: whether dopaminergic neurons die or their postsynaptic target is blocked, the striatum loses its dopamine signal and the symptoms are identical: antipsychotics cause parkinsonism, not Parkinson's. Not the others: the neurons are blocked, not destroyed; drug-induced parkinsonism occurs at any age; tardive dyskinesia is late, hyperkinetic and involves the face.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man on haloperidol has cogwheel rigidity and a shuffling gait. Which medication is the classic treatment for this side effect, and why does it work?
options: Benztropine, an anticholinergic, because acetylcholine in the striatum influences dopamine signalling
A higher dose of haloperidol, to overcome the block
questions.explain: Why: the striatal cholinergic interneuron modulates the nigrostriatal terminal, so anticholinergics such as benztropine, trihexyphenidyl or procyclidine treat drug-induced parkinsonism; propranolol, lorazepam, amantadine and diphenhydramine are also used across the extrapyramidal syndromes. Not the others: levodopa would worsen the psychosis; raising the dose worsens the EPS; serotonin has no role here.

questions.stem: Which statement about dopamine receptors is correct?
options: All five subtypes are G-protein-coupled; D1-like receptors raise adenylyl cyclase activity and D2-like receptors lower it
D2 receptors are ligand-gated ion channels
D1 and D2 receptors both raise cyclic AMP
Dopamine receptors share no homology with histamine or adrenergic receptors
questions.explain: Why: D1 to D5 are all GPCRs; D1-like (D1, D5) stimulate and D2-like (D2, D3, D4) inhibit adenylyl cyclase; their homology with H1, adrenergic, serotonin and muscarinic receptors is why low-potency antipsychotics hit those targets. Not the others: no dopamine receptor is an ion channel; the two families have opposite effects on cAMP; the homology is the whole basis of the off-target side effects.

questions.stem: A resident asks what makes clozapine "atypical." Which answer best reflects the evidence?
options: Proposed criteria such as less EPS, benefit for negative symptoms and 5-HT2 to D2 affinity are not consistently associated with atypicality; clozapine is the only truly atypical drug because it works when other antipsychotics have failed
Atypicals are more effective than typicals for positive symptoms
Clozapine is atypical because it has the highest D2 affinity
questions.explain: Why: the four proposed criteria for atypicality do not hold consistently, and first- and second-generation drugs are equally effective; what is genuinely different is clozapine's efficacy in treatment resistance. Not the others: efficacy does not differ by generation; second-generation drugs can cause TD; clozapine is a low-affinity, high-dose drug.

guide.s: clozapine is the only truly atypical antipsychotic

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who has taken a first-generation antipsychotic for twenty years has developed constant chewing movements, lip pursing and tongue protrusion. Which statement about this condition is correct?
options: It is tardive dyskinesia, typically irreversible, though symptoms may lessen after the drug is stopped
It is acute dystonia and will resolve within hours of an anticholinergic
It is akathisia and is treated with propranolol
questions.explain: Why: facial dyskinesia after prolonged antipsychotic exposure is tardive dyskinesia: puffing of the cheeks, tongue protrusion, chewing and pursing, typically irreversible. Not the others: acute dystonia is an early, painful spasm; akathisia is inner restlessness; NMS is rigidity with fever and autonomic instability.

questions.stem: Which dopamine pathway is the site of the antipsychotic effect itself, as opposed to a site of side effects?
options: Mesolimbic, where blockade produces feeling bad
questions.explain: Why: antipsychotic and cognitive effects belong to the mesocortical tract, feeling bad and low motivation to the mesolimbic, EPS to the nigrostriatal and prolactin to the tuberoinfundibular. Not the others: each is a side-effect site in that scheme; the mesolimbic tract's blockade is what makes patients feel bad, the reason antipsychotics have no street value.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a first episode of schizophrenia has taken risperidone 4 mg daily for four weeks with little improvement. According to the algorithm taught this week, what is the next step?
options: Switch to a different antipsychotic and repeat the trial for four to six weeks
Give a loading dose of the same drug
questions.explain: Why: little or no improvement after four weeks means switch and repeat for four to six weeks; only after that second failure does clozapine follow, and ECT after clozapine. Not the others: NICE and Choosing Wisely both forbid antipsychotic combinations and loading doses; clozapine requires two failed adequate trials.

guide.s: switch antipsychotic and repeat the trial for four to six weeks

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with schizophrenia has failed adequate trials of olanzapine and paliperidone and is started on clozapine. Which monitoring schedule is required?
options: Complete blood count weekly for six months, every two weeks for six months, then monthly
Fasting glucose weekly for a year
questions.explain: Why: clozapine causes agranulocytosis, so the count is checked weekly for six months, fortnightly for the next six, then monthly, and the drug is prescribed only by a psychiatrist. Not the others: glucose and lipids belong to the metabolic schedule shared by all second-generation drugs; there is no lifelong monthly ECG requirement; it is first-generation drugs that need no laboratory monitoring.

guide.s: complete blood count weekly for six months

questions.stem: A patient with schizophrenia has been rehospitalised twice after stopping oral antipsychotics. The team proposes a long-acting injectable. What is the best explanation for why depots reduce rehospitalisation?
options: The drug is reliably in the body, since only about a third of patients take oral medication as prescribed
Injectable formulations have higher D2 affinity
Depots have fewer metabolic side effects
Depots treat negative symptoms better than oral drugs
questions.explain: Why: a drug does not work if it is not in the body; a monthly injection means daily medication, and in a within-individual cohort every long-acting injectable beat its own oral form on rehospitalisation. Not the others: depots are not superior pharmacology; their side-effect and efficacy profiles are those of the parent drug.

guide.s: one third of patients take medication as prescribed

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with a first psychotic episode is worried about weight gain. Which of the following antipsychotics produced the least weight change against placebo in the network meta-analysis shown this week?
questions.explain: Why: ziprasidone was the only drug with a negative point estimate (−0.16 kg, interval crossing zero); lurasidone and aripiprazole were next best. Not the others: olanzapine gained about 2.8 kg, quetiapine about 1.9 kg and clozapine about 1.9 kg.

guide.t: 3 · Choosing among the drugs: efficacy against weight

questions.stem: Which antipsychotic had the largest effect on overall symptoms in the 2019 network meta-analysis, and where did it sit for weight gain?
options: Clozapine, the most effective drug, is mid-table for weight gain
Olanzapine, the most effective drug, gains the least weight
Haloperidol, the most effective drug, gains the most weight
Ziprasidone, the most effective drug, gains no weight
questions.explain: Why: clozapine (standardised mean difference −0.89) and amisulpride (−0.73) top the efficacy plot, and clozapine's weight gain (+1.89 kg) is in the middle of the facing plot, the efficacy-against-side-effects trade-off the two slides are designed to show. Not the others: olanzapine is mid-table for efficacy and gains the most weight of the common drugs; haloperidol and ziprasidone are mid to low for efficacy.

guide.t: 3 · Choosing among the drugs: efficacy against weight

questions.stem: A family physician takes over the care of a stable patient on olanzapine with normal baseline metabolic values. After the first twelve weeks, how often should fasting glucose and lipids be checked?
options: Only if the dose is increased
questions.explain: Why: the screening table checks glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks, then annually if values are normal, with blood pressure, BMI and counselling also quarterly. Not the others: six-weekly checks belong to the initiation phase; quarterly is for BP and BMI, not bloods; metabolic effects are not dose-dependent, so dose changes do not set the schedule.

guide.t: 3 · Choosing among the drugs: efficacy against weight

questions.stem: Which psychosocial intervention has evidence for reducing relapse and hospitalisation specifically in severely ill patients with schizophrenia?
questions.explain: Why: ACT teams are for relapse and hospitalisation in the severely ill; family psychoeducation for relapse prevention; CBT for symptom reduction or relapse prevention, though uncommon. Not the others: family psychoeducation and CBT have different stated indications; supported employment is not named in the sources.

questions.stem: Which statement about the course of schizophrenia under treatment is correct?
options: Only about a quarter of patients are still taking an antipsychotic at 18 months, and fewer than 15% of first-episode patients are in remission at five years
Most patients achieve symptomatic and functional remission within 18 months of treatment
Antipsychotics improve functional outcome as much as they improve psychotic symptoms
Outcomes are clearly better in low-income countries
questions.explain: Why: the outcome slide gives 25% continuation at 18 months, under 10% remission in chronic illness at 18 months, and under 15% first-episode remission at five years. Not the others: remission is the exception; antipsychotics treat psychosis without much changing functional outcome; the low-income-country finding is named and doubted as a measurement artefact.

questions.stem: A family physician is asked to start an antipsychotic for a 20-year-old who presented yesterday with new sustained hallucinations and delusions. Which action follows the NICE guidance summarised this week?
options: Refer urgently to mental health services and initiate an antipsychotic only in consultation with a psychiatrist
Start two antipsychotics at low dose to cover both generations
Give a loading dose of olanzapine and review in a month
questions.explain: Why: a first presentation with sustained psychotic symptoms is urgently referred, and primary care does not initiate an antipsychotic unless in consultation with a psychiatrist. Not the others: combinations and loading doses are both prohibited; CBT is offered to all but alongside, not instead of, an antipsychotic.

guide.s: No combination of antipsychotics; no loading dose

questions.stem: A pharmacology question asks for an antipsychotic that does not act by D2 blockade. Which is correct?
options: Xanomeline-trospium: an M1/M4 muscarinic agonist that reduces ventral tegmental dopamine firing, paired with a peripheral anticholinergic
Paliperidone: the active metabolite of risperidone
questions.explain: Why: xanomeline is an orthosteric M1/M4 agonist, the rationale being that norclozapine is an M1 agonist; trospium blocks the peripheral diarrhoea, sweating and drooling. Ulotaront, a TAAR1 and 5-HT1A agonist, is the other non-D2 drug. Not the others: paliperidone, amisulpride and zuclopenthixol are all D2 antagonists.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with known schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department acutely psychotic and agitated. Which pharmacological combination is named for this situation?
options: Haloperidol with lorazepam, oral or injected
questions.explain: Why: agitation with psychosis is treated with an antipsychotic plus a benzodiazepine; the two combinations named are loxapine with lorazepam and haloperidol with lorazepam, oral or by injection, after de-escalation. Not the others: clozapine is never an emergency drug; combinations of antipsychotics are prohibited; propranolol and benztropine treat extrapyramidal effects.

guide.s: loxapine with lorazepam, or haloperidol with lorazepam

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman on St. John's Wort and L-tryptophan for two months takes a single 20 mg tablet of citalopram and within hours is hyperthermic, agitated and hyperreflexic. What type of adverse drug reaction is this?
options: Type A, augmented: a predictable pharmacodynamic interaction producing too much serotonin
Type B, bizarre: an idiosyncratic host-dependent reaction
Gell and Coombs Type IV: delayed hypersensitivity
questions.explain: Why: three drugs act on the same target, serotonin regulation, so the reaction is an extension of expected pharmacology and therefore Type A; the dose is the cumulative serotonergic burden, not the milligrams of any one drug. Not the others: it is predictable and not host-dependent, so not B; nothing was stopped, so not E; Type IV needs days and gives a rash.

guide.t: 3 · The case: one tablet, three serotonergic drugs

questions.stem: A hyperthermic, diaphoretic, confused patient has increased tone in the legs, brisk reflexes with clonus, dilated pupils and hyperactive bowel sounds. Which diagnosis do the physical findings support?
questions.explain: Why: the distinct features of serotonin syndrome are hyperreflexia with clonus, dilated pupils and hyperactive bowel sounds, with tone greatest in the lower limbs. Not the others: NMS gives lead-pipe rigidity in all muscle groups, hyporeflexia, normal pupils and normal or decreased bowel sounds; malignant hyperthermia follows anaesthetics in the operating room; dystonia has no fever or autonomic instability.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man whose haloperidol dose was doubled four days ago has become progressively confused, then rigid, febrile and tachycardic. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what feature of the history supports it?
options: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, because it follows a dopamine antagonist with gradual onset over one to three days beginning with mental status change
Serotonin syndrome, because onset was within hours
Type E withdrawal reaction, because the dose was changed
Malignant hyperthermia, because he is rigid
questions.explain: Why: NMS is precipitated by dopamine antagonists, develops gradually over 1 to 3 days, and usually starts with mental status changes before rigidity, autonomic instability and hyperthermia. Not the others: serotonin syndrome is abrupt, under 12 hours, after a serotonergic agent; the dose went up, not down; malignant hyperthermia needs anaesthetic exposure.

guide.s: usually starts with mental status changes

questions.stem: After the serotonin syndrome case resolves, a resident asks whether to file an individual adverse-reaction report with Health Canada. What is the correct answer?
options: No: it is a well-documented reaction to an older medication; the hospital reports under Vanessa's Law, and individual reports are prioritised for new drugs, bizarre reactions and severe or lethal reactions
Yes: every adverse reaction must be reported by the treating physician within 24 hours
Yes, because serotonin syndrome is a Type B reaction
No, because adverse reactions to natural products are never reportable
questions.explain: Why: the individual practitioner does not report this case; the hospital reports under Vanessa's Law, and individual priority goes to drugs under five years on the market, bizarre (Type B) reactions and severe or lethal reactions. Not the others: there is no universal 24-hour duty for individuals; serotonin syndrome is Type A; the natural-product point is invented.

guide.t: 2 · Managing, grading and reporting a reaction

questions.stem: A patient who abruptly stopped paroxetine develops dizziness, nausea and electric-shock sensations. Of the four ADR management strategies, what is the appropriate dose action and why?
options: Increase the dose and monitor, because this is a Type E withdrawal reaction
Decrease the dose and monitor, because this is a Type A reaction
Discontinue the drug, because the reaction is severe
Add a second drug to treat the symptoms and continue the current dose of zero
questions.explain: Why: strategy 2 is bidirectional: decrease for a dose-related reaction, increase for a withdrawal reaction; a discontinuation syndrome is Type E, so the dose goes up. Not the others: calling it Type A would move the dose the wrong way; the drug is already stopped; adding a drug is the treat-through strategy for a needed drug's side effect.

guide.t: 2 · Managing, grading and reporting a reaction

questions.stem: Two days after starting a new antibiotic a patient develops a maculopapular rash. Which hypersensitivity type is this, and what mediates it?
options: Type IV, delayed hypersensitivity, mediated by T-helper cells
Type I, anaphylaxis, mediated by IgE
Type II, cytotoxic, mediated by IgG against cell surfaces
Type III, immune complex, mediated by IgG complexes
questions.explain: Why: onset in days with a maculopapular rash or contact dermatitis is Type IV, the only cell-mediated type, which is why it is delayed. Not the others: Type I is minutes with urticaria and shock; Type II is minutes to hours with cytopenias; Type III is hours with serum sickness, glomerulonephritis and vasculitis.

guide.t: 1 · Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems

questions.stem: Which statement about the diagnosis of serotonin syndrome is correct?
options: It is a clinical diagnosis based on medication review and examination; serum serotonin levels are unreliable
A serum serotonin level above the reference range confirms it
It requires a positive toxicology screen
It is excluded if symptoms began within an hour of the dose
questions.explain: Why: it is a clinical diagnosis requiring thorough medication review and physical examination, and that serum serotonin does not correlate with the presentation. Not the others: no blood test confirms it; toxicology is pending and never reported in the case; onset is within one hour in 28% and within six hours in 61%.

questions.stem: A patient on sertraline is prescribed an antibiotic for a resistant skin infection and develops serotonin syndrome. Which antibiotic is the likely precipitant, and by which mechanism?
options: Linezolid, which decreases serotonin breakdown by inhibiting monoamine oxidase
Ciprofloxacin, which is a serotonin precursor
questions.explain: Why: linezolid is listed with the MAO inhibitors under decrease serotonin breakdown, the second of the five mechanisms. Not the others: none of the other antibiotics is serotonergic; release is the amphetamine mechanism, precursor is tryptophan, reuptake inhibition is the SSRI, tramadol and St. John's Wort mechanism.

questions.stem: Which of the following citalopram orders is written correctly?
questions.explain: Why: the correct order has the drug, a dose with unit and no trailing zero, the route and a spelled-out frequency. Not the others: a trailing zero reads as 200 mg and OD reads as right eye; .5 lacks a leading zero and reads as 5; QD reads as QID and the route is missing.

guide.t: 2 · Managing, grading and reporting a reaction

questions.stem: Which statement about neuroleptic malignant syndrome is correct?
options: It is fatal in 6 to 10% if untreated, and about 30% of patients develop rhabdomyolysis
Its incidence is about 5% of antipsychotic-treated patients
It is a Type B reaction because it is idiosyncratic
It is caused by increased central dopamine
questions.explain: Why: mortality untreated is 6 to 10%, rhabdomyolysis in 30% and progression to acute kidney injury in 30%, and incidence of 0.01 to 0.2%. Not the others: it is rare; it is Type A, linked directly to the drug's effects; the mechanism is D2 blockade with decreased dopaminergic transmission.

questions.stem: In the serotonin syndrome case, the treatment slide asks which drug is the offender. What is the correct acute management?
options: Stop all three drugs, because the reaction is an additive interaction with no single offender
Stop citalopram only, since it was the last drug added
Stop St. John's Wort only, since it is not a prescribed drug
Halve the citalopram dose and continue the natural products
questions.explain: Why: the reaction is the product of three agents acting on one pathway in a patient already at 39 °C; removing one leaves a dangerous load, so the rule is acutely, stop all three. Not the others: any single-agent strategy leaves two serotonergic drugs on board; a severe reaction requires discontinuation, not dose adjustment.

guide.t: 3 · The case: one tablet, three serotonergic drugs

questions.stem: How does the risk of adverse drug reactions with antipsychotics compare with other drugs?
options: About three times higher, although psychiatry's overall rate is similar to the general population's 5 to 15%
About the same as all other drugs
questions.explain: Why: ADRs complicate 5 to 15% of drug management, rates in psychiatry are similar, but the risk with antipsychotics is about three times that of other drugs. Not the others: the threefold figure is specific to antipsychotics, not psychiatric drugs generally, and the 10% figure is the share of drugs withdrawn or black-boxed in 25 years.

guide.t: 1 · Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder says angrily, "You started me on this medication and now my vision is all messed up and nobody is taking me seriously." Which response is the most validating according to the DBT hierarchy taught this week?
options: "I can see why you're so worried about your vision. Anyone would be."
"You've told me before that doctors have missed things, so I see why you'd expect that again."
"Why do you feel nobody is taking you seriously?"
questions.explain: Why: level 5, makes sense for anyone, is the most validating level, and is preferred over level 4 when both apply. Not the others: the history-based statement is level 4, which can itself invalidate; the reflection is level 2; a question is a change strategy in DBT and can dysregulate the patient further.

questions.stem: A resident opens an encounter with a distressed patient by asking a series of clarifying questions, and the patient becomes more agitated. What does the DBT teaching say about this?
options: Questions are a change strategy and can dysregulate a patient who has not first been validated
Questions are the highest form of validation because they show interest
The patient should be asked more specific questions until she calms
Agreement with the patient's view should be offered before any question
questions.explain: Why: validation is not praise or agreement, not asking questions, and not problem-solving; in DBT a question pushes for change, which a shut-down patient cannot handle in the moment. Not the others: appearing interested is non-verbal; more questions worsen the dysregulation; agreement is not validation either, since you can disagree and still validate.

questions.stem: A clinician guesses that a patient's anger conceals fear and says, "You're really scared." The patient snaps, "I'm not scared, I'm furious." What was the error, and what should the clinician do now?
options: The mind-reading statement was not tentative; back off and correct it, since a wrong guess is invalidating
Nothing was wrong; the clinician should repeat the interpretation more firmly
The clinician should move to problem-solving immediately
The clinician should apologise for validating at all
questions.explain: Why: level 3, mind reading, is more validating but riskier; it must be tentative ("I'm guessing you must be worried") and when wrong the clinician backs off: "OK, so angry. Sorry, I misread that." Not the others: insisting compounds the invalidation; problem-solving before validation fails; the aim is to validate accurately, not to stop validating.

questions.stem: A patient with schizophrenia refuses hospital food, convinced staff are poisoning it, and is terrified. How can the clinician validate without reinforcing the delusion?
options: Validate the emotion given the belief: it makes sense to be scared if you think people are putting poison in the food
Agree that the food might be poisoned to build rapport
Tell the patient the fear is irrational because the belief is false
Avoid validation entirely, since the belief cannot be validated
questions.explain: Why: emotions are always valid; validate the emotion given the belief, not the belief. Not the others: agreeing validates the delusion; dismissing the fear invalidates the patient; the fallback rule exists precisely so that validation is always possible.

guide.s: the emotion given the belief, without the belief

questions.stem: A patient in the emergency department demands admission the clinician does not think will help. Which phrasing is the validating one?
options: "It makes sense to me that you want to be admitted, and at the same time I don't think that's going to be helpful for you."
"It makes sense that you want to be admitted, but I don't think it will help."
"I don't think admission will help, so let's not discuss it."
questions.explain: Why: pair validation with an and-statement to add your own view; "but" dismisses all the validation that preceded it. Not the others: the second uses "but"; the third skips validation; the fourth is agreement, which is not validation and is not the clinical judgement.

questions.stem: According to the personality-disorders workshop, which diagnostic criteria set must be memorised for the exam and for clinical practice?
questions.explain: Why: the only criteria to memorise are the borderline criteria, which can appear on an exam, an OSCE station and the licensing examination. Not the others: the other disorders are examined by gestalt with obvious prompts; narcissistic disorder is often asked but by gestalt, not criteria.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders
guide.s: The only criteria to memorise are the borderline criteria

questions.stem: A student suggests that personality disorders are less pathological than other psychiatric disorders because they are traits rather than states. Which reply is correct?
options: Not less pathological: borderline personality disorder carries functioning comparable to schizophrenia and an estimated 12 to 20 years of reduced life expectancy
Correct: personality disorders are stable traits without mortality risk
Correct: they remain on a separate axis for that reason
Partly: only Cluster B disorders are pathological
questions.explain: Why: they are not less pathological; borderline patients function at levels comparable to schizophrenia and life expectancy is 12 to 20 years lower depending on the study. Not the others: the separate axis is gone and personality disorders are ordinary DSM disorders; no cluster is exempt.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has odd beliefs about telepathy and sometimes sees shadows at the edge of vision that he acknowledges may not be real; he has never had a fixed delusion or a clear voice. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.explain: Why: schizotypal personality disorder has sub-syndromal positive symptoms only: unusual beliefs and illusions the person can question, not full hallucinations. Not the others: schizoid disorder has no positive symptoms at all, only affective flattening; schizophrenia needs full delusions and hallucinations in a constellation; delusional disorder needs a fixed delusion.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders
guide.s: Schizotypal personality disorder has sub-syndromal positive symptoms only

questions.stem: A patient with borderline personality disorder reports a new episode of self-harm at a clinic visit. Which response is correct?
options: Brief genuine disappointment, "oh, shoot, that's too bad," followed by an and-statement about the work they have been doing
Warm reassurance and extra time, to show unconditional support
Silence, to avoid reinforcing the behaviour
A lecture on the risks of self-harm
questions.explain: Why: warmth after self-harm can reinforce it; a little genuine disappointment is useful, then an and-statement: "I know you've been working on this really hard, and let's see what we can do." Not the others: moving in with "poor thing" reinforces; silence and lectures are neither validating nor effective.

guide.s: a little genuine disappointment is also useful

questions.stem: Which statement about the classification of personality disorders is correct?
options: The ICD has moved to dimensional diagnosis for personality disorders but kept borderline personality disorder as a category; the DSM has not changed
The DSM-5 has abolished all personality-disorder categories in favour of dimensions
Borderline personality disorder is likely to be removed from the next edition
Personality disorders remain on a separate axis in the current DSM
questions.explain: Why: the ICD went dimensional for the other personality disorders and kept borderline disorder as it is in the DSM, because it is well studied with established treatments; the DSM has not changed, though there is talk of it. Not the others: the DSM categories still exist; borderline disorder is not going anywhere soon; the separate axis is gone.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders
guide.s: kept borderline personality disorder as a category

questions.stem: A 14-year-old tells a family physician during a confidential interview that her stepfather hits her when he drinks. She begs the physician not to tell anyone. What must the physician do?
options: Immediately and directly report to a Children's Aid Society, without relying on anyone else to do so
Ask the school counsellor to make the report
Investigate further to confirm the allegation before reporting
Respect confidentiality, since she is a capable minor
questions.explain: Why: reasonable grounds to suspect abuse of a child under 16 triggers a mandatory, immediate, direct and personal report to the CAS under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act. Not the others: the duty is non-delegable; the threshold is suspicion, not proof; the safety of children under 16 is a stated limit of confidentiality.

guide.s: not rely on anyone else to report on their behalf

questions.stem: A physician suspects that a 17-year-old patient is being neglected at home. What is the physician's reporting obligation in Ontario?
options: Permitted, but not required, to report to a Children's Aid Society
Prohibited from reporting without the patient's consent
Required to report only if the patient agrees
questions.explain: Why: for a child aged 16 or 17, physicians are permitted but not required to report. Not the others: the mandatory duty applies under 16; nothing prohibits a report; the patient's agreement is not the test.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with moderate depression wants to start psychotherapy but does not want her parents to decide for her. Under Ontario law, who consents?
options: She does, if she understands the treatment and appreciates the consequences of treatment versus no treatment; there is no minimum age
Her parents, because she is under 16
Her parents, because she is under 18
A capacity assessor must be appointed first
questions.explain: Why: the Health Care Consent Act sets no fixed minimum age; capacity is presumed, decision-specific, and means understand and appreciate; the mature-minor doctrine applies. Not the others: 16 and 18 are not consent thresholds in Ontario; capacity is presumed, so no assessor is needed by default.

guide.s: There is no fixed minimum age

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the four stated limits to confidentiality when interviewing a youth alone?
questions.explain: Why: the four limits are harm to yourself, harm to others, safety of young children under 16, and driving safety; the last two are the ones people forget. Not the others: substance use and sexual behaviour are high-risk topics kept confidential unless unsafe; school attendance is not a limit.

questions.stem: In what order does the child and adolescent psychiatric interview proceed?
options: Together, then the child alone, then the parents alone, then together for feedback
Parents alone, then child alone, then together
Child alone throughout, with parents by phone
questions.explain: Why: start together to set the frame and observe the parent-child interaction, then the child separately for confidential material, then the parents for collateral, then reconvene for summary and feedback. Not the others: observing the dyad requires the joint start; the confidential segment requires the child alone.

guide.s: come back together for summary and feedback

questions.stem: How should a clinician ask a 9-year-old about suicidal thoughts?
options: "Do you ever think about not wanting to be alive?"
"Have you ever made a plan to end your life?"
Safety should not be asked directly at this age
questions.explain: Why: the script for a 9-year-old is "do you ever think about not wanting to be alive?"; the 15-year-old is asked about suicidal thoughts. Not the others: the adult phrasing is for adolescents; safety is always asked, in developmental language.

questions.stem: A parent reports that their daughter spoke her first words at 2.5 years but met other milestones on time. Against the milestone norms taught this week, how is this interpreted?
options: A speech delay, since first words are expected at 12 to 18 months
Normal, since first words are expected by 3 years
A sign of autism spectrum disorder
questions.explain: Why: walking and first words are expected at 12 to 18 months, two words together at 2 years, a tricycle at 3; 2.5 years is a speech delay. Not the others: the language norm is not 3 years; it is not a motor milestone; isolated speech delay with normal other milestones is a neurodevelopmental marker, not a diagnosis of autism.

questions.stem: Which domain is added to the mental status examination when assessing a child, beyond the adult domains?
questions.explain: Why: parent-child interaction is the paediatric extra domain, observed during the joint segment of the interview, and is the item an adult-trained examiner forgets. Not the others: cognition, insight and perceptions are standard adult domains.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination in youth

questions.stem: A 15-year-old is diagnosed with moderate major depressive disorder in primary care. According to the management framework taught this week, what comes first?
options: Safety: a safety plan with coping strategies, the emergency department if acutely unsafe, and crisis resources
questions.explain: Why: the framework is numbered: safety first, then investigations (collateral before scales before bloodwork), then medication, therapy, school, community and other. Not the others: bloodwork sits inside investigations; SSRIs and school accommodations come later in the list.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination in youth

questions.stem: A 15-year-old has had low mood for 8 weeks. Her friends dropped her 10 weeks ago; she stopped competitive swimming a year ago; she has ADHD and a reading disability; there is a family history of bipolar disorder; her parents found searches about self-harm. Which is the most likely precipitating factor?
questions.explain: Why: a precipitating factor is the proximate trigger, and the friend-group rupture at 10 weeks tightly precedes the 8-week mood change; the model impression says so. Not the others: stopping swimming is a remote, perpetuating loss of a protective activity; family history and ADHD are predisposing; the searches are a consequence, a symptom.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination in youth

questions.stem: What proportion of adults with psychiatric disorders report that their symptoms began before age 18?
questions.explain: Why: 70% of adult psychiatric illness declares itself before 18, and up to 75% by age 25 with a peak onset at 15. Not the others: 20% is the share of children with a mental health disorder and the share of youth admissions that are psychiatric; the other figures are not in the source.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the four most common paediatric anxiety disorders by their typical age of emergence, earliest first?
options: Separation anxiety, specific phobia, social anxiety, generalised anxiety
Specific phobia, separation anxiety, generalised anxiety, social anxiety
Social anxiety, separation anxiety, specific phobia, generalised anxiety
Generalised anxiety, social anxiety, specific phobia, separation anxiety
questions.explain: Why: the sequence runs separation anxiety (early childhood), specific phobia (early school age), social anxiety (late school age, early teens), generalised anxiety (mid to late teens): anxiety moves outward from caregiver to object to peers to abstract worry. Not the others: each scrambles the order.

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

questions.stem: A 14-year-old has had excessive, hard-to-control worry about school and sports for eight months, with reassurance seeking, and reports only one associated symptom: difficulty sleeping. Does she meet the criteria for generalised anxiety disorder?
options: Yes: in children and adolescents only one of the six associated symptoms is required
No: three of six associated symptoms are required at any age
No: the worry must exceed twelve months in youth
Yes, but only if a specific phobia is also present
questions.explain: Why: the youth criterion is excessive anxiety, difficult to control, over 6 months, plus only 1 of 6 associated symptoms; adults need three. Not the others: the duration is six months; comorbidity is common but not required.

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy has refused to attend school for three weeks. How should this presentation be handled diagnostically?
options: School avoidance is not a DSM diagnosis; identify the underlying disorder such as separation anxiety, social anxiety or depression
No diagnosis is needed since it is a behavioural choice
questions.explain: Why: school avoidance is clinically common but not a DSM diagnosis; the task is to name the disorder driving it. Not the others: there is no such DSM entity; oppositional defiant disorder is not implied; the presentation needs assessment.

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth
