questions.stem: Which of the following is a paediatric modification of the diagnostic criteria for depressive disorders?
options: Irritable mood may replace low mood, and persistent depressive disorder requires only one year
Anhedonia is not required in youth
Two weeks of symptoms is shortened to one week
Six of nine symptoms are required instead of five
questions.explain: Why: the criteria are the same as adult major depressive disorder except that mood can be irritable instead of low and youth dysthymia needs one year, not two. Not the others: the duration and symptom-count rules are unchanged.

questions.stem: Which statement about depression in adolescents is correct?
options: Cumulative incidence reaches about 20% by age 18 and about 60% of those with an episode have a recurrence by 21
Fewer than 20% of depressed youth have a comorbid diagnosis
Recurrence after a first episode is uncommon before adulthood
questions.explain: Why: cumulative incidence by 18 is 20% and recurrence by 21 is 60%; lifetime prevalence is 11%. Not the others: more than 60% of youth with major depression have a comorbid diagnosis; recurrence is the rule, not the exception.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old presents with new anxiety, palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. Which organic cause should be ruled out first?
questions.explain: Why: anxiety points to hyperthyroidism (with sympathomimetics, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma, caffeine and substances); depression points to hypothyroidism, anaemia and vitamin deficiencies. Not the others: those are depression mimics.

questions.stem: An SSRI is started for a 17-year-old with moderate depression that has not responded to CBT. According to the warning cited this week, until what age does close observation for emergent suicidality apply?
questions.explain: Why: the FDA black-box warning of 2004 recommends close observation for emergence of suicidality up to 24 years, extending past the paediatric range. Not the others: 18 is the trap; the warning is age-bounded.

questions.stem: Before prescribing an SSRI to a 15-year-old with severe anxiety, what must the consent discussion include about its regulatory status in Canada?
options: No SSRI is approved by Health Canada for paediatric anxiety or depression, so the prescription is off-label
Fluoxetine is approved by Health Canada for paediatric depression
All SSRIs are approved for youth over 12
Health Canada requires a boxed warning but permits routine use
questions.explain: Why: there are no approved SSRIs by Health Canada; clinical use for moderate to severe anxiety and depression is off-label. Not the others: fluoxetine's paediatric approval is an FDA approval, not a Health Canada one; the boxed warning is the FDA's.

guide.s: no SSRI is approved by Health Canada

questions.stem: Which of the following is a stated indication for adding medication to psychotherapy in a youth with anxiety or depression?
options: To increase the effectiveness of CBT
Parental preference for a quick result
questions.explain: Why: the three printed indications are high impairment, limited progress with CBT, and to increase CBT effectiveness. Not the others: family history, age and parental preference are not indications.

questions.stem: Why does the paediatric psychiatric interview require both the youth's self-report and the parents' collateral?
options: Youth often do not share their parents' opinion of their mental health, so the two accounts disagree and both are needed
Parents are legally required to be present for all history taking
Youth self-report is unreliable and is used only for rapport
Collateral is needed only when the youth refuses to speak
questions.explain: Why: the survey finding is a clinical instruction: youth often don't share the same opinion as their parents on their mental health, which is why the interview separates them. Not the others: no law requires parental presence; self-report is essential, not decorative.

guide.s: do not share their parents' opinion

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy often loses things, is forgetful, does not seem to listen and fails to finish schoolwork; the pattern has lasted a year and is reported by both his parents and his teacher. Which framing criterion is still required for a diagnosis of ADHD?
options: Symptoms in three or more settings
Symptoms for at least two years
A positive response to a stimulant
questions.explain: Why: the framing criteria are often, at least 6 months, 2 or more settings, and several symptoms before age 12, with 6 of 9 in a domain. Not the others: two settings suffice; six months suffice; stimulant response is never diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old university student endorses five inattention symptoms on the CADDRA checklist, with childhood onset, impairment in two settings, and six months' duration. Does she meet the symptom-count threshold?
options: Yes: at age 17 and older, five symptoms in a domain suffice
No: six of nine are required at every age
No: adults require symptoms in both domains
Yes, but only if a stimulant challenge is positive
questions.explain: Why: DSM-5-TR requires 6 of 9 in children and 5 of 9 at age 17 and older; the CADDRA form prints 6 of 9 for both domains but the adult threshold is five. Not the others: a single domain suffices for an inattentive presentation; stimulant challenge tests are not part of assessment.

guide.s: 5 or more at age 17 and older

questions.stem: A second-year medical student asks whether she could have ADHD despite excellent grades throughout school. Which reply is correct?
options: Doing well in school does not rule out ADHD: hyperfocus and high IQ compensate for the impairment and forestall the diagnosis
ADHD cannot be diagnosed after age 18
Only the hyperactive presentation persists into adulthood
questions.explain: Why: people with ADHD can hyperfocus when interested or under pressure, and higher IQ correlates with later diagnosis. Not the others: grades do not exclude it; adult diagnosis is routine; the inattentive presentation persists and often worsens while hyperactivity internalises.

guide.s: IQ compensates for the impairments and forestalls diagnosis

questions.stem: A first-year student who managed well at home decompensates in her first term in residence. Which factor does the transition model rank first in unmasking ADHD?
options: Increased available distraction and immediate reward
questions.explain: Why: the podium ranks abrupt loss of structure first, then rising self-regulation demands, then more distraction and immediate reward. Not the others: the second and third are the lower tiers; sleep is not on the podium.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with poor concentration, restlessness and low motivation is being assessed for ADHD versus major depressive disorder. Which question best discriminates?
options: Whether there are distinct depressive episodes with wellness between them, and whether the attentional difficulties persisted during the well periods
Whether she has trouble falling asleep
questions.explain: Why: restlessness, motivation and concentration belong to both; the discriminator is episodic disturbance: depression comes in episodes, ADHD is continuous. Not the others: sleep-onset difficulty, demoralisation and irregular fatigue occur in ADHD as well.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with ADHD also reports anxiety in social settings and difficulty switching off at night. What is the relationship between her ADHD and her anxiety?
options: Treating the ADHD can mitigate ADHD-related anxiety; distractibility can masquerade as social anxiety and difficulty switching off as generalised anxiety
The anxiety must be treated first, before any ADHD treatment
Anxiety excludes a diagnosis of ADHD
Anxiety is rarer in women with ADHD than in men
questions.explain: Why: ADHD correlates with anxiety especially in girls and women, and treatment of ADHD can help to mitigate ADHD-related anxiety; anxiety is a collection of signs whose cause must be determined. Not the others: there is no rule to treat anxiety first; anxiety is a common comorbidity, more so in women.

guide.s: Treating the ADHD mitigates ADHD-related anxiety

questions.stem: What proportion of adults with ADHD score in the 95th percentile of emotion dysregulation on self-report?
questions.explain: Why: 55% of adults with ADHD sit in the top 5% of the population distribution, so most self-rate it as extreme; a patient presenting with emotion dysregulation should be asked about untreated ADHD. Not the others: 5% is the population share of that percentile; the other figures are not in the source.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man scores 5 of 6 on Part A of the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. How should this result be interpreted?
options: A positive screen, which should lead to the DSM criteria on the CADDRA checklist with childhood and current columns; the scale rules out better than it rules in
A false positive, since the scale has low negative predictive value
An indication to start a stimulant trial as a diagnostic test
questions.explain: Why: 4 or more on Part A is positive, but the scale has higher negative than positive predictive value, so it is followed by the criteria-based checklist and a thorough history. Not the others: no questionnaire diagnoses; the weakness is false positives, not false negatives; stimulant challenge is not diagnostic.

guide.s: 4 or more positive on Part A

questions.stem: A 45-year-old reports inability to start tasks, poor organisation and forgetfulness. Why is this presentation not sufficient to diagnose ADHD?
options: Executive dysfunction is non-specific and is not itself a diagnosis; it occurs in anxiety, psychosis, substance use, mood, neurocognitive and medical disorders as well as ADHD
Executive dysfunction only occurs in children
Executive dysfunction is diagnostic of hypothyroidism
questions.explain: Why: the same complaint belongs to seven categories: neurodevelopmental, anxiety, psychosis, substance, mood, neurocognitive and other medical (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency). Not the others: it occurs at any age; the inattentive presentation needs no hyperactivity; hypothyroidism is one cause among many.

guide.s: Executive dysfunction is not itself a diagnosis

questions.stem: A patient with depression on an SSRI reports emotional flatness and worsening concentration despite improved mood. What does the ADHD module suggest?
options: Raised serotonin can lower dopamine, producing serotonergic fogging, to which people with ADHD may be more vulnerable; assess for ADHD
This is serotonin syndrome and the SSRI must be stopped
The SSRI dose should be doubled
questions.explain: Why: increased serotonin can decrease dopamine, giving cognitive fogging or amotivation, and given the dopamine hypothesis of ADHD those with ADHD may be more susceptible; emotional blunting on an SSRI is a cue to assess for ADHD. Not the others: serotonin syndrome is an acute toxidrome; dose escalation and a bipolar diagnosis are not suggested.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old is newly diagnosed with ADHD. According to the CADDRA guidance, what is the first intervention?
questions.explain: Why: psychoeducation should be the first intervention; treatment is multimodal and collaborative and a stimulant should build on strategies. Not the others: medication and CBT come after education, and atomoxetine is second line.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD in the CADDRA October 2024 table?
questions.explain: Why: first line is the long-acting stimulants: mixed amphetamine salts XR, lisdexamfetamine, Biphentin, Concerta, Foquest and Quillivant ER. Not the others: short-acting stimulants, dextroamphetamine, atomoxetine and guanfacine XR are second line.

questions.stem: Which statement about lisdexamfetamine is correct according to the CADDRA table?
options: It is a prodrug with a duration of about 13 to 14 hours, started at 20 to 30 mg and capped at 60 mg at all ages
It is released 50/50 immediate and delayed with a maximum of 70 mg
It is a non-stimulant with 24-hour coverage
It is second line because of abuse potential
questions.explain: Why: lisdexamfetamine's release profile is not applicable because it is a prodrug; duration about 13 to 14 hours; start 20 to 30 mg in the morning; maximum 60 mg for all ages. Not the others: 50/50 release describes mixed amphetamine salts XR; 70 mg was a generic figure superseded by the CADDRA chart; it is a first-line stimulant.

questions.stem: How do amphetamine-based stimulants increase synaptic dopamine and noradrenaline?
options: They enter the terminal, inhibit VMAT2 so monoamines are not stored in vesicles, and the build-up makes the transporters run in reverse
They block dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake only
They bind postsynaptic alpha-2A receptors in the prefrontal cortex
They inhibit noradrenaline reuptake to reach steady state over 24 hours
questions.explain: Why: amphetamines bind monoamine transporters, inhibit VMAT2 and reverse the transporter, releasing dopamine and noradrenaline, and may also inhibit monoamine oxidase; the same mechanism by which methamphetamine causes psychosis. Not the others: reuptake inhibition alone is methylphenidate; alpha-2A is guanfacine; noradrenaline reuptake with steady state is atomoxetine.

questions.stem: A student starting methylphenidate OROS reports feeling irritable and unable to concentrate every afternoon around four. Which counselling point most directly addresses this?
options: Set a lunch alarm and take the drug after food, because appetite suppression means hunger is no longer a cue to eat and poor intake causes irritability at wear-off
Stop the stimulant, since irritability indicates intolerance
Add caffeine in the afternoon to extend the effect
Switch to cannabis in the evening to switch off
questions.explain: Why: stimulants can backfire through appetite suppression: the patient forgets to eat and irritability appears at wear-off, so the advice is to take it after food, remember lunch with an alarm, and take it early. Not the others: caffeine compounds side effects and cannabis reduces stimulant effectiveness; stopping is not the first move.

guide.s: hunger can no longer be the only cue to eat

questions.stem: Which substance is said to reduce the effectiveness of a stimulant in a patient with ADHD?
questions.explain: Why: the four points before starting a stimulant include watching substances: cannabis may reduce stimulant effectiveness, caffeine may compound side effects, and alcohol may feel more potent. Not the others: alcohol and caffeine carry different warnings; nicotine is not one of the four points.

questions.stem: A patient on a morning stimulant uses 25-minute timed work blocks and notices pages read fall sharply after 3 p.m. What is this information for?
options: It flags medication wear-off, prompting a different time of day or a divided dose
It shows the stimulant is ineffective and should be stopped
It indicates the dose should be doubled
It is irrelevant to medication decisions
questions.explain: Why: Pomodoro blocks flag the best time of day for each task and flag medication wear-off; if pages read fall by late afternoon, consider a different time or a divided dose. Not the others: the response earlier in the day shows efficacy; doubling is not the response to wear-off.

questions.stem: Which statement about cognitive behavioural therapy for adult ADHD is supported by the trials?
options: Higher baseline severity predicted more response to CBT, and response was independent of medication status
CBT was no better than relaxation and educational support
CBT works only in patients already on a stimulant
Individual CBT is the best-supported intervention for adolescents
questions.explain: Why: CBT beat relaxation and education (67% versus 33% response) and supportive therapy (53% versus 28%); higher baseline severity predicted more response to CBT but not to supportive therapy, and response was independent of medication status. Not the others: the effect is larger when added to a stimulant but not dependent on it; adolescents have less evidence for individual CBT and more for school- and family-based interventions.

guide.s: Higher baseline severity predicted more response to CBT

questions.stem: What is the value of exercise as a motivation strategy in ADHD?
options: One hour of effective exercise may contribute up to four hours of improved concentration and reduced hyperactivity and impulsivity
Exercise has no measurable effect on ADHD symptoms
Exercise replaces the need for medication in most adults
Exercise should be avoided in the evening because it worsens hyperactivity
questions.explain: Why: the ratio is 1 to 4: one hour of exercise, up to four hours of improved concentration, one of the healthier sources of motivation compared with negative self-talk, procrastination, caffeine and cannabis. Not the others: the other claims are unsupported.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with ADHD and tics is started on guanfacine XR. Which statement about this drug is correct?
options: It binds postsynaptic alpha-2A receptors in the prefrontal cortex, gives 24-hour coverage, starts at 1 mg and has a monotherapy maximum of 4 mg at ages 6 to 12
It inhibits dopamine reuptake and lasts 12 hours
Its maximum dose is 7 mg at any age
questions.explain: Why: guanfacine XR is a second-line alpha-2A agonist acting in the prefrontal cortex on behavioural inhibition and impulsivity, with 24-hour coverage; start 1 mg, titrate up to 1 mg weekly, maximum 4 mg at 6 to 12, 7 mg at 13 to 17, and 4 mg as an adjunct to a stimulant. Not the others: reuptake inhibition is methylphenidate; it is a non-stimulant; the 7 mg maximum is age-banded.

guide.s: postsynaptic alpha-2A adrenergic receptors in the prefrontal cortex

questions.stem: Which statement about atomoxetine is correct?
options: It inhibits noradrenaline reuptake and aims for 24-hour coverage at steady state, starting at 0.5 mg/kg/day in youth with a maximum of 1.4 mg/kg or 100 mg
It is a first-line long-acting stimulant
It should be opened and sprinkled on food
Its dose is adjusted every two days until response
questions.explain: Why: atomoxetine is a second-line selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor giving 24-hour coverage like a once-daily antidepressant; youth start at 0.5 mg/kg/day and hold 7 to 14 days before each step to 0.8 then 1.2 mg/kg, adults 40 then 60 then 80 mg, maximum 1.4 mg/kg or 100 mg. Not the others: it is a non-stimulant; capsules are swallowed whole because of gastrointestinal effects; steps are held at least a week.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old's history includes: her father's loud emotional outbursts; not being close to her 10-year-old brother; an eight-week separation from her parents at age 5; her mother's reactivity when she tries to share; and frequent parental arguments. Which item is LEAST related to attachment?
options: Not being close to her brother
Her mother's reactivity when she shares
questions.explain: Why: attachment is the bond formed through interactions with primary caregivers; a sibling relationship is a peer-like relationship, not an attachment relationship. Not the others: frightening caregiver behaviour, a literal separation from caregivers, and caregiver non-responsiveness at a bid for comfort are textbook attachment mechanisms.

guide.s: A sibling relationship is not an attachment relationship

questions.stem: An infant in the Strange Situation is highly anxious about abandonment and also highly avoidant of closeness, with contradictory behaviour on reunion. Which attachment classification fits?
questions.explain: Why: the grid runs on two orthogonal axes; disorganised is high on both anxiety and avoidance, and is the pattern most linked to frightening caregiving and later psychopathology. Not the others: secure is low on both; preoccupied is high anxiety with low avoidance; dismissive is high avoidance with low anxiety.

questions.stem: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, which moment is used to classify the infant's attachment style?
options: The infant's reaction on reunion with the returning caregiver
The infant's play while the caregiver is present
The infant's reaction to the stranger's arrival
questions.explain: Why: the key moments are separations and reunions and how the infant behaves when the caregiver is absent and returns; the classification comes from the reunion. Not the others: play, the stranger and separation distress are manipulated elements, not the classifying moment.

questions.stem: What was the central methodological point of the Felitti adverse childhood experiences study?
options: The number of categories of adversity, not any single event, was compared with adult health risk
A single severe event predicted adult disease better than multiple mild ones
Only sexual abuse predicted adult mortality
Children were followed prospectively from birth
questions.explain: Why: a questionnaire to 13,494 adults (9,508 responded, 70.5%) at a health maintenance organisation studied seven categories and compared the number of categories with adult risk: a dose-response relationship. Not the others: it was retrospective and cumulative, not event-specific.

guide.t: 2 · Social determinants and adverse childhood experiences

questions.stem: How many items are on the CDC adverse childhood experiences list, and how are they grouped?
options: Ten: three abuse, two neglect, five household challenges
Seven: three abuse, two neglect, two household challenges
Twelve: four in each of three domains
questions.explain: Why: physical, emotional and sexual abuse; physical and emotional neglect; and mental illness, divorce, a parent treated violently, an incarcerated relative and substance abuse: 3 plus 2 plus 5 equals 10. Not the others: seven is Felitti's category count, not the CDC list.

guide.t: 2 · Social determinants and adverse childhood experiences

questions.stem: On the ACE pyramid, which mechanism links disrupted social, emotional and cognitive functioning to health-risk behaviours?
questions.explain: Why: the upper arrow, adaptations, runs from functioning into health-risk behaviours, framing them as adaptations to adversity rather than moral failings. Not the others: neurodevelopment and epigenetics is the lower arrow from intergenerational adversity into ACEs; historical trauma is the base tier and early death the apex.

guide.t: 2 · Social determinants and adverse childhood experiences

questions.stem: Where does toxic stress sit on the stress-performance curve?
options: At the far right of the high-stress zone, where performance collapses
At the peak of the curve, in the optimal zone
In the low-stress zone of boredom and inactivity
It is not represented on the curve
questions.explain: Why: the inverted U rises through boredom to an optimal zone of productivity and focus and falls through burnout, anxiety and breakdown; toxic stress is marked at the far right tail. Not the others: some stress enhances performance; toxic stress is the extreme of high stress.

guide.t: 2 · Social determinants and adverse childhood experiences
guide.s: toxic stress sits at the far right

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about social media use in teenagers is TRUE?
options: Girls are more negatively affected by social media than boys
Around 75% of adolescents use social media
Youth play video games about as much as they use social media
Time spent on social media does not correlate with its impact
questions.explain: Why: the take-home names higher relative concern of harm in adolescent girls. Not the others: up to 95% of 13- to 17-year-olds use social media; gaming is 3.57% of online activity against 42.86% for social networking; more than 3 hours a day doubles the risk and limiting use improves outcomes.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health
guide.s: that girls are more negatively affected than boys is true

questions.stem: How much daily social media use is associated with a doubled risk of mental health outcomes such as anxiety and depression in teens?
questions.explain: Why: teens who spend more than 3 hours a day have twice the risk. Not the others: 30 minutes a day is the level to which a trial limited use and saw improvement; there is no threshold at any use.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health
guide.s: More than 3 hours a day doubles the risk

questions.stem: A depressed 19-year-old spends five hours a day on social media. What is the evidence-based advice about social media?
options: Limit use to 30 minutes a day; a randomised trial of that limit for three weeks significantly improved depression severity in transitional-aged youth
Continue, since social media has only benefits for marginalised youth
Switch to video games, which are safer
questions.explain: Why: limits on use benefited transitional-aged youth and adults, especially those with more severe problems: 30 minutes a day for three weeks improved depression, and four weeks' deactivation improved well-being. Not the others: the advice is not anti-screen; benefits exist but so do dose-dependent harms; gaming is not the recommended substitute.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health
guide.s: limiting social media to 30 minutes a day for three weeks

questions.stem: A 19-year-old is struck on the temple with a baseball. Which artery is at greatest risk, and why?
options: The anterior division of the middle meningeal artery, which lies deep to the pterion, the thinnest part of the vault
The internal carotid artery in the carotid canal
The superficial temporal artery in the scalp
The vertebral artery at the foramen magnum
questions.explain: Why: the pterion overlies the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery; a fracture there lacerates it and arterial blood strips the periosteal dura off the inner table. Not the others: the carotid and vertebral arteries enter at the base; the superficial temporal artery bleeds externally, not into the epidural space.

guide.s: The pterion overlies the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery

questions.stem: Which bony feature serves as the anterior attachment of the tentorium cerebelli?
options: The petrous ridge of the temporal bone
The posterior clinoid processes of the sphenoid
The clivus of the occipital bone
The squamous part of the temporal bone
questions.explain: Why: the tentorium's attached margin runs along the superior border of the petrous temporal bone, with the superior petrosal sinus, and its posterior attachment is the occipital bone along the transverse sinus grooves. Not the others: the clinoids are the endpoints of the attached and free margins, not the attachment line; no dural reflection attaches to the clivus or the squamous temporal.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses
guide.s: anterior attachment is the petrous ridge

questions.stem: A patient with a cavernous sinus thrombosis develops an isolated inability to abduct the right eye before any other cranial nerve sign. Which anatomical fact explains the order?
options: The abducens nerve runs free in the lumen beside the internal carotid artery, while cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and V2 are protected in the lateral wall
The abducens nerve is the most superior nerve in the lateral wall
The abducens nerve passes through the optic canal with the internal carotid
The abducens nerve is the longest cranial nerve and therefore the most fragile
questions.explain: Why: inside the lumen: internal carotid artery and CN VI; in the lateral wall, top to bottom, III, IV, V1, V2. Free in the venous space, the abducens is the most vulnerable. Not the others: the most superior wall nerve is the oculomotor; the optic canal carries CN II and the ophthalmic artery.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses
guide.s: inside the lumen: the internal carotid artery with the abducens nerve

questions.stem: Starting at the superior sagittal sinus, which sequence carries venous blood to the internal jugular vein?
options: Confluence of sinuses, transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, jugular foramen
Straight sinus, cavernous sinus, inferior petrosal sinus
Inferior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, jugular foramen
Transverse sinus, cavernous sinus, superior petrosal sinus
questions.explain: Why: the superficial route is superior sagittal sinus, confluence, transverse, sigmoid, jugular foramen, internal jugular vein; the deep route joins at the straight sinus and confluence; the cavernous sinus drains by the petrosal sinuses. Not the others: each mixes routes or reverses direction.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses
guide.s: superior sagittal sinus, confluence of sinuses, transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, jugular foramen, internal jugular vein

questions.stem: Which statement about the epidural space is correct?
options: Cranially it is a potential space between the periosteal dura and the inner table; in the spine it is a real space containing fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus
It is a real space at both levels, filled with CSF
It lies between the meningeal dura and the arachnoid
questions.explain: Why: the cranial epidural space is potential, created by arterial bleeding beneath the periosteal dura; the spinal epidural space is real, with fat and venous plexus, where epidural anaesthesia is placed. Not the others: CSF fills the subarachnoid space; dura-to-arachnoid is subdural; bridging veins cross the subdural interval.

questions.stem: Through which opening does the internal carotid artery enter the cranial cavity?
questions.explain: Why: internal carotid via the carotid canal; vertebral arteries via the foramen magnum; middle meningeal via the foramen spinosum. Not the others: the jugular foramen is the exit of the internal jugular vein.

guide.s: internal carotid through the carotid canal

questions.stem: An 85-year-old woman presents with bleeding from the right ear and confusion after a fall. Which bone is most likely fractured?
questions.explain: Why: otorrhagia localises to the temporal bone, which houses the external acoustic meatus and middle ear; associated findings are CSF otorrhoea, Battle's sign, facial and vestibulocochlear nerve injury and middle meningeal injury. Not the others: none contains the ear.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerves lie in the supratentorial compartment?
options: None; all cranial nerves are infratentorial
questions.explain: Why: the supratentorial compartment holds the cerebral hemispheres, the diencephalon and the intracranial parts of CN I and II, which are forebrain outgrowths; the infratentorial compartment holds the brainstem, cerebellum and CN III to XII. Not the others: every nerve from III onward arises from the brainstem.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses

questions.stem: A patient squeezes an infected pimple beside the nose and days later develops fever, proptosis and ophthalmoplegia. Which venous pathway explains the spread?
options: Facial vein tributaries anastomose without valves through the ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus
The facial vein drains directly into the superior sagittal sinus
The external jugular vein communicates with the sigmoid sinus
The pterygoid plexus drains into the transverse sinus
questions.explain: Why: the danger triangle from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose drains via the facial vein, which anastomoses valvelessly with the ophthalmic veins, and via the pterygoid plexus and deep facial vein, into the cavernous sinus. Not the others: the facial vein does not reach the sagittal sinus; the external jugular and transverse sinus are not the route.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses

questions.stem: On a child's skull radiograph, how is a linear fracture distinguished from a suture?
options: A fracture is sharper, straighter, non-serrated and not in an anatomically expected location
A fracture is always wider than 5 mm
A fracture is serrated and interdigitating
A fracture always crosses the midline
questions.explain: Why: sutures are serrated and lie between bones in expected places; a fracture is sharper, straighter, non-serrated and in the wrong place, and the child's skull shows open sutures, fontanelles, tooth buds and a thin diploë. Not the others: width and midline crossing are not discriminators; serration marks a suture.

questions.stem: Which lobes are accommodated in the middle cranial fossa?
questions.explain: Why: anterior fossa holds the frontal lobes; middle fossa the temporal lobes and, in the sella, the pituitary; posterior fossa the cerebellum, pons and medulla. Not the others: the occipital lobes sit on the tentorium above the posterior fossa.

questions.stem: Which statement is most accurate regarding the organisation of grey and white matter in the central nervous system?
options: Grey matter in the spinal cord is organised into horns, whereas grey matter in the forebrain is organised into a cerebral cortex and deep nuclei
Grey matter in the spinal cord and forebrain is organised exclusively into nuclei
Grey matter is superficial and white matter deep in both the spinal cord and the forebrain
Grey matter in the forebrain is organised into horns, whereas grey matter in the spinal cord is organised into cortical layers
questions.explain: Why: the arrangement is inverted: forebrain grey is superficial cortex plus deep nuclei with white matter deep; cord grey is central horns with white matter in peripheral columns. Not the others: the cortex is laminar, not nuclear; grey is not superficial in the cord; the last option reverses the truth.

guide.t: 3 · Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres

questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid leaving the third ventricle passes next through which structure?
questions.explain: Why: the chain runs lateral ventricles, foramina of Monro, third ventricle, aqueduct of Sylvius through the midbrain, fourth ventricle, then Magendie and Luschka into the subarachnoid space. Not the others: Monro precedes the third ventricle; the apertures leave the fourth.

questions.stem: A CT shows markedly dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle. Where is the obstruction, and what type of hydrocephalus is this?
options: At the cerebral aqueduct; obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus
At the arachnoid granulations; communicating hydrocephalus
At the foramen of Magendie; communicating hydrocephalus
At the foramina of Monro; obstructive hydrocephalus
questions.explain: Why: ventricles upstream of a block dilate and those downstream do not; lateral and third dilated with a normal fourth places the block at the aqueduct, obstructive hydrocephalus. Not the others: failure at the granulations dilates all ventricles; a block at the fourth ventricle outlets would dilate the fourth; a Monro block spares the third.

guide.s: aqueductal stenosis dilates the lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth

questions.stem: Which structures form the limbic lobe?
options: Cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus and uncus
Precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus and paracentral lobule
questions.explain: Why: the limbic lobe is not a discrete lobe; it is formed by the cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus and uncus. Not the others: hippocampus, amygdala and fornix belong to the limbic system as a circuit, not the lobe; the insula is a separate lobe; the pre- and postcentral gyri are motor and sensory.

guide.s: cingulate gyrus, the parahippocampal gyrus and the uncus

questions.stem: A small lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule produces a dense right hemiparesis. Why is the deficit so disproportionate to the lesion's size?
options: The posterior limb carries the corticospinal tract and somatosensory thalamocortical fibres in a compact bundle between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus
The posterior limb contains the primary motor cortex
The lesion interrupts the corpus callosum's forceps major
The posterior limb carries the association fibres for the whole hemisphere
questions.explain: Why: projection fibres funnel from the corona radiata into the internal capsule; the posterior limb, between thalamus medially and lentiform laterally, carries the corticospinal tract, so a tiny lesion cuts the whole descending motor output. Not the others: the motor cortex is the precentral gyrus; forceps major is callosal to the occipital lobes; association fibres stay within a hemisphere and are not capsular.

guide.t: 3 · Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres
guide.s: The posterior limb carries the corticospinal tract

questions.stem: Which structure separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explain: Why: the longitudinal fissure divides the hemispheres and holds the falx cerebri. Not the others: the lateral fissure separates the temporal lobe from frontal and parietal; the central sulcus separates frontal from parietal; the transverse fissure separates cerebrum from cerebellum and holds the tentorium.

guide.t: 1 · From neural tube to adult brain

questions.stem: From which secondary brain vesicle do the pons and cerebellum develop?
questions.explain: Why: the rhombencephalon divides into the metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) and the myelencephalon (medulla). Not the others: the medulla is myelencephalic; the diencephalon gives the thalamus and hypothalamus; the telencephalon gives the hemispheres.

guide.t: 1 · From neural tube to adult brain

questions.stem: Why is the insular lobe not visible on an intact lateral view of the brain?
options: It lies deep to the lateral fissure
It lies on the medial surface beneath the corpus callosum
It is part of the diencephalon
It is covered by the tentorium cerebelli
questions.explain: Why: the insula is buried in the depths of the lateral fissure, beneath the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. Not the others: the medial surface shows the cingulate gyrus; the insula is cortex, not diencephalon; the tentorium covers the cerebellum.

guide.s: lies deep to the lateral fissure

questions.stem: A right-handed patient has a lesion of the left precentral gyrus. Which deficits are predicted?
options: Right-sided weakness, with a possible language deficit because the left hemisphere is dominant in most people
questions.explain: Why: each hemisphere controls voluntary movement of the contralateral side, and the dominant hemisphere controls language, the left in most people. Not the others: weakness is contralateral, not ipsilateral or bilateral; the precentral gyrus is motor, not sensory.

questions.stem: Which cistern lies between the cerebellum and the medulla, below the fourth ventricle?
questions.explain: Why: the cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) sits between cerebellum and medulla and is the target of suboccipital puncture. Not the others: interpeduncular is between the peduncles in front of the midbrain; ambient wraps around the midbrain; superior sits behind it beneath the splenium.

questions.stem: On a wet brain specimen, how can the arachnoid mater be distinguished from the pia mater?
options: The arachnoid bridges over sulci and strips off easily; the pia dips into every sulcus and cannot be peeled
The arachnoid dips into every sulcus; the pia bridges over them
The arachnoid is thick and vascular; the pia is thin and avascular
They cannot be distinguished on a specimen
questions.explain: Why: the arachnoid is thin, avascular and translucent and bridges over sulci; the pia is adherent, carries the cortical vessels and dips into every sulcus. Not the others: the descriptions are reversed; the arachnoid is the avascular one.

guide.t: 5 · Lab specimens and the wet brain

questions.stem: A 24-year-old cyclist is struck on the side of the head. CT shows a hyperdense lens-shaped collection against the inner table that does not cross the adjacent suture. Which vessel is the likely source?
options: A ruptured aneurysm of the circle of Willis
questions.explain: Why: an epidural haematoma is arterial, classically the middle meningeal artery, higher pressure, biconvex, suture-bounded and often accompanied by a fracture. Not the others: bridging veins give a crescentic subdural; an aneurysm gives subarachnoid blood in sulci and cisterns; lenticulostriate arteries bleed into the parenchyma.

guide.s: Arterial, classically the middle meningeal artery

questions.stem: A 72-year-old presents three days after a fall with a gradually worsening headache, intermittent confusion, drowsiness and mild left-sided weakness. Non-contrast CT shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over the right hemisphere. What is the mechanism?
options: Stretching and tearing of bridging cortical veins as they cross the subdural space to a dural sinus, made likelier by atrophy
Rupture of the middle meningeal artery under a fracture
Aneurysmal bleeding into the subarachnoid space
Hypertensive rupture of a deep perforating artery
questions.explain: Why: a crescentic collection that crosses sutures is a subdural haematoma from torn bridging veins; generalised volume loss in the elderly leaves the brain mobile and the veins stretched, and the venous, low-pressure bleed evolves over days. Not the others: the middle meningeal gives a lens; aneurysms bleed into sulci; hypertension bleeds into the parenchyma.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a sudden, severe headache she describes as the worst of her life. CT shows hyperdense material layering in the cortical sulci and basal cisterns. What is the most likely cause, and what test finds the source?
options: A torn middle meningeal artery; skull radiograph
questions.explain: Why: thunderclap headache with serpiginous blood in the sulci is subarachnoid haemorrhage, typically from trauma or a ruptured aneurysm, and angiography finds the vascular source. Not the others: the middle meningeal gives an epidural lens; bridging veins give a subdural crescent; amyloid angiopathy causes parenchymal bleeding.

questions.stem: After a subarachnoid haemorrhage a patient's CT shows enlargement of all four ventricles. What is the mechanism?
options: Blood products block the arachnoid villi and granulations, preventing absorption: non-obstructive hydrocephalus
Blood clot obstructs the cerebral aqueduct: obstructive hydrocephalus
Blood obstructs the foramen of Monro on both sides
Blood raises CSF production by the choroid plexus
questions.explain: Why: diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage blocks reabsorption at the granulations, so CSF exits the ventricles normally but is not absorbed and all ventricles enlarge. Not the others: an aqueductal block spares the fourth ventricle; a Monro block spares the third and fourth; production is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which statement about imaging modalities for the brain is correct?
options: CT is the primary initial tool despite limited sensitivity for some pathologies, and MRI is the problem-solving tool for parenchyma
MRI is the first-line study for acute head trauma because it shows bone best
Ultrasound is the initial study for adult headache
Plain radiography reliably shows intracranial haemorrhage
questions.explain: Why: CT is the primary initial tool and MRI visualises parenchyma better and is used as a problem-solving tool, with contrast on either for vessels, inflammation and lesions. Not the others: MRI cannot see cortical bone well; ultrasound is blocked by bone except in neonates; radiography shows bone, not blood.

guide.s: CT is the primary initial tool for brain imaging

questions.stem: Two patients have skull fractures. One has a depressed fracture; the other has a fracture through the anterior skull base with clear fluid from the nose. How do their intracranial pressures differ?
options: The depressed fracture immediately raises intracranial pressure; the dural tear with CSF leak lowers it, producing sagging of the brain
questions.explain: Why: a depressed fracture immediately increases intracranial pressure and needs emergent repair; a fracture that damages the dura lets CSF leak, which decreases pressure, causing sagging and downward cerebellar tonsillar descent. Not the others: the pressure change runs in opposite directions, though both can show tonsillar descent.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a headache red flag that mandates emergent head imaging?
options: New onset of severe headache in a patient over 50
Bilateral pressing headache lasting hours in a 25-year-old
questions.explain: Why: the six red flags are thunderclap headache, new neurological deficit, fever with neck stiffness, recent head trauma, immunosuppression, and new severe headache over 50. Not the others: features of benign, transitory headache.

questions.stem: A contrast MRI shows a 1 cm enhancing lesion with a very large surrounding zone of oedema and mass effect. Which diagnosis does the oedema favour?
questions.explain: Why: metastases create extensive inflammation and far more oedema and mass effect than primary lesions of similar size; primary tumours have relatively little inflammation unless they necrose or bleed. Not the others: a low-grade glioma and a meningioma show proportionate or little oedema; an old infarct does not enhance with mass effect.

questions.stem: A contrast MRI shows a solitary ring-enhancing intra-axial lesion with surrounding oedema. The differential includes metastasis, abscess and glioblastoma. What is true about distinguishing them?
options: Even with MRI they can all appear very similar; imaging alone may not separate them and tissue may be needed
The thickness of the rim reliably identifies the abscess
Glioblastoma is excluded by the presence of oedema
questions.explain: Why: set side by side, even with MRI these can all appear very similar; often only pathology determines the tumour type. Not the others: rim features are not a reliable discriminator; metastases and glioblastoma both ring-enhance with oedema.

guide.s: cannot be reliably distinguished on imaging

questions.stem: A CT shows displacement of the ventricles across the midline beneath the falx by a large hemispheric mass. Which herniation is this?
options: Cingulate (subfalcine) herniation, seen as midline shift
questions.explain: Why: the cingulate gyrus swept beneath the falx is subfalcine herniation, captioned on the CT as midline shift with displacement of the ventricles. Not the others: uncal herniation is the medial temporal lobe over the tentorial edge; tonsillar is through the foramen magnum; transcalvarial is out through a skull defect.

questions.stem: A bone-window CT of a depressed frontal fracture shows a small focus of gas just deep to the inner table. What does this finding mean?
options: The fracture is open, with a high risk of eventual infection
The fracture is old and healing
The patient has an arterial bleed
questions.explain: Why: intracranial gas means the fracture communicates with the outside or a sinus: an open fracture with a high infection risk. Not the others: gas does not date the fracture, indicate pressure, or signal arterial bleeding.

guide.s: intracranial gas means an open fracture

questions.stem: A small group is appraising a randomised controlled trial with the CASP checklist. Which sections answer whether the trial is valid?
questions.explain: Why: for the RCT checklist, validity is sections A and B, results section C, relevance section D; for the cohort checklist validity is A, results B, relevance C. Not the others: A alone is the cohort mapping; C and D are results and relevance.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research
guide.s: in sections A and B for validity

questions.stem: Both papers appraised this week studied patients with chronic schizophrenia on maintenance treatment. To which of the four cases of the week are they LEAST relevant?
options: The 33-year-old woman brought by police, positive for cannabis and methamphetamine, with substance-induced psychosis
The 54-year-old in family practice remitted on long-acting paliperidone
The 33-year-old game designer in remission on risperidone who wants to stop
The 23-year-old student with a first psychosis
questions.explain: Why: relevance turns on population match; the substance-induced case is the clearest mismatch with a chronic-schizophrenia population. Not the others: the family-practice case fits both papers best; the discontinuation question fits a real-world cohort; first psychosis is a partial match.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the limitations of the two antipsychotic papers?
options: Newer antipsychotics were not included and the doses may be outdated
Neither paper used a control group
Both papers were funded by industry
The sample sizes were too small to detect a difference
questions.explain: Why: the four bullets are: are the articles outdated (doses used; newer antipsychotics not included) and are they generalisable (different health care systems; only one point in time). Not the others: none of these was raised, and the cohort had 29,823 patients.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

questions.stem: On the evidence pyramid, which of the following counts as filtered information?
options: Critically appraised topics such as evidence syntheses and guidelines
questions.explain: Why: filtered information is the top three tiers: systematic reviews, critically appraised topics, and critically appraised individual articles; unfiltered is RCTs, cohorts, and case-control, series and reports. Not the others: all three are unfiltered primary designs.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

questions.stem: A 60-year-old presents with new persecutory delusions, disorientation to time and place, and fluctuating alertness. According to the diagnostic hierarchy taught for the psychiatric interview, which rung must be considered first?
options: Physical or drug-induced conditions, whose hallmark is confusion
The psychoses, whose hallmark is impaired reality-testing
questions.explain: Why: the hierarchy runs top down: physical and drug-induced conditions (hallmark confusion) can show every sign of the rungs below and are most open to specific, sometimes life-saving treatment; only then psychosis, then mood. Not the others: the delusions may be secondary; disorientation flags rung one.

questions.stem: A patient says her mood is "empty, about 3 out of 10", while the interviewer observes a restricted, depressed affect. Which statement correctly assigns these findings?
options: Mood is subjective and reported by the patient, rated 0 to 10 with 0 worst; affect is objective and observed by the interviewer
Mood is what the interviewer observes; affect is what the patient reports
A rating of 3 out of 10 indicates a mildly elevated mood
questions.explain: Why: mood is subjective, in the patient's words, on a 0 to 10 scale where 0 is worst and 10 is well; affect is objective, with four axes: quality, range, stability, congruence. Not the others: the definitions are reversed; the scale runs the reverse of most, so 3 is low.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk

questions.stem: After a patient admits thinking about death, which is the next question in the scripted suicide assessment?
options: "Are you thinking about ways that you would end your life?"
"What are some reasons for staying alive?"
"Have you attempted suicide in the past?"
"How would you describe your level of intent?"
questions.explain: Why: the ladder is ideation, then method, then means or preparation, then intent, then past attempts; then acute against chronic and active against passive; and it ends on protective factors. Not the others: reasons for living is the closing question; past attempts and intent come later.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk
guide.s: Are you thinking about ways that you would end your life

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the six risk domains the interview guide requires, beyond suicide?
questions.explain: Why: the six domains are suicide, other deliberate self-harm, violence to others, inability to look after oneself, self-neglect, and neglect of dependents, with safe driving and cooking added. Not the others: none is a listed risk domain.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk

questions.stem: Which wording does the interview guide prescribe when discussing suicide?
options: "Die by suicide" or "complete suicide", not "commit suicide"
"Successful suicide", to distinguish it from attempts
questions.explain: Why: the one explicit language rule replaces words with a negative connotation: "complete suicide" or "die by suicide" for "commit suicide", and "drug use" for "drug abuse". Not the others: the topic is raised plainly with calm interest, not avoided.

questions.stem: A patient reports hearing a voice. Which sequence of probes does the guide script, and what is the final instruction?
options: Screen, quality (conscience? inside or outside the head?), number and recognisability, commentary, command including harm to self or others; then ask about substance use and symptoms when abstinent
Command first, then screen for visual hallucinations
Quality, then a formal cognitive test
Number of voices, then whether they are pleasant
questions.explain: Why: the run is screen, quality, number, commentary, command, the command probe doubling as a risk question, followed by the substance-induced-versus-primary discriminator: concurrent substance use and intensity of symptoms when abstinent. Not the others: the order and the closing instruction are the examinable content.

questions.stem: In the formulation model taught, what are the three components of a working diagnosis?
options: Classify the illness, discern the predicament, discover the disease
questions.explain: Why: the Taylor triad: illness (the symptoms and signs brought to the encounter), predicament (the context), disease (the underlying pathophysiology, if discoverable); the plan is biopsychosocial, feasible and mitigates safety concerns. Not the others: the four Ps are not in this guide; biopsychosocial describes the plan, not the diagnosis.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with lupus, hypertension and a depressive episode five years ago is brought in by his wife with several days of pressured speech, irritability and hearing voices. He has taken ramipril for years; prednisone 50 mg was started a week ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Recurrence of depression with psychotic features
questions.explain: Why: the timeline names the drug: symptoms began days after prednisone 50 mg, and the picture is manic-flavoured with hallucinations, the classic corticosteroid presentation. Not the others: schizophreniform needs no substance cause and one to six months; a depressive recurrence would not be pressured and irritable; lupus psychosis needs evidence of a flare, and the drug is the more proximate cause.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease, admitted for pyelonephritis, wants to leave because he dislikes hospital food and does not believe in Western medicine. The medical team asks the on-call psychiatry resident to complete a Form 1. What is the best response?
options: He should be assessed by the internal medicine team first to determine whether he understands and appreciates the risks and benefits of refusing antibiotics
A Form 1 cannot be completed because dementia is not a mental illness under the Mental Health Act
He should be detained under a Form 1 because he is refusing necessary treatment
He should be detained under a Form 1 because he risks physical impairment without antibiotics
questions.explain: Why: refusal of treatment is a capacity question for the treating team under the Health Care Consent Act (understand and appreciate); if capable he may refuse, if incapable a substitute decision-maker decides, and neither needs a Form 1. Not the others: dementia is a mental disorder under the Mental Health Act; a Form 1 requires a mental disorder plus risk of serious harm arising from it warranting psychiatric assessment, not a medical treatment dispute.

guide.s: understand and appreciate the risks and benefits of refusing antibiotics

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease is brought by his daughter because he has begun swatting at things no one else sees and muttering that a fairy is here, worse in the evenings; he is sleepy and cannot focus on questions. Which action is LEAST appropriate?
options: Prescribe an antipsychotic and see him again in one month
Examine the chest, abdomen and nervous system
Order urinalysis, complete blood count and electrolytes
Consider urgent referral to the emergency department
questions.explain: Why: acute visual hallucinations, evening worsening, somnolence and inattention in dementia are delirium until proven otherwise; the cause must be found, and antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for mortality in dementia-related psychosis. Not the others: examination, basic investigations and urgent referral are all appropriate.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old construction worker, referred by his family physician, insists there is nothing wrong with him. Which finding would warrant starting an antipsychotic?
options: A belief, held for nine months, that the FBI hired him to protect the prime minister
Ringing in his ears since standing beside the speakers at a concert yesterday
Low mood for two months since losing his job
Fear of being followed by criminals since he was mugged three weeks ago
questions.explain: Why: only the FBI belief is a delusion: fixed, implausible and past both the one-month and six-month thresholds. Not the others: tinnitus has a real stimulus; low mood after job loss is a mood symptom with a precipitant; fear after a real mugging is a plausible, reality-based worry.

guide.s: fixed, implausible, past both duration thresholds

questions.stem: Which statement about evidence-based treatment for schizophrenia is correct?
options: Assertive community treatment teams can reduce hospitalisations
Assertive community treatment teams improve employment rates
Cognitive behavioural therapy can stop hallucinations
questions.explain: Why: ACT teams reduce admissions and days in hospital; employment is the domain of supported employment; CBT reduces distress attached to hallucinations without stopping them; family psychoeducation reduces relapse. Not the others: each attaches an outcome to the wrong intervention.

guide.s: Assertive community treatment teams reduce hospitalisations

questions.stem: What is the main difference between delusional disorder and schizophrenia?
options: Delusional disorder does not include hallucinations
Delusional disorder is preceded by a prodrome of functional decline
Patients with delusional disorder usually recover spontaneously
Delusional disorder is treated with psychotherapy rather than antipsychotics
questions.explain: Why: delusional disorder is delusions without hallucinations, with nonbizarre delusions and no disorganisation or negative symptoms. Not the others: functioning is preserved apart from the delusion's impact, so no prodromal decline; the course is chronic; antipsychotics treat both.

guide.s: Delusional disorder does not include hallucinations

questions.stem: Which statement about the epidemiology of schizophrenia is correct?
options: Most cases occur late in life
The male to female ratio is 1 to 1.5
questions.explain: Why: the keyed range brackets 0.5% (lecture) and 1% (textbooks). Not the others: incidence is about 15 to 20 per 100,000 person-years; 80% of cases begin before 30; men are affected more, about 2 to 1.

questions.stem: According to the patient-educator panel, why should coercive measures be avoided whenever possible in a psychotic crisis?
options: Coercion damages the person's future relationship with the illness, its treatment and its service providers
questions.explain: Why: the patient-educators' key message is to listen deeply, understand the person's perspective on the crisis and avoid coercion whenever possible, because coercion damages the future working relationship with illness, treatment and providers; the long game is a safe, meaningful, dignified, self-determined life. Not the others: the argument is relational, not legal or pharmacological, and "whenever possible" concedes it is sometimes needed.

questions.stem: A question asks how many cerebral lobes there are. Which answer strategy reflects the week's sources?
options: Six including the insula and limbic lobe on a lab-based question; five with the limbic lobe not a discrete lobe on a lecture-based question
questions.explain: Why: the lab manual counts six lobes including insula and limbic; five (lecture), with the limbic lobe not a discrete lobe; standard texts describe four classical lobes plus the insula with the limbic lobe as a functional sixth. Not the others: the cerebellum is not a cerebral lobe; a single number ignores the examiner's source.

guide.s: Six on a lab question including insula and limbic

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is brought by police in January wearing one shoe, screaming that people want to murder her and talking to the walls; she has presented before and improved after a single antipsychotic dose, and her urine is positive for methamphetamine. What is the most likely diagnosis, and why?
options: Substance-induced psychosis: a found cause moves the case out of the schizophrenias, and methamphetamine is now the commonest cause of acute drug-induced psychosis
Schizophrenia, because she has persecutory delusions and hallucinations
Delusional disorder, because the belief is persecutory
Brief psychotic disorder, because she improves within a day
questions.explain: Why: as soon as a cause is found it is no longer schizophrenia; methamphetamine raises synaptic dopamine and is the commonest cause of acute drug-induced psychosis, and rapid improvement after one dose fits. Not the others: schizophrenia requires the absence of a substance cause; delusional disorder excludes prominent hallucinations; brief psychotic disorder also requires no substance cause.

guide.s: a found cause is no longer schizophrenia

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with severe haemophilia falls down a flight of stairs and is drowsy on arrival. Non-contrast CT of the head shows no hyperdense collection. Which statement best guides interpretation?
options: Haemorrhage is bright on CT only once blood has clotted, so a patient who cannot form a clot may bleed without the bright sign
Absence of hyperdensity excludes intracranial haemorrhage
Flowing blood in vessels is normally hyperdense, so any bleed would be visible
Haemophilia makes haemorrhage more hyperdense than usual
questions.explain: Why: clot is denser than brain, which is why haemorrhage is bright; the sign assumes the patient can clot, and in a coagulopathic patient the bleed can be isodense. Not the others: a normal-looking CT does not exclude a bleed in this setting; circulating blood is not bright; coagulopathy makes the bleed less, not more, conspicuous.

guide.s: a coagulopathic patient can bleed without the bright sign

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden left hemiparesis. CT shows a hyperdense haematoma deep in the right hemisphere. Which location and mechanism fit best?
options: Basal ganglia; small feeder vessels arising near the circle of Willis fail under the highest pressure in the brain
Cortical convexity; bridging veins torn by atrophy
Extradural space; the middle meningeal artery sheared by a fracture
questions.explain: Why: hypertensive bleeds sit centrally, in the basal ganglia, because their fine perforating feeders come off the circle of Willis, where pressure is highest, and cannot take the load. Not the others: bridging veins give a subdural crescent; the middle meningeal gives an epidural lens; an aneurysm gives subarachnoid blood.

guide.s: Hypertensive bleeds sit centrally, in the basal ganglia

questions.stem: Two head-injured patients arrive together. One has a lens-shaped extradural collection under a temporal fracture; the other, an anticoagulated 80-year-old, has a bilateral crescentic collection. Which statement about their prognosis and management is most accurate?
options: The epidural expands fastest and kills soonest but is the more fixable, since the artery can be occluded and the clot evacuated; the subdural is harder to control
The subdural expands fastest because venous bleeding is under higher pressure
The epidural cannot be treated surgically
Both carry the same mortality and the same operative options
questions.explain: Why: the arterial epidural strips the dura and grows rapidly, so it kills fastest, but the vessel can be clipped, coiled or ligated and the clot removed; the subdural involves many torn veins in a potential space with no tamponade, recurs, and afflicts elderly or anticoagulated patients, so it is the harder problem. Not the others: venous bleeding is low pressure and slow; epidurals are eminently operable; the two differ in both mortality and options.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old is hit on the head by a baseball, is briefly dazed, then converses normally and is sent home. Twelve hours later he is found unrousable. Which haemorrhage does this course illustrate, and why?
options: A subdural haematoma: a slow, insidious venous bleed from bridging veins torn in an atrophic brain, even after a low-energy blow
An epidural haematoma: subdural blood is never associated with a lucid period
A subarachnoid haemorrhage from an aneurysm
questions.explain: Why: this is the subdural story: the atrophic brain sits in a pool of CSF, rotates, tears veins, and the low-pressure bleed accumulates over hours. Standard texts attach the classic lucid interval to the epidural, and both are true; in an elderly patient after minor trauma the answer is the subdural. Not the others: aneurysmal bleeding presents with thunderclap headache; a hypertensive bleed has no trauma.

guide.s: the elderly patient with a low-energy injury who deteriorates hours later has a subdural

questions.stem: Which statement about the causes of subarachnoid haemorrhage is correct?
options: Trauma is the commonest cause overall; a ruptured aneurysm is the commonest cause of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage
A ruptured aneurysm is the commonest cause overall, and trauma rarely produces subarachnoid blood
Hypertension is the commonest cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage
Bridging vein rupture is the commonest cause
questions.explain: Why: the two causes are trauma and ruptured aneurysm; trauma is the more common overall, while an aneurysm accounts for about 85% of spontaneous cases. Not the others: trauma frequently produces subarachnoid blood; hypertension bleeds into the parenchyma; bridging veins bleed into the subdural space.

guide.s: trauma is the commonest cause overall

questions.stem: A man with a depressed frontal fracture and a small focus of intracranial gas is admitted for observation of his haematoma. Which management point follows from the gas?
options: The fracture is open; infection is a risk that can declare itself as meningitis days later, so antibiotics that cross the blood-brain barrier should be started early
The gas confirms low intracranial pressure and no antibiotics are needed
The gas means the bleed is arterial
Routine oral antibiotics are sufficient because the skull is fractured
questions.explain: Why: intracranial gas means the fracture communicates with the outside or a sinus; attention goes to the haemorrhage while meningitis develops over days, and routine agents may not cross the blood-brain barrier, so the gas is the cue to start a penetrating antibiotic early. Not the others: gas says nothing about pressure or about the vessel; drug choice must account for the barrier.

questions.stem: Three days after a fall onto his face, a 30-year-old reports a persistent clear drip from one nostril without other cold symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?
options: CSF rhinorrhoea from a fracture through the cribriform plate
questions.explain: Why: a fracture through the cribriform plate tears the dura and CSF drips from the nose; the leak lowers intracranial pressure, lets the brain sag and opens a route for infection. Not the others: post-traumatic unilateral clear drip is not a cold; aneurysm and epidural haematoma do not produce nasal fluid.

questions.stem: After an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage with blood in the ventricles, a patient develops ventriculomegaly. Which statement about the mechanism is most accurate?
options: Blood can cause both types at once, clotting inside the ventricular system and clogging the arachnoid granulations, and the mass effect matters more than which mechanism dominates
questions.explain: Why: clot is sticky: it can block a ventricular pathway (obstructive) and plug the granulations (non-obstructive), and both often coexist after a bleed. Not the others: neither mechanism is exclusive, and production is not the issue.

guide.s: Blood can cause both types at once

questions.stem: MRI shows a smooth, well-defined mass in the posterior fossa with a thin rim of CSF between it and the indented cerebellum. Which diagnosis and reasoning fit best?
options: Meningioma: the CSF cleft shows the mass is extra-axial, outside the brain and pushing it away
Glioblastoma: the cleft proves the mass arises within the parenchyma
Brain abscess: the cleft is the abscess wall
Metastasis: extra-axial masses are always metastatic
questions.explain: Why: a rind of CSF separating a mass from brain marks it as extra-axial, and the classic example is a meningioma; such lesions are generally easier to treat because the surgeon need not go through brain. Not the others: glioblastoma is intra-axial; an abscess is an intra-axial ring-enhancing lesion; extra-axial does not mean metastatic.

questions.stem: A patient with an open skull fracture develops fever. Over the following week imaging shows first meningeal enhancement, then a hazy area in the basal ganglia. Which entity is expected next in the cascade, and how does it kill?
options: Ventriculitis, which clogs the arachnoid villi with protein and kills through hydrocephalus and mass effect
Brain abscess, which kills by direct toxin release
Meningitis again, which kills by dehydration
questions.explain: Why: the cascade runs meningitis, cerebritis, ventriculitis, abscess, progressively more serious; infection in the ventricles produces proteins that block the villi, so the killer is the resulting hydrocephalus. Not the others: abscess is the last step and kills by mass effect and rupture; the other options are not part of the cascade.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has three weeks of progressive headache and a new focal seizure. The emergency physician orders a non-contrast CT head to look for a tumour. What is the limitation of that order?
options: Very large tumours can be invisible on non-contrast CT because they are soft-tissue density; a suspected tumour should be imaged with contrast CT or MRI
CT cannot be performed with a seizure history
MRI is contraindicated in tumour work-up
questions.explain: Why: most neoplasms are soft-tissue density, so a non-contrast CT can miss even a large tumour; contrast enhancement, on CT or MRI, is what reveals it. Not the others: CT is the best modality for bone; seizures do not preclude CT; MRI is the problem-solving tool.

cards.prompt: Match each condition to its typical hallucination modality.
pairs: Auditory: human voices in a meaningful language

cards.prompt: Define hallucination and delusion, and give the physical test that separates a hallucination from a disagreement about what was heard.
cards.answer: Hallucination: a sensory perception in the absence of a stimulus. Delusion: a fixed false belief. Test: a real stimulus leaves a trace an instrument could record (a waveform); a hallucinated voice leaves none.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are negative symptoms of schizophrenia?

cards.text: Schizophrenia is defined purely by {{symptoms}}; there are no objective tests, no scan and no biochemistry, and its course is {{chronic and episodic}}.

cards.prompt: Match each spectrum to the entities laid along it.
pairs: Schizophrenia, schizophreniform, delusional disorder, schizotypal and schizoid PD
Schizophrenia with obsessions, OCD with poor insight, OCD, Tourette's
Schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, depression

cards.prompt: How do the Cluster A personality disorders relate to schizophrenia, and can one develop into the other?
cards.answer: They are a less severe phenotype of the same illness: odd beliefs not quite delusional, social dysfunction overlapping with autism, and a genetic relationship to schizophrenia. A Cluster A picture that later becomes schizophrenia was schizophrenia before its age of onset, not one disorder turning into another.

cards.prompt: In the older formal nosology, which delusions fall under the umbrella term paranoid delusions?
Grandiose delusions are most characteristic of which condition?
What does the mood congruence of a delusion tell you about the diagnosis?
cards.answer: Content that fits the mood (hyper-negative and self-referential in depression; talent, wealth and power in mania) points to a mood disorder with psychotic features; content orthogonal to mood, or present with euthymic mood, points to a primary psychotic disorder.

cards.text: The number of people needed in a room for a 50% chance that two share a birthday is {{23}}; most people guess {{183}}.

cards.prompt: In the Redelmeier and Tversky study of arthritis pain and weather, what was the mean correlation between pain and the weather variables?
Which features were already present in Kraepelin's 1919 description of dementia praecox?
options: Loss of the ability to keep attention fixed
The feeling of one's thoughts being influenced

cards.prompt: Why is schizophrenia called a leftover diagnosis of exclusion, and which conditions illustrate the point?
cards.answer: It is a clinical syndrome with many causes; once a cause is found (neurosyphilis, complex partial epilepsy, metachromatic leukodystrophy, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, a structural lesion, 22q11 deletion) the condition is no longer called schizophrenia.

cards.prompt: Place the components of the mental status examination in the conventional order.

cards.text: On the MSE, mood is the patient's {{subjective}} report of emotional state, while affect is the physician's {{objective}} observation, described by range, intensity, stability, congruence and appropriateness.

cards.prompt: Which conditions are characterised by lack of insight on the MSE, and what does unawareness track with in schizophrenia?
cards.answer: Schizophrenia (often unaware of the illness, with poorer treatment response) and frontotemporal dementia; mania shows little insight, depression over-emphasises problems. In schizophrenia, unawareness tracks with executive dysfunction.

cards.prompt: What does LEAP stand for as an approach to a relative who does not accept a diagnosis of psychosis?
cards.answer: Listen, empathise, agree where you can, partner.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are Criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia?

cards.text: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for at least {{six months}}, including at least {{one month}} of active-phase symptoms.

cards.prompt: Name three changes DSM-5 made to the schizophrenia criteria compared with DSM-IV-TR.
cards.answer: At least one Criterion A symptom must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech; the one-symptom exception for bizarre delusions and Schneiderian hallucinations was removed; the five subtypes were removed (and negative symptoms are worded as diminished emotional expression or avolition).

cards.prompt: Which features belong to the prodromal phase of schizophrenia?
options: Loss of interest in work or school

cards.prompt: Match each disorder to its duration criterion.
pairs: At least one day, less than one month
At least one month, less than six months
Six months or more, with one month active

cards.prompt: Order these diagnoses from the shortest to the longest required duration of psychotic symptoms.

cards.text: Schizoaffective disorder requires a mood episode concurrent with active-phase symptoms, mood symptoms for a substantial portion of the illness, and delusions or hallucinations for {{two weeks}} without prominent mood symptoms.

cards.prompt: List the defining features of delusional disorder.
cards.answer: Nonbizarre delusions; absence of hallucinations, disorganized speech or behaviour, and negative symptoms; functioning largely preserved apart from the delusion's direct impact.

guide.s: exclusively during periods of mood disturbance

cards.prompt: In depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features, when do the psychotic symptoms occur?
options: Exclusively during periods of mood disturbance
For at least two weeks without mood symptoms
Only after the mood episode remits

cards.prompt: How do schizotypal and schizoid personality disorder differ from each other and from schizophrenia?
cards.answer: Schizotypal: sub-threshold positive features (unusual beliefs, illusions such as shadows) without full delusions or hallucinations. Schizoid: no positive symptoms, only affective flattening and negative-type features. Schizophrenia: full delusions and hallucinations in a constellation; flattening alone is not sufficient.

cards.prompt: Match each medical cause of psychosis to its characteristic finding.
pairs: Kayser-Fleischer rings; basal ganglia lesions on MRI
Moon face, striae; elevated 24-hour urine cortisol
Malar rash, oral ulcers; elevated ANA

cards.prompt: Which two substances are the most common causes of drug-induced psychosis today, and how does their time course differ?
cards.answer: Methamphetamine, which produces psychosis acutely (and resolves quickly), and cannabis, which does so less acutely.

cards.prompt: Which steps belong to the evaluation of a first psychosis before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed?
options: Screen for delirium, mood disorder with psychosis, Cushing syndrome and drug use
Observe in a controlled setting for an extended time where feasible
Perform a physical examination for organic causes

guide.t: 4 · Referral, admission and the first steps

cards.text: For agitation with psychosis the emergency department combines an antipsychotic with a benzodiazepine: {{loxapine}} with lorazepam, or {{haloperidol}} with lorazepam, oral or injected.

guide.t: 4 · Referral, admission and the first steps

cards.prompt: What is the recommended stance toward a patient's delusions during de-escalation?
options: Do not argue with them, but do not agree with or support them either
Agree with them to build rapport
Ignore them and redirect to medication

guide.t: 4 · Referral, admission and the first steps

cards.prompt: Who with psychosis is referred to psychiatry, and who is admitted?
cards.answer: All patients presenting with psychosis or newly diagnosed with schizophrenia are urgently referred for psychiatric evaluation; admission is considered for those who may pose a danger to themselves or others.

cards.text: Lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia is about {{0.5%}}; peak onset is age {{23}} in males and {{40}} in females; 80% of cases begin before age 30.

cards.prompt: Match each age band to the male to female ratio.
The week's sources give different prevalence figures for schizophrenia. What are they, and what should be answered?
