cards.answer: 0.5% (lecture); 0.3 to 0.7% (AFP review, DSM-5-TR); about 1% (older texts); 0.5 to 1% (quiz key). Any value within 0.5 to 1% is defensible; expect 0.5% on a lecture-based item.

cards.prompt: Match each risk factor to its magnitude.
pairs: Smoking and lung cancer, for calibration

cards.prompt: Which of the following are environmental risk factors for schizophrenia named this week?
Describe the design of the maternal influenza study and its result.
cards.answer: Archived maternal serum samples drawn about forty years earlier and stored at minus 80 degrees; offspring were traced and their diagnoses established; influenza-antibody-positive mothers had offspring with a sevenfold higher rate of schizophrenia.

cards.prompt: Match each degree of relationship to the lifetime risk of schizophrenia.
pairs: Monozygotic twin or both parents affected

cards.text: Schizophrenia risk combines {{rare, large-effect}} mutations with {{common}} variants of individually small effect, most of them in non-coding regions of the genome.

cards.prompt: Which genetic variant carries a genotype relative risk for schizophrenia of about 20 but is too rare to be useful in general practice?
How does the heritability of schizophrenia compare with other conditions, and to what does the 80% figure apply?
cards.answer: About 80%, comparable to autism and higher than height, heart disease and depression (about 30 to 35%). It applies to schizophrenia alone, not to the whole spectrum.

cards.text: The strongest SNP-based genetic correlation among psychiatric disorders is between schizophrenia and {{bipolar disorder}} at about {{0.70}}; the only uncorrelated pair is anorexia and ADHD.

cards.prompt: What did the Minnesota study of twins reared apart show about personality, and what was the negative control?
cards.answer: Identical twins correlated equally whether reared apart or together on personality questionnaires (ratios about 1.0), so genetics accounts for about 50% of personality variation and shared family environment for 1 to 9%; fingerprint ridge count (ratio 1.01) was the negative control. IQ did not follow the pattern (ratio 0.78).

cards.prompt: Which of the following are predictors of violence that operate across diagnoses?
options: Paranoia associated with a specific threat
Poor impulse control and threatened narcissism

cards.prompt: Match each forensic trajectory to its description and proportion.
pairs: Violent before the illness; conduct disorder, adversity, drugs
Violent only at or after onset; symptom-related
Violent after years of illness; treatment-resistant; often intra-familial homicide

cards.text: {{85%}} of forensic psychiatry patients have a psychotic illness; about {{40%}} of first-episode patients could have had criminal charges at presentation; {{one third}} of homicides by psychotic patients occur in the first episode.

cards.prompt: In what proportion of homicides is the perpetrator intoxicated with alcohol or other substances?

cards.text: Suicide risk in schizophrenia is about {{13}} times the general population with a lifetime risk near {{5%}}; overall mortality is two to three times, mostly from cardiovascular disease.

cards.prompt: Which features raise suicide risk in schizophrenia?
Where does schizophrenia rank as a cause of disability, and why is its burden out of proportion to its prevalence?
cards.answer: Fifth in established market economies, ninth worldwide. Early onset, lifetime disability and high medical burden mean many disability-adjusted life years per case.

cards.prompt: Why does finding an abnormality at every level of organisation in schizophrenia fail to explain the illness?
cards.answer: Because if every tool finds something, the findings do not identify a cause; behaviour is controlled at every level, unlike an atherosclerotic plaque, which has a simple pathophysiology.

cards.prompt: Match each mechanism to the symptom domain it produces in the integrated model.
pairs: Developmental cortical abnormality disrupting networks and learning
Working-memory deficit and generalised cognitive impairment
Aberrant dopamine release assigning importance to spurious events
Disturbed dopamine role in motivated behaviour

cards.text: The coarsest summary of the gross pathology of schizophrenia is {{bigger}} ventricles and {{smaller}} cortex, with the hippocampus and frontal cortex most affected.

cards.prompt: Which statements about the hippocampus are correct?
options: It contains place cells for spatial navigation
It encodes short-term memory of under two weeks
It shows ongoing adult neurogenesis and cell death
Its atrophy is specific to schizophrenia

cards.prompt: Which histological findings are described in schizophrenia?
options: Pyramidal neurons less dense in superficial layers and shifted deeper
Reduced GAD67 and GAT-1 interneuron markers

cards.prompt: Match each neuronal population to its migration route.
pairs: Radial migration along radial glia, inside-out
Tangential migration from the ganglionic eminences

cards.prompt: What evolutionary advantage did inside-out cortical lamination confer, and at what cost?
cards.answer: It allowed the brain to incorporate mutations that enlarge the cortex (outside-in lamination, found below the teleost fishes, cannot expand). The cost is fragility: the two migrating populations must intersect at the right time and place, so assembly can go wrong.

cards.text: In Walker's study, paediatric neurologists blind to adult diagnosis rated childhood home movies and found subtle {{soft neurological signs}} in the children who later developed schizophrenia, {{ten to fifteen}} years before onset; they cannot be used to screen because they are non-specific.

Cocaine and amphetamine act on the {{dopamine transporter}} much as an SSRI acts on the serotonin transporter; methamphetamine is also taken up by monoamine transporters and targets {{VMAT2}}, raising synaptic dopamine.

cards.prompt: Match each drug to its primary target.
What did Abi-Dargham's amphetamine-challenge study find in schizophrenia?
options: Equal baseline D2 availability but greater amphetamine-induced dopamine release (13.8% vs 7.1%)

cards.prompt: List four facts about ketamine given this week.
cards.answer: A veterinary and paediatric anaesthetic; an NMDA channel blocker that produces hallucinations at higher doses; used for ECT anaesthesia because it spares respiration; a one-dose antidepressant whose effect lasts about two weeks but can precipitate psychosis.

cards.prompt: Order the catecholamine synthetic pathway from precursor to final product.
How does dopamine encode reward expectancy?
cards.answer: An unexpected reward produces a spike of dopamine; an unexpected absence of reward produces a dip. Dopamine signals what to expect, and where to focus effort, rather than managing the movement itself.

cards.prompt: What relationship did Seeman's 1975 study establish across two dozen antipsychotics?
options: Clinical dose is inversely proportional to D2 receptor affinity
Clinical dose is proportional to serotonin affinity
Efficacy is proportional to molecular weight
Side effects are independent of dose

cards.prompt: In what order did the antipsychotics and the dopamine hypothesis arrive, and why does it matter?
cards.answer: The drugs were discovered by accident and the neuroscience was learned from them, not the reverse; the same is true of the antidepressants. Seeman's dose-affinity relationship then supplied an inductive proof that D2 is the target.

cards.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Neurons that fire together wire together
Strengthening through recruitment of AMPA receptors, instructed by NMDA
Weakening through internalisation of AMPA receptors
The smallest unit of memory Lashley searched for; the modern answer is the synapse

cards.prompt: What does the neural-net simulation of hallucination demonstrate?
cards.answer: That perturbing a simple speech-recognition network, trained by a pruning function like a real synapse, makes it report a word it was never shown: simple changes in circuits can generate complex symptoms.

cards.prompt: Match each dopamine pathway to the consequence of D2 blockade.
Match each pathway to its origin and terminus.
pairs: Ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens

cards.prompt: Three dopamine tracts or four pathways: how do the two counts reconcile?
cards.answer: Three tracts (mesolimbic and mesocortical combined) is one count; the standard four pathways are mesolimbic, mesocortical, nigrostriatal and tuberoinfundibular. Answer three tracts, four pathways; the practice quiz keys nigrostriatal for neurological side effects.

cards.text: The corticospinal tract was called the pyramidal tract because it {{decussates at the pyramids}}; motor inputs outside it are extrapyramidal, and the striatum stores the {{unconscious motor programs}} learned by practice.

cards.prompt: Which anticholinergic drugs are named for treating extrapyramidal side effects?
Why do high-potency antipsychotics raise prolactin, and what does it cause?
cards.answer: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release in the tuberoinfundibular pathway; D2 blockade removes the inhibition, producing hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea and menstrual disturbance.

cards.text: All dopamine receptors are G-protein-coupled; D1-like receptors {{raise}} adenylyl cyclase activity and D2-like receptors {{lower}} it.

cards.prompt: Dopamine receptors share homology with which receptor families, explaining the off-target effects of low-potency antipsychotics?
At which receptor do benzodiazepines act?

cards.text: D2 receptor binding is {{inversely}} proportional to the clinical dose: low-dose drugs have {{high}} affinity and their side effects come from decreased dopamine signalling; high-dose drugs have low affinity and their side effects come from non-dopamine receptor binding.

cards.prompt: Match each drug to its dose band and expected side-effect profile.
pairs: Single digits: EPS and prolactin elevation
Hundreds: sedation, hypotension, constipation, no EPS

cards.prompt: Match each off-target receptor to the side effect of a low-potency antipsychotic.
pairs: Constipation, dry mouth, dry eyes, and no EPS

cards.prompt: List the ten drugs on the potency slide with their daily dose ranges, from highest to lowest affinity.
cards.answer: Haloperidol 2 to 5; risperidone 6 to 9; paliperidone 6 to 12; fluphenazine 5 to 10; flupenthixol 10; olanzapine 20 to 30; loxapine 50 to 100; chlorpromazine 300 to 800; clozapine 300 to 600; quetiapine 600 to 900 mg.

cards.prompt: How do first- and second-generation antipsychotics differ in effectiveness and in adverse effects?
cards.answer: There is no difference in effectiveness and quality of life is similar at one year. First-generation drugs most commonly cause extrapyramidal symptoms; second-generation drugs most commonly cause weight gain and metabolic change. Laboratory monitoring is not needed for first-generation drugs.

cards.prompt: Which criteria have been proposed to define atypical antipsychotics?
Match each antipsychotic to its distinguishing note.
pairs: More effective for positive symptoms but high risk of EPS; QT prolongation
Agranulocytosis, myocarditis, seizures; reserved for refractory illness
Most weight gain but a lower discontinuation rate

cards.prompt: What boxed warning applies to every antipsychotic?
options: Increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis

cards.prompt: Match each extrapyramidal syndrome to its description.
pairs: Inner restlessness and inability to be still
Late chewing, lip pursing, tongue protrusion; typically irreversible

guide.s: propranolol, lorazepam, amantadine, benztropine and diphenhydramine

cards.prompt: Which drugs are used to treat extrapyramidal symptoms?
Define remission in schizophrenia as the review does.
cards.answer: A period of six months with no symptoms or mild symptoms that do not interfere with the person's behaviours.

cards.prompt: Put the steps of the refractory schizophrenia algorithm in order.
items: Little or no improvement after four weeks of treatment
Switch antipsychotic and repeat the trial for four to six weeks

cards.text: Response in the first {{two to four weeks}} is highly predictive of long-term response, but an adequate trial is at least {{four weeks}} at a therapeutic dose before stopping or switching.

cards.prompt: Which of the following does NICE guidance say should not be done?
options: Prescribe a loading dose of an antipsychotic
Start an antipsychotic in primary care for a first presentation without a psychiatrist
Offer CBT to all patients with schizophrenia

cards.prompt: What should patients be told about stopping antipsychotic therapy early?
cards.answer: There is a high risk of relapse if therapy is discontinued within one to two years.

cards.prompt: Match each formulation to its hazard ratio for rehospitalisation compared with no antipsychotic.
How often are long-acting injectable antipsychotics given?
cards.answer: Every two weeks or every month; the longest last up to three months.

cards.prompt: Which are serious adverse effects of clozapine?
options: QT prolongation as its signature effect

cards.prompt: List the de-escalation strategies for an agitated psychotic patient.
cards.answer: Casual, friendly, respectful, non-judgemental, non-confrontational approach; say you're not in trouble, we're here to help; find common ground; do not argue with delusions but do not agree with or support them; listen actively.

cards.prompt: Which two drugs top both the overall-symptom and positive-symptom efficacy plots?

guide.t: 3 · Choosing among the drugs: efficacy against weight

cards.prompt: Match each antipsychotic to its weight change against placebo.

guide.t: 3 · Choosing among the drugs: efficacy against weight

cards.text: Second-generation weight gain is usually {{rapid in the first few weeks}} and then plateaus, but can continue for {{a year or more}}; metabolic effects are not dose-dependent.

guide.t: 3 · Choosing among the drugs: efficacy against weight

cards.prompt: Match each screening component to its schedule on a second-generation antipsychotic.
Match each psychosocial intervention to its stated indication.
pairs: Reduce relapse and hospitalisation in the severely ill
Symptom reduction or relapse prevention, though uncommon

guide.s: numbers needed to treat of 7 and 12

cards.prompt: What did combining psychosocial treatment with medication do to discontinuation and relapse in the Chinese trial cited by the review?
cards.answer: Reduced both: absolute risk reductions of 14% and 8%, numbers needed to treat of 7 and 12; it also improved adherence, insight and quality of life and reduced admissions.

cards.prompt: Which comorbid disorders are more common in schizophrenia, and what do SSRIs do for them?
cards.answer: Anxiety disorders, panic symptoms, PTSD and OCD; SSRIs and anxiolytics help the comorbid mood and anxiety symptoms but do not treat schizophrenia itself.

cards.text: Only {{25%}} of patients stay on an antipsychotic for 18 months; in chronic schizophrenia under {{10%}} reach symptomatic and functional remission at 18 months; in first-episode schizophrenia under {{15%}} are in remission at five years.

cards.prompt: What does the review say about the proportion with a positive outcome and the proportion who remain symptomatic?
cards.answer: About 20% can expect a positive outcome; despite adequate treatment one third remain symptomatic; most need some support but most live independently; predictors of outcome are not understood.

cards.prompt: How should the finding that schizophrenia has better outcomes in low- and middle-income countries be read?
options: It names it and doubts it as likely an artefact of measurement biased toward higher-income countries
It accepts it as evidence that family structure cures schizophrenia
It attributes it to lower antipsychotic use

cards.prompt: Match each new antipsychotic to its mechanism.
pairs: Orthosteric M1/M4 muscarinic agonist; reduces VTA dopamine firing
Peripheral anticholinergic that blocks xanomeline's diarrhoea, sweating and drooling

cards.prompt: What point does the bar chart of mechanistically distinct drugs since the 1950s make?
cards.answer: Schizophrenia has stayed at about three distinct mechanisms while heart disease went from three or four to about fifteen; virtually all new antipsychotics are variations on old themes, hence the need for better treatments.

guide.t: 1 · Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems

cards.prompt: Match each WHO adverse-reaction type to its defining features.
pairs: Failure of therapy; absence of the intended effect

guide.t: 1 · Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems

cards.prompt: How do the WHO and Gell and Coombs classifications relate to each other?
cards.answer: Non-immune reactions use WHO Types A to F; immune reactions use Gell and Coombs Types I to IV. Every Gell and Coombs reaction is non-dose-related, unexpected and host-dependent, so every one is a WHO Type B.

guide.t: 1 · Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems

cards.text: Adverse drug reactions complicate {{5 to 15%}} of all drug management; the risk with antipsychotics is about {{three}} times that of other drugs; in 25 years {{10%}} of drugs have been withdrawn or given a black-box warning.

guide.t: 1 · Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems
guide.s: Onset time is the fastest discriminator

cards.prompt: Match each hypersensitivity type to its onset, reactant and name.
pairs: Minutes to hours; IgG against cell surfaces; cytotoxic
Hours; IgG immune complexes; serum sickness

guide.t: 1 · Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems
guide.s: II attacks a cell, III deposits a clump

cards.prompt: Both Type II and Type III reactions use IgG. How are they distinguished?
cards.answer: By the target: Type II antibody binds a cell-surface antigen and destroys that cell line (haemolytic anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia); Type III forms soluble immune complexes that deposit in tissue (serum sickness, glomerulonephritis, vasculitis). II attacks a cell, III deposits a clump.

cards.prompt: Put the four ADR management strategies in order, from least to most disruptive.
items: Continue the drug and add another to treat the symptoms

cards.prompt: Match each severity tier to its criteria.
pairs: No antidote or treatment; no medical attention
Change in treatment but not discontinuation; medical attention may or may not be needed
Discontinuation, specific treatment and medical attention required
Contributed directly or indirectly to death

guide.s: new drugs (under five years on the market)

cards.prompt: For which reactions should an individual practitioner prioritise a report to Health Canada?
options: A drug under five years on the market
A well-documented reaction to an older medication

cards.prompt: Match each prescription-writing error to the harm it causes.

guide.t: 3 · The case: one tablet, three serotonergic drugs
guide.s: one 20 mg tablet is a standard starting dose

cards.prompt: Why is the finding that only one citalopram tablet is missing the most important object in the case?
cards.answer: One 20 mg tablet is a standard starting dose, so the presentation is not an overdose and not citalopram toxicity alone; it must be an interaction with something already on board, which converts the question from how much she took to what else she is on.

guide.t: 3 · The case: one tablet, three serotonergic drugs

cards.prompt: Match each of the case's three agents to its serotonergic mechanism.

guide.t: 3 · The case: one tablet, three serotonergic drugs

cards.text: The patient's vitals were heart rate 115, blood pressure 150/100, respiratory rate 26 and temperature {{39 °C}}; she was oriented to {{person only}}, with logical thought and no hallucinations, showing the altered mental status was {{toxidrome-driven}}, not psychiatric.

cards.prompt: What is the clinical triad of serotonin syndrome, and how quickly does it begin?
cards.answer: Neuromuscular excitation, altered mental status and autonomic dysfunction; onset within one hour in about 28% of patients and within six hours in 61%.

cards.prompt: Match each finding to its tier on the serotonergic toxicity spectrum.
pairs: Hyperreflexia, tremor, myoclonus, diaphoresis, mydriasis, tachycardia
Inducible clonus, agitation, hypertension, hyperthermia under 40 °C, hyperactive bowel sounds
Rigidity, seizure, coma, confusion, hyperthermia at or above 40 °C

cards.prompt: Match each agent to its mechanism of raising serotonin.
pairs: A CYP inhibitor raising SSRI levels

cards.prompt: Which of these non-psychiatric drugs are listed as serotonergic?
What are the three principles for minimising the risk of serotonin syndrome?
cards.answer: A complete medication history including over-the-counter and natural products before prescribing; education and awareness, telling patients to check with a pharmacist before self-selecting products; and safe washout periods when switching agents, most concerning with MAO inhibitors.

cards.prompt: Beyond stopping the drugs, how is serotonin syndrome managed, and why do antipyretics fail?
cards.answer: Supportive care with fluids and monitoring, benzodiazepines for agitation, active cooling, cyproheptadine in moderate to severe cases, and sedation with intubation in the severest; antipyretics fail because the heat comes from muscle activity, not a hypothalamic set point, and restraints make it worse.

cards.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome has an incidence of {{0.01 to 0.2%}}, is fatal in {{6 to 10%}} if untreated, and {{30%}} of patients get rhabdomyolysis, with progression to acute kidney injury.

cards.prompt: Put the usual sequence of neuroleptic malignant syndrome in order.
What is the accepted mechanism of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: Decreased central dopaminergic transmission from D2 blockade or abrupt withdrawal of a dopamine agonist

cards.prompt: Match each distinct feature to the syndrome.
pairs: Lead-pipe rigidity in all muscle groups

cards.prompt: Which features are identical in serotonin syndrome and NMS, and what does that imply for a stem that gives only vitals?
cards.answer: Hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hyperthermia over 40 °C and hypersalivation are identical. A stem giving only vitals is undecidable; go back to the drug history, then the onset clock, then the reflexes.

cards.text: Serotonin syndrome begins abruptly within {{12 hours}}; NMS begins gradually over {{1 to 3 days}}.

guide.s: Malignant hyperthermia is the operating-room cousin

cards.prompt: How is malignant hyperthermia distinguished from serotonin syndrome and NMS?
cards.answer: It is a pharmacogenetic ryanodine-receptor reaction triggered by volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine in the operating room, with masseter spasm and rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, and no psychotropic exposure.

cards.prompt: Outline the management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
cards.answer: Stop the dopamine antagonist (or restart a withdrawn dopamine agonist), aggressive intravenous fluids to protect the kidneys, cooling, benzodiazepines, dantrolene for severe rigidity and hyperthermia, bromocriptine or amantadine, and ECT if refractory; check creatine kinase and renal function; restart a lower-potency agent no sooner than two weeks after resolution.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders

cards.prompt: How are personality disorders other than borderline examined, and which two are asked most often?
cards.answer: By gestalt, with obvious prompts, rather than by criteria; narcissistic personality disorder and borderline personality disorder are the two most commonly asked.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders

cards.text: Two acronyms exist for the borderline criteria, in the way {{MSIGECAPS}} serves depression and {{GSTPAID}} serves bipolar disorder.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders

cards.prompt: Are personality disorders different in kind from other psychiatric disorders?
cards.answer: No. Older DSM editions put them on a separate axis with lifelong conditions such as what is now intellectual disability; that is gone and they are ordinary DSM disorders.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders

cards.text: Patients with borderline personality disorder function at levels comparable to {{schizophrenia}}, and life expectancy is reduced by an estimated {{12 to 20}} years.

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders

cards.prompt: Match each condition to its positive-symptom picture.
pairs: Full delusions and full hallucinations in a constellation
Unusual beliefs and illusions the person can question; no full hallucinations
No positive symptoms; affective flattening and negative-type symptoms only

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders

cards.prompt: Can a person with a Cluster A personality disorder go on to develop schizophrenia?
options: No: if they develop schizophrenia, it was schizophrenia all along, before the age of onset
Yes, in about half of cases

guide.t: 1 · What the examiners want from personality disorders
guide.s: need not run across every relationship

cards.prompt: Must the unstable relationships of borderline personality disorder be present in every kind of relationship?
cards.answer: No. Romantic only, family only, or across the board all satisfy the criterion; the popular "favourite person" idea has no evidence base yet and may relate more to autism.

cards.prompt: Define validation and state its effect.
cards.answer: Expressing an understanding of what makes sense about what is going on for someone else; receiving validation decreases emotional arousal.

cards.text: Borderline personality disorder develops in part from {{emotional invalidation}}, so these patients are more sensitive to it; validation is the clinical corollary of the {{invalidating environment}} half of the biosocial model.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are NOT validation, according to the DBT teaching?
options: Reflecting back what the patient said

guide.s: The levels get more validating up the list

cards.prompt: Put the levels of validation in order from least to most validating.
items: Makes sense for this person given their context

guide.s: do not look at your computer

cards.prompt: What does the first level of validation consist of, and what practical advice comes with it?
cards.answer: Appearing interested: facial expression, posture, full attention; make eye contact, do not look bored, do not look at your computer. With a dysregulating patient, write the note afterwards, which may save time overall.

cards.prompt: How is simple reflection done well?
cards.answer: Reflect back a chunk of exactly what the person said, choosing the understandable part, then leave it there without jumping into questions or problem-solving; it feels uncomfortable at first, so practise it.

cards.text: Mind reading guesses at something the person has not said; often underneath anger is {{fear}}. It is riskier, so use {{tentative}} wording and back off if wrong.

cards.prompt: Why is "of course you're upset, anyone would be" preferred to "that makes sense, you've had a lot of breakups"?
cards.answer: The second is level 4, grounded in the person's history, and can itself invalidate by implying the reaction is about their pattern; the first is level 5, makes sense for anyone, the most validating level. Prefer 5 over 4 when both apply.

cards.prompt: List the six ways to be validating.
cards.answer: Show interest; reflective statements; mindreading statements; statements that show something makes sense in a context; normalizing statements; be genuine, authentic, cheerleading. The live teaching presented the first five as levels and omitted the sixth.

guide.s: validate the emotion, not its size

cards.prompt: How do you validate a patient whose emotion is wildly out of proportion, for example throwing chairs?
cards.answer: There is always a grain of truth; validate the emotion, not its size: not "it makes sense you're so angry you're throwing chairs" but "I can see how angry you are right now, and it seems it's because I'm going on vacation."

cards.text: When nothing else fits, {{emotions are always valid}}: with a patient with schizophrenia the delusion is not validated, but "I can see how {{scared}} you are" is.

cards.prompt: Why "and" rather than "but" after a validating statement?
options: "But" dismisses all the validation that came before it
"But" is too informal for clinical use

guide.s: weave a validating statement in before anything else

cards.prompt: What was the lesson of the two-take fracture-clinic role play?
cards.answer: Weave a validating statement in before anything else, then use the and-statement to be helpful: validate the patient's wish to cover her whole list and to take her diuretic properly, and at the same time propose one item at a time and restarting the drug even if doses are sometimes missed; some doses beat none.

cards.prompt: Why is validation not merely a nice soft skill?
cards.answer: It makes assessment faster and more effective: a vomiting, suicidal patient too distressed to be examined settled once validated, and the medical assessment could then proceed.

cards.text: {{20%}} of children experience a mental health disorder; {{70%}} of adults with psychiatric disorders had onset before 18; only {{one in five}} Canadian children receive appropriate mental health services.

cards.prompt: What are the peak age of onset of mental illness and the proportion with onset by 25, and which age group accesses services least?
cards.answer: Peak onset at 15; up to 75% by age 25; youth are less likely than any other age group to access mental health services, blocked by stigma, low literacy, poor access and system structure.

cards.prompt: Which early-intervention programmes are named?
options: Universal school screening with the PHQ-9

cards.prompt: Match each developmental stage to the interview technique.
pairs: Play remains important but the child is more capable of dialogue

cards.prompt: List the rapport-building techniques for a child interview.
cards.answer: Age-appropriate plain language without jargon; play, art and drawing; offer a break, water or a snack; a friendly introduction such as "I am a doctor who helps kids and teens with big feelings"; structure and frame.

guide.s: three wishes, hopes for the future

cards.prompt: Which items are specific additions to the paediatric psychiatric history?
options: Three wishes, hopes for the future
Past personal history of pregnancy, delivery and temperament

cards.prompt: Expand the HEADSS mnemonic.
cards.answer: Home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide and self-harm.

cards.text: In the history of presenting illness, listen for at least the {{first five minutes}}, then enquire about each symptom category and ask about safety: suicidal ideation with {{plan and intent}}, homicidal ideation, and self-harm past and present.

cards.prompt: Match each milestone to its age.
Which three medical conditions does the paediatric history template single out, and why?
cards.answer: Asthma, seizures and traumatic brain injury: the conditions that change psychiatric management or mimic psychiatric illness.

cards.answer: Concern about safety: harm to yourself, harm to others, safety of young children under 16, and driving safety.

cards.text: Under the Health Care Consent Act, 1996, capacity means the ability to {{understand}} the treatment and {{appreciate}} the consequences of treatment versus no treatment; it is {{presumed}} and there is no minimum age.

cards.prompt: Which statements about mandatory reporting under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017 are correct?
options: The threshold is reasonable grounds to suspect, not proof
The report is made immediately and directly to a Children's Aid Society
The physician must not rely on anyone else to report
A further report is required on new grounds
The duty applies to children under 16
The duty applies to all patients under 18

cards.prompt: In the case, who consented to sharing the diagnostic impression with the parents, and why?
cards.answer: The 15-year-old herself, because a capable minor consents to her own care and disclosure in Ontario; she hardly spoke with parents present, shared alone, then gave informed consent to discuss the impression all together.

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

cards.text: Anxiety disorders affect {{6 to 10%}} of children with a median onset at {{11}}; lifetime prevalence is 20 to 30%, female more than male after {{puberty}}.

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

cards.prompt: How does social anxiety disorder present in a child?
cards.answer: Crying, tantrums, freezing, clinging or shrinking in peer settings; difficulty with school participation and presentations, ordering food, eating in public, using the phone.

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

cards.prompt: Match each disorder to its duration threshold.

guide.t: 1 · Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

cards.prompt: What paediatric clues point to generalised anxiety disorder?
cards.answer: Worries about performance, school and sports; somatic symptoms; reassurance seeking; perfectionism and high standards; difficulty with transitions.

guide.s: mood, sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicide

cards.prompt: Expand the depression symptom mnemonic MSIGECAPS.
cards.answer: Mood, sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicide.

cards.prompt: How does the youth depression phenotype differ from the adult one?
cards.answer: More irritability, labile mood, loss of energy, somatic symptoms, appetite and sleep change, as against adult anhedonia and low mood; children show more somatic concern, anxiety and psychomotor agitation, adolescents more hypersomnia and mood reactivity.

cards.text: More than {{60%}} of youth with major depressive disorder have a comorbid mental health diagnosis, and onset before adulthood predicts more episodes, admissions, self-harm and worse {{physical health}} including obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

cards.prompt: Match each depression statistic to its figure.
What proportion of youth self-report suicidal ideation, by sex?
cards.answer: 5.5% of males and 10.7% of females.

cards.prompt: What did the 2023 and 2024 Canadian data show about youth mental health?
cards.answer: In 2023 about a fifth of youth who reported good mental health in 2019 now reported fair or poor, with bigger declines in girls, older teens and transitional-aged youth; in 2024, 36% of children and youth aged 2 to 17 who needed mental health care had partially or completely unmet needs, more so for girls.

cards.prompt: Match each organic cause to the presentation it mimics.
pairs: Hypothyroidism, anaemia, vitamin deficiencies, chronic pain

cards.text: The baseline panel for anxiety and depression includes CBC, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, liver and lipid profiles, {{ferritin}}, {{TSH}}, and {{B12 and folate}}.

cards.prompt: Which psychotherapy is the gold standard for youth anxiety and depression, and which is the named alternative for depression?

guide.s: sleeping enough, eating enough and moving enough

cards.prompt: What is the lifestyle prescription for youth with anxiety or depression?
cards.answer: Sleeping enough, eating enough and moving enough, alongside psychoeducation, safety planning, and school and family involvement.

cards.prompt: Which are printed indications for adding an SSRI to CBT in youth?
Which side effects of SSRIs in youth are listed?
options: Suicidal ideation, mania and serotonin syndrome (rare, serious)

cards.prompt: What is the difference between the FDA black-box warning and Health Canada's position on SSRIs in youth?
cards.answer: The FDA's 2004 boxed warning calls for close observation for emergent suicidality up to age 24; Health Canada has approved no SSRI for paediatric depression or anxiety, so prescribing is off-label. Two regulators, two distinct facts.

cards.prompt: How does the case resolution tie back to the management framework?
cards.answer: The youth shares alone and consents to a joint discussion; the family accepts major depressive disorder and is open to individual and family therapy; medication is considered; follow-up in two weeks reflects the black-box observation; and the safety plan names the emergency department if acutely unsafe, distraction and asking for help.

cards.prompt: Define executive functioning.
cards.answer: Processes for managing ourselves and our internal resources in order to achieve a goal.

cards.prompt: Which are among the nine executive-function domains?
Match each executive-function domain to its clinical example.
pairs: Not checking the phone during rounds
Managing several patients' acuity at once in the emergency department
Remembering the history until you can chart
Spotting holes in a history and going after them
Keeping track of the stethoscope on the wards

cards.text: Executive functioning runs on distributed networks: the {{prefrontal cortex}} is the mainframe, the {{parietal cortex}} decides what holds attention, and the basal ganglia, thalamus and {{cerebellum}} complete the network.

cards.prompt: Match each category behind executive dysfunction to its example.

cards.text: ADHD symptoms occur often, for at least {{6 months}}, in {{2 or more}} settings, with several present before age {{12}}; 6 or more of 9 in a domain, or 5 or more at age 17 and older.

guide.s: 5 to 8% of youth and 2 to 4% of adults

cards.prompt: What is the prevalence of ADHD in youth and in adults, and how stable is it across cultures?
cards.answer: 5 to 8% of youth and 2 to 4% of adults; prevalence is similar across cultures and has been stable for thirty years.

cards.prompt: Which are inattention symptoms of ADHD?
How are the hyperactivity items rephrased for adults?
cards.answer: A child's running and climbing becomes feeling restless; difficulty playing quietly becomes difficulty doing fun things quietly; the internal need to move is suppressed with effort.

cards.text: Across the lifespan hyperactivity and impulsivity become {{more internalised}}; {{female and gender-diverse}} patients have more internalised symptoms that are harder to spot or attributed to other diagnoses.

cards.prompt: Rank the three factors that unmask ADHD at a transition, most important first.
items: Increased available distraction and immediate rewards

cards.prompt: Which academic effects of ADHD are cited?
options: Lower writing quality even after controlling for impulsive mistakes
Less secondary-school support than students with learning disabilities

cards.prompt: Match each substance use pattern to what it suggests in a patient with possible ADHD.
pairs: Cannabis at the end of the day
Ten caffeinated drinks a day with minimal or paradoxical effect
Self-medication of ADHD via adenosine antagonism

cards.prompt: How does caffeine act, and what response patterns suggest ADHD?
cards.answer: Caffeine antagonises adenosine, an inhibitory transmitter, raising dopamine and glutamate; extensive use without a use disorder, a minimal response (asleep despite late caffeine) or a paradoxical response (fatigue) all suggest ADHD.

cards.prompt: What is the effect of cannabis in ADHD?
cards.answer: Some perceive short-term improvement of the scattered mind and almost as many perceive worsening; the majority of both groups eventually report problems with motivation, sometimes called marijuana amotivation syndrome.

cards.text: In a 2019 survey of over 55,000 Canadian post-secondary students, {{4.5%}} had taken a stimulant not prescribed to them; stimulant challenge tests are {{not}} part of an ADHD assessment and a positive response is not diagnostic.

cards.prompt: How does the menstrual cycle affect ADHD symptoms?
cards.answer: In the follicular phase rising oestrogen and testosterone bring motivation, confidence and focus; premenstrually falling oestrogen and progesterone bring poor focus and dysregulated mood, and some patients need a dose adjustment across the cycle.

cards.prompt: Which are the screening principles for adult ADHD?
options: Physician interview, collateral and mental status examination
No perfect questionnaire; questionnaires are age-specific
Past and present symptoms on the same form
Collateral from report cards and a parent or partner
A positive stimulant trial confirms the diagnosis

guide.s: higher negative than positive predictive value

cards.prompt: Describe the structure and scoring of the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, and its predictive limits.
cards.answer: 18 items rated never to very often over the past six months; items 1 to 6 are Part A, and 4 or more positive on Part A is a positive screen; higher negative than positive predictive value, so it rules out better than it rules in and false positives are common.

cards.prompt: What does the CADDRA ADHD checklist add after a positive screen, and why are childhood and current symptoms rated on one form?
cards.answer: The DSM criteria rated 0 to 3 in each domain, with columns for retrospective childhood symptoms and current symptoms; rating both together is how onset before age 12 is confirmed, and it shows which symptoms improved or worsened entering adulthood.

cards.prompt: The worked checklist scored 6 of 9 for attention and 2 of 9 for hyperactivity. Which presentation is that?

guide.s: Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults

cards.prompt: Which structured interview is named for the adult ADHD assessment?
cards.answer: The Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults (DIVA).

cards.text: ADHD treatment is {{multimodal}}, combining education, medication and behavioural or psychotherapeutic work, and {{collaborative}} among physician, patient and family; {{psychoeducation}} is the first intervention.

cards.prompt: Which are among the twelve psychoeducation moves?
options: Promote exercise, sleep hygiene and nutrition
Prescribe a stimulant at the first visit

guide.s: Suffering does not correlate with functional impairment

cards.prompt: Why does grieving the ADHD diagnosis matter, and what three questions guide treatment?
cards.answer: Diagnosis can be stigmatising, brings mourning for past struggles and questions about the true self; suffering does not correlate with functional impairment, priorities differ by developmental task, and grief is under-addressed. Ask what the diagnosis has meant, what they believe about themselves (unreliable, unmotivated, incapable versus creative, spontaneous, flexible), and what they are good at, what is not needing treatment.

cards.prompt: What are the sources of motivation in ADHD, and which are unhealthy?
cards.answer: Negative self-talk (brief motivation, worse self-concept), procrastination pressure (overcomes inertia, lowers quality), caffeine and other stimulants, cannabis to switch off, and exercise; the question is whether motivation can be made healthier.

cards.prompt: By what system does body doubling build motivation?

guide.s: higher motivation than others when stimulated

cards.text: Gamification turns the mundane into something interesting so the goal becomes {{salient}}; patients with ADHD often have {{higher}} motivation than others when stimulated. Streak charts and time trials are examples.

guide.s: decrease the distance to the reward

cards.prompt: What two distances does the distraction strategy adjust?
cards.answer: Increase the distance between the student and the distraction (noise-cancelling headphones, coping cards, sitting at the front) and decrease the distance between the student and the reward.

guide.s: risk of derailing with every task switch

cards.prompt: What is the reality of multitasking for a person with ADHD?
cards.answer: Risk of derailing with every task switch, less efficiency than we think, tasks started but not finished, and further guilt.

cards.text: Pomodoro: a specific goal, {{25}} minutes of work, {{5}} minutes of break, typically {{four}} cycles before a longer 30-minute break, with breaks spent standing or fetching water rather than on screens.

cards.prompt: Match each quadrant of the Eisenhower matrix to its example or handling.
pairs: Exams and taxes, neglected until they become crises
Circle it to make it salient, then break it down
Keep it visual on a whiteboard updated each evening

cards.prompt: What is wrong with guilt reminders, and what replaces them?
cards.answer: Guilt reminders ("I should be in bed by now") are unrealistic; sequential reminders replace them: 9 p.m. "Have I had dinner?", 10 p.m. "Bedtime in an hour, is what I'm doing aligned with that?" Ask where the reminder is, whether it can be more salient, and when the student gets derailed.

cards.text: Anxiety distracts the {{auditory-verbal}} working memory; methylphenidate may improve auditory working memory but with {{less}} effect when anxiety is comorbid, so use {{visual}} strategies instead of verbal.

cards.prompt: Match each CBT comparison to its response rates.
pairs: CBT versus relaxation and educational support
CBT versus supportive therapy without strategies
CBT added to a stimulant for comorbid depression and anxiety
Larger effect size; gains persist at 6 and 12 months

cards.prompt: How does the evidence for CBT differ between adults and adolescents with ADHD?
cards.answer: Adults have evidence for individual and group CBT, group mindfulness and coaching; adolescents have less evidence for individual CBT and more for school- and family-based interventions.

cards.prompt: Which products are first line in the CADDRA October 2024 table?
Match each product to its maximum dose on the CADDRA chart.
pairs: 30 mg children; 20 to 30 mg adolescents and adults
4 mg at 6 to 12; 7 mg at 13 to 17

cards.prompt: Match each product to its duration of action.
Match each drug class to its mechanism.
pairs: Inhibits VMAT2 and reverses the monoamine transporter, releasing dopamine and noradrenaline
Inhibits reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline
Postsynaptic alpha-2A agonist in the prefrontal cortex

cards.prompt: Recall the four points to share before starting a stimulant.
Turn "I want to be better with my readings and get better grades" into a SMART goal and say how it is monitored.
cards.answer: Four Pomodoro cycles of reading from a textbook: specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, time-based; monitored in 25-minute blocks by pages read, whether a page had to be reread for mind-wandering, note-taking afterwards and general attentiveness.

cards.prompt: What stimulant monitoring do the week's decks omit, and what does standard practice add?
cards.answer: Neither deck gives an adverse-effect list or schedule; standard practice monitors height, weight, heart rate and blood pressure at each visit, plus sleep, appetite, mood, tics and psychotic symptoms, and takes a cardiac history and family history of sudden death before starting.

cards.prompt: Which two resources are recommended for adult ADHD, and why do resources matter?
cards.answer: The Centre for ADHD Awareness, Canada (peer-led groups including for comorbid substance use, webinars on trauma, relationships and perimenopause, a resource navigator, a reading list) and eConsult, answered within seven days; a strategy effective in one environment can fail in another and ADHD bites at transitions, so supports must outlast the episode of care.

cards.prompt: Define attachment, and name the source of the definition.
cards.answer: The deep emotional bond that connects one person to another across time and space (Bowlby, 1958), shaped in early childhood through interactions with primary caregivers.

guide.s: caregiver presence, a stranger, and an exit

cards.prompt: What three elements does the Strange Situation manipulate, and who designed it?
cards.answer: Caregiver presence, a stranger, and an exit; Mary Ainsworth, 1970s. The classification is made from the reunion.

cards.prompt: Match each attachment style to its position on the anxiety and avoidance axes.

cards.text: Disorganised attachment is high on both axes and is the pattern most associated with {{frightening or frightened caregiver behaviour}}, maltreatment and later {{psychopathology}}.

cards.prompt: Match each feature of the case family to the attachment axis it loads.
pairs: Mother reacts and instructs when her daughter tries to share
Father's outbursts; parents avoid talking about emotions
Eight-week stay with grandparents at age 5
"Does not trust them, feels like a burden"

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health

cards.text: Up to {{95%}} of 13- to 17-year-olds use social media and almost a {{third}} use it almost constantly; nearly {{40%}} of 8- to 12-year-olds use it despite a minimum age of 13, for about 1.5 hours a day.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health

cards.prompt: Match each platform category to its share of youth online activity.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health

cards.prompt: Why are youth particularly vulnerable to social media?
cards.answer: Self-regulatory abilities are still developing; platforms are constantly accessible and immersive by design; and ages 10 to 19 are a critical, highly sensitive period of brain development.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health

cards.prompt: Which are the benefits of social media for youth?
options: Community with others who share identities and interests
Social support, especially for marginalised groups

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health

cards.prompt: What did the natural experiment of a new platform among US college students show?
cards.answer: Depression rose 9% and anxiety 12% over baseline, with 300,000 new cases of depression.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health

cards.prompt: Match each trial to its finding.
pairs: Limiting social media to 30 minutes a day for three weeks
Significant improvement in depression severity in transitional-aged youth
Deactivating social media for four weeks

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health

cards.prompt: State the take-home on social media harm.
cards.answer: Higher relative concern of harm in adolescent girls and those already experiencing poor mental health; cyberbullying-related depression, body image and disordered eating, and poor sleep quality related to use.

guide.t: 3 · Social media and youth mental health
guide.s: how much, on what, and is it displacing sleep

cards.prompt: What screening question and intervention does the social media evidence support?
cards.answer: Ask how much, on what, and whether it is displacing sleep and physical activity; the intervention is to cap use at about 30 minutes a day.

guide.s: Eight bones form the calvaria and cranial base

cards.prompt: Name the eight bones of the calvaria and cranial base.
cards.answer: Frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid.

cards.prompt: Match each suture to the bones it separates.

cards.text: The anterior fontanelle lies at the future {{bregma}}, where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet; the posterior fontanelle at the future {{lambda}}, where the sagittal and lambdoid sutures meet.

guide.s: Frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of sphenoid

cards.prompt: Which four bones meet at the pterion?
cards.answer: Frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and the greater wing of the sphenoid; it is the thinnest part of the vault.

cards.prompt: Order the route of the middle meningeal artery from its origin to the dura.
items: Periosteal layer of the dura, grooving the parietal bone

cards.prompt: Match each cranial fossa to its bones and contents.
pairs: Frontal, ethmoid, lesser wing of sphenoid; frontal lobes
Sphenoid and temporal; temporal lobes and pituitary
Occipital and petrous temporal; cerebellum, pons, medulla

guide.s: Three arteries enter through three openings

cards.prompt: Match each artery to its opening into the cranial cavity.
Which arterial systems supply the brain and which supplies the dura, and what follows for epidural bleeding?
cards.answer: The brain is supplied by the internal carotid and vertebral systems; the dura by the external carotid system through the middle meningeal artery; an epidural bleed is therefore an extracerebral, external-carotid-territory bleed.

cards.prompt: Which openings are in the sphenoid bone?
What are granular foveolae?
cards.answer: Pits in the inner table of the parietal bone beside the sagittal suture, made by arachnoid granulations; a dry-skull sign of CSF reabsorption.

cards.prompt: Match each internal bony landmark to the dural structure attached or related to it.
pairs: Tentorium cerebelli and superior petrosal sinus

guide.s: open sutures, patent fontanelles, tooth buds

cards.prompt: Which features indicate a skull radiograph is from a child?
options: Large vault relative to the face

cards.prompt: Match each meningeal layer to its description.
pairs: External layer of two layers, periosteal and meningeal
Thin avascular membrane lining the meningeal dura, with trabeculae to the pia; bridges sulci and strips easily
Innermost, adherent to the brain, dips into every sulcus, cannot be peeled

cards.prompt: Match each space to its status and pathological content.
pairs: Potential; arterial blood from a torn meningeal artery
Potential; venous blood from torn bridging veins
Real; fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus

cards.prompt: Order the layers from outside in.

guide.s: continuous with the pericranium through the sutures

cards.text: The periosteal dura is continuous with the {{pericranium}} through the sutures, which is why epidural blood {{stops at sutures}} while subdural blood crosses them.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses

cards.prompt: Match each dural partition to its description.
pairs: Separates the hemispheres; sits in the longitudinal fissure
Overlies the cerebellum; sits in the transverse fissure
Roofs the sella turcica and stabilises the pituitary
Separates the cerebellar hemispheres; named only in the lab

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses

cards.prompt: What passes through the tentorial notch, and what is the clinical consequence?
cards.answer: The midbrain; a supratentorial mass pushes the uncus through the notch, compressing the midbrain and the oculomotor nerve: ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral hemiparesis and falling consciousness.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses
guide.s: superior sagittal sinus in its upper margin

cards.text: The falx cerebri carries the {{superior sagittal}} sinus in its upper margin and the {{inferior sagittal}} sinus in its free margin; the {{straight}} sinus runs where falx meets tentorium.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses

cards.prompt: Match each sinus to the groove it leaves on the skull.
pairs: Deep S-shaped groove behind the petrous and mastoid temporal, heading to the jugular foramen
Horizontal groove on the internal occipital squama

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses
guide.s: from superior to inferior: oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic, maxillary

cards.prompt: Order the nerves in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus from superior to inferior.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses

cards.prompt: What does a pituitary macroadenoma produce as it grows upward, and as it grows laterally?
cards.answer: Upward: compression of the optic chiasm and bitemporal hemianopia. Laterally: invasion of the cavernous sinus with ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI) and ophthalmic and maxillary sensory loss. The sphenoidal sinus below is the trans-sphenoidal corridor.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses
guide.s: CSF is extruded into venous blood across the arachnoid granulations

cards.prompt: Where does CSF re-enter the venous system, and what marks the site on the skull?
cards.answer: Across the arachnoid granulations projecting into the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral venous lacunae; the granular foveolae are their imprints on the parietal bone.

guide.t: 3 · Dural reflections and the venous sinuses
guide.s: pterygoid plexus and deep facial vein

cards.prompt: Besides the ophthalmic veins, what is the second venous route from the face to the cavernous sinus?
cards.answer: The pterygoid plexus and the deep facial vein, labelled on the danger-triangle diagram.

guide.t: 1 · From neural tube to adult brain

cards.prompt: Match each secondary vesicle to its adult derivative.

guide.t: 1 · From neural tube to adult brain

cards.text: By the {{fourth}} week there are three primary brain vesicles: the {{prosencephalon}} (forebrain), the mesencephalon (midbrain) and the {{rhombencephalon}} (hindbrain).

guide.t: 1 · From neural tube to adult brain

cards.prompt: State the adult groupings of forebrain, hindbrain and brainstem.
cards.answer: Forebrain is the cerebral hemispheres plus the diencephalon; hindbrain is the brainstem plus the cerebellum; the brainstem is midbrain, pons and medulla.

guide.t: 1 · From neural tube to adult brain

cards.prompt: Why do dorsal and ventral mean different things in the forebrain and the brainstem?
cards.answer: The human nervous system has two longitudinal axes bent at the midbrain, so rostral, caudal, dorsal and ventral each appear twice: dorsal is superior in the forebrain and posterior in the brainstem and cord; superior, inferior, anterior and posterior are absolute.

guide.t: 1 · From neural tube to adult brain
guide.s: Two fissures pair with two dural partitions

cards.prompt: Match each fissure to the dural partition that occupies it.

guide.s: Three sulci divide the lateral surface

cards.prompt: Match each sulcus or fissure to the lobes it separates.
Which sulci are named on the medial surface?

cards.text: The {{calcarine}} sulcus lies in the occipital lobe on the medial surface, and the primary {{visual}} cortex lies on its banks.

guide.s: cerebral cortex (grey matter), subcortical white matter and basal nuclei

cards.prompt: What are the three components of a cerebral hemisphere?
cards.answer: Cerebral cortex (grey matter), subcortical white matter, and basal nuclei (grey matter).

cards.prompt: Match each gyrus to its function and position.
pairs: Primary motor area, anterior to the central sulcus
Primary somatosensory area, posterior to the central sulcus

cards.prompt: State the three lateralisation rules.
cards.answer: The hemispheres are anatomically similar but functionally different; the dominant hemisphere controls language, the left in most people; each hemisphere controls voluntary movement of, and receives sensation from, the contralateral side.

guide.t: 3 · Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres

cards.prompt: Match each region to its grey and white matter arrangement.
pairs: Grey superficial as cortex plus deep nuclei; white matter deep
Grey central in horns; white matter superficial in columns or funiculi

guide.t: 3 · Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres

cards.prompt: Match each class of subcortical fibre to what it connects and its named example.
pairs: Homologous regions of the two hemispheres; corpus callosum, anterior commissure
Cortex to subcortical structures, brainstem and cord; corona radiata and internal capsule
Regions within one hemisphere; no named bundle

guide.t: 3 · Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres

cards.prompt: Order the parts of the corpus callosum and its forceps from front to back.
items: Forceps minor into the frontal lobes
Forceps major into the occipital lobes

guide.t: 3 · Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres

cards.prompt: Match each part of the internal capsule to its boundaries or content.
pairs: Between the head of the caudate medially and the lentiform laterally
The medial apex of the V; corticobulbar fibres
Between the thalamus medially and the lentiform laterally; corticospinal tract

guide.t: 3 · Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres

cards.text: On an axial section the internal capsule appears as a {{V pointing medially}}, with the {{lentiform}} nucleus in its angle laterally.

cards.prompt: List the three functions of cerebrospinal fluid, and where it is produced.
cards.answer: It supports and cushions the brain, transports nutrients to and waste from it, and exchanges continuously with the parenchyma; it is produced by the choroid plexus within the ventricles.

cards.prompt: Which are parts of the lateral ventricle?
Match each ventricular passage to its eponym and number.
pairs: Foramen of Monro; one each side
Aqueduct of Sylvius; through the midbrain

cards.prompt: Order the flow of cerebrospinal fluid from production to venous return.
items: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricles

cards.text: The third ventricle is surrounded by the {{thalamus}}; the lateral ventricles are separated by the {{septum pellucidum}}.

cards.prompt: Match each cistern to its location.
pairs: Between the cerebral peduncles, in front of the midbrain
Behind the midbrain, beneath the splenium
Between the cerebellum and the medulla

cards.prompt: Match each hydrocephalus type to its mechanism and ventricular pattern.
pairs: Block within the ventricular system; upstream ventricles dilate, downstream do not
Absorption fails at the arachnoid granulations, after subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis; all ventricles dilate

guide.t: 5 · Lab specimens and the wet brain

cards.prompt: Which subdivision of the brainstem passes through the tentorial notch?
cards.answer: The midbrain.

guide.t: 5 · Lab specimens and the wet brain

cards.prompt: Which structures are identified in the cranial meninges dissection?

guide.s: brain tissue, blood within vessels, CSF, and "other"

cards.prompt: Name the four non-compressible components of the Monro-Kellie hypothesis.
cards.answer: Brain tissue, blood within vessels, CSF, and "other", the added pathology such as a haematoma, tumour, abscess or oedema.

cards.prompt: Which pathologies throw off the intracranial pressure-volume relationship?

cards.text: Ultrasound is useless for the adult brain because it is blocked by {{cortical bone}}; the exception is the {{neonate}}, imaged through the fontanelle.

cards.prompt: What are the three stated indications for contrast on CT or MRI of the brain?
cards.answer: To examine vasculature, and to improve the visibility of underlying inflammation or of lesions.

cards.prompt: A trauma patient needs the facial bones assessed. What must be done beyond a CT head?
cards.answer: Request a CT facial bones separately; a CT head does not include all the facial structures by default.

guide.s: direct brain injury, haemorrhage and herniation, infection, and CSF leakage

cards.prompt: Which are the four concerns about a skull fracture's impact?
options: Direct injury to the underlying brain

cards.prompt: Which are headache red flags requiring emergent imaging?
Which are the six herniation routes?

guide.s: direct compression or by vascular compromise

cards.prompt: By what two mechanisms does herniation damage the brain?
cards.answer: Direct compression of the fragile parenchyma, and secondary vascular compromise when supplying vessels are crushed.

guide.s: the brainstem sits at its outlet

cards.text: A relatively small posterior fossa bleed is disproportionately dangerous because the {{compartment}} is small and the {{brainstem}} sits at its outlet; the tonsils descend through the foramen magnum.

guide.s: tonsillar descent appears with both high pressure

cards.prompt: Why is cerebellar tonsillar descent not exclusively a high-pressure sign?
cards.answer: It appears with high pressure from a posterior fossa mass, and with low pressure when a dural tear leaks CSF and the brain sags.

cards.prompt: Order the meningeal layers from outside in.
Match each haemorrhage to its shape and suture behaviour.
pairs: Lens-shaped, biconvex; does not cross sutures
Serpiginous, layering in the sulci along the gyri
Round hyperdense lesion within the brain substance

cards.prompt: Which are the five common causes of intraparenchymal haemorrhage?

cards.text: On CT, haemorrhage is usually {{bright}} because the clot is {{denser}} than the surrounding brain; localising the space tells you the cause.

cards.prompt: Why does epidural blood stop at sutures while subdural blood crosses them?
cards.answer: The dura is stuck to the skull at the sutures, so blood beneath the periosteal dura is trapped between sutures as a lens, while blood under the dura spreads freely across sutures as a crescent.

guide.s: A single trauma CT can carry all four

cards.prompt: Give the one-liner for naming each compartment of blood on a trauma CT.
cards.answer: Lens and suture-bounded: epidural. Crescent following the inner table: subdural. Blood in sulci, fissures and cisterns: subarachnoid. Blood inside the brain: intraparenchymal.

guide.s: increase in the volume of CSF

cards.prompt: Define hydrocephalus and state where CSF is absorbed.
cards.answer: An increase in the volume of CSF causing distension of the cerebral ventricles, producing mass effect that can lead to herniation; CSF is absorbed into the venous system through the arachnoid villi and granulations.

guide.s: Look at which ventricles are big

cards.prompt: Match each ventricular pattern to its cause.
pairs: Lateral and third dilated, fourth normal
All ventricles dilated after a bleed
Lateral ventricles dilated with a mass at the foramen of Monro

cards.prompt: How is obstructive hydrocephalus treated?
cards.answer: Remove the obstruction, or place a ventricular drain to provide an alternative pathway for drainage.

cards.prompt: Match each mass location to its description.
pairs: Outside the parenchyma, seen pushing the brain away and buckling the cortex inward

cards.text: Most brain neoplasms are soft-tissue density and hard to characterise on non-contrast CT, so {{contrast CT or MRI}} is usually required, and often only {{pathology}} determines the type.

cards.prompt: Match each brain infection to its imaging appearance.
pairs: Thickened enhancing meninges over the cortex
Hazy parenchymal signal without a discrete rim
A bright rim lining the ventricle
A thick ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema

cards.prompt: How does infection reach the brain, and why is treatment difficult?
cards.answer: By violating the blood-brain barrier or the skull, through trauma or advanced superficial infection such as sinusitis or mastoiditis; treatment is difficult because many drugs cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: Define critical appraisal.
cards.answer: The process that allows us to evaluate medical evidence to decide whether a research article is useful for informed decisions about care that is unique, and relevant to the individual patient we are caring for.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: Which inputs have equal footing in evidence-informed practice?
options: Clinical expertise (the integrator, not an input)

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: Order the evidence pyramid from top to bottom.
items: Case-control studies, case series and reports

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.text: CASP, the {{Critical Appraisal Skills Programme}}, is a set of {{ten}} checklists, one per study design; the spine is valid, results, {{relevant}} to the specific cases.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: Match each checklist to its section mapping.
pairs: Valid A; results B; relevance C
Valid A and B; results C; relevance D

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: Match each paper to its design and detail.
pairs: Cohort of 29,823 patients with schizophrenia; Finnish register, within-individual comparison
Lieberman, New England Journal of Medicine 2005
Randomised controlled trial in chronic schizophrenia; CATIE; high discontinuation

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: Match each case of the week to its label.
pairs: 23-year-old student, months of withdrawal, devices watching him, father with schizophrenia
33-year-old brought by police in one shoe, positive for cannabis and methamphetamine
54-year-old on long-acting paliperidone, 30 pounds heavier, lip puckering
33-year-old game designer in remission on risperidone, sexual side effects

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: What are the two limitation headings and their four bullets?
cards.answer: Are the articles outdated: the doses used, and newer antipsychotics not included. Are they generalisable: different health care systems, and applicability to only one point in time.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: What are the central threats to a register-based cohort of antipsychotic effectiveness?
cards.answer: Confounding by indication, where sicker patients get the newer or stronger drug, and immortal time bias; ask what confounder would explain the result and whether it was measured.

guide.t: 1 · Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

cards.prompt: Which methodological problems are specific to psychiatry trials?
options: Rating-scale outcomes whose significance may be clinically trivial
Blinding that fails when a drug sedates or causes weight gain
Depot-versus-oral comparisons confounding pharmacology with adherence

guide.s: forget the idea of interviewing from a checklist

cards.prompt: What is the rule about checklists and the order of presentation?
cards.answer: Do not confuse the order of the presentation with the sequence of information-gathering: gather organically, never interview from a checklist, but use one towards the end or afterwards to check what you have.

cards.prompt: Match each history domain to its mental status examination counterpart.
pairs: Speech, thought process, thought content, perception

cards.prompt: Order the diagnostic hierarchy from the top rung down.
State the five appraisal questions of the psychiatric assessment.
cards.answer: How dangerous is the condition; how great is the functional impairment; what is the immediate psychosocial context; what physical factors are at play; who is the person with the sickness.

cards.prompt: Which are the key phrases for the interview?
options: You're doing well, let's keep going
In the interest of time, I may ask questions more quickly
I apologise if I interrupt you
What you're talking about is important

cards.prompt: What does the interview opening contain?
cards.answer: Name and role, purpose, circumstances, the limits of confidentiality, and thanks; identifying data then include living situation, relationship status, children, income and occupation, and inpatient or outpatient with voluntary or involuntary status.

guide.s: describe for me what that's like

cards.prompt: Give the two scripted lines for the chief concern and the phenomenology probe.
cards.answer: "Please tell me about the concerns that you've had recently" and "describe for me what that's like; how do you experience it?"

guide.s: number, severity, medical intervention and most recent

cards.text: Past suicide attempts are quantified by {{number}}, {{severity}}, medical intervention and {{most recent}}; substance use records first, typical and last use and periods of abstinence.

guide.s: most of the day, nearly every day

cards.prompt: Give the two scripted depression screening stems.
cards.answer: "Have you ever had 2 weeks or more when you felt sad or low, for most of the day, nearly every day?" and "Have you ever had 2 weeks or more when you lost interest in things, for most of the day, nearly every day?"

cards.prompt: Match each delusion type to its scripted probe, each beginning "Has it ever seemed that".
pairs: people are after you or doing bad things to you
some outside force is controlling your actions or thoughts
you have special traits or abilities
things happen because of you, or people are talking about you
your thoughts are taken out of your head by some outside force
something has changed in your body recently

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk

cards.prompt: Order the twelve headings of the mental status examination write-up.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk

cards.prompt: Which are the four axes of affect?
options: Congruence with mood and thought content

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk
guide.s: circumstantial, tangential, loosening of associations, word salad

cards.prompt: Order the disorganisation of thought process from least to most severe.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk

cards.prompt: Define insight and judgement as the guide does, and state the grading.
cards.answer: Insight is the ability to realise one has a mental health concern and to appreciate its implications, two parts; judgement is recent behaviour as it relates to safety, social functioning and treatment decisions; both are graded none or impaired, partial, intact or full.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk
guide.s: active (plans for suicide) against passive (thoughts of death)

cards.text: Suicidal ideation is classified as acute against chronic, and as active, meaning {{plans for suicide}}, against passive, meaning {{thoughts of death}}; the script ends on {{protective factors}}.

guide.t: 3 · The mental status examination and risk

cards.prompt: What does the case presentation require after the history and mental status examination?
cards.answer: A two- to three-sentence summary of the most pertinent historical and mental state findings, a diagnostic impression, and a biopsychosocial plan covering medication, therapy and lifestyle that is feasible and mitigates safety concerns.

guide.s: two of five symptoms for a month

cards.prompt: State the schizophrenia criteria in one line.
cards.answer: Two of five symptoms for a month within six months of disturbance with functional decline; schizophreniform under six months; delusional disorder without hallucinations; a found cause moves the case out of the schizophrenias.

cards.prompt: What prevalence of schizophrenia should be answered, and what does the patient-educators' "1 in 10" refer to?
cards.answer: 0.5% on a lecture-based item, 0.5 to 1% on a quiz-style item; 1 in 10 refers to psychotic experiences in the population, not to any disorder.

cards.prompt: The criteria taught are DSM-IV-TR. What did DSM-5 change?
cards.answer: At least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech is required; the single bizarre-delusion or Schneiderian carve-out was removed; the subtypes were removed.

cards.prompt: Which antipsychotic dose figures should be used for the digit rule, and which when a stem quotes licensed ranges?
cards.answer: Haloperidol 2 to 5, olanzapine 20 to 30, clozapine 300 to 600, quetiapine 600 to 900 mg for the digit rule; the licensed ranges (AFP review) when a stem quotes them.

cards.prompt: Match each disputed point to the answer to give.
pairs: Median aperture plus paired lateral apertures

cards.prompt: Which dopamine pathway is responsible for the neurological side effects of antipsychotics?
Which is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
Quetiapine is used at low doses as a sleep agent. What best explains its sedating properties?
options: More effective blockade of acetylcholine transmission
Low-dose blockade of the mesocortical pathway

guide.s: Haloperidol: single-digit, highest affinity, most EPS

cards.prompt: A 19-year-old on a new antipsychotic in its typical dose range cannot sit still and has muscle contractions, tremor, stiffness and facial movements. Which drug is most likely responsible?

guide.s: an order of magnitude below 1 per 1,000

cards.prompt: Why are the incidence, age and sex-ratio distractors in the epidemiology question wrong?
cards.answer: Incidence is about 15 to 20 per 100,000 person-years, an order of magnitude below 1 per 1,000; 80% of cases begin before 30, not late in life; men are affected more, about 2 to 1, not 1 to 1.5.

cards.text: Refusing treatment is not grounds for a Form 1; capacity to refuse is assessed by the {{treating team}} under the Health Care Consent Act; an incapable patient's decisions pass to a {{substitute decision-maker}}; dementia {{is}} a mental disorder under the Mental Health Act.

guide.s: none of the week's material carries

cards.prompt: Which two formative quiz topics are not taught in any Week 42 file?
cards.answer: Assertive community treatment (question 1) and the Mental Health Act's Form 1 criteria (question 6); both are answered in the walkthrough from general teaching.

cards.prompt: In which frameworks do people make meaning of psychotic experiences?
Which four adverse-effect domains of antipsychotics did the patient-educators name?
What are the three forms of stigma, and what should a clinician do when giving a diagnosis?
cards.answer: Self-stigma, structural stigma, and discrimination in work, housing and social settings; explain what the diagnosis means and what it does not mean.

guide.s: peer support, CBT, alternative medicine and the Hearing Voices movement

cards.prompt: Which four non-pharmacological supports did the patient-educators name?
cards.answer: Peer support, CBT, alternative medicine and the Hearing Voices movement.

cards.prompt: Why might a patient withhold symptoms from their psychiatrist?
cards.answer: Because disclosure has a cost: one educator never disclosed what he shared with the class because he knew his medication would be increased; the alliance implication is the point.

cards.text: Most people with schizophrenia are {{victims}}, not perpetrators; clinicians facilitate healing by holding and instilling {{hope}}; validate without insisting, connecting to the {{emotion}}, not the content.

cards.prompt: Match each presentation to its diagnosis and first management step.
pairs: Hours after a first SSRI dose on St. John's Wort and tryptophan, 39 °C, hyperreflexic
Serotonin syndrome; stop all three drugs
Four days after an antipsychotic dose increase, confused then rigid and febrile
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; check creatine kinase, stop the drug, fluids, cooling, dantrolene

cards.prompt: Match each CT appearance after a fall to its vessel.
pairs: Lens against the inner table, bounded by a suture
Crescent crossing sutures, three days later

guide.s: Find the cause before calling it schizophrenia

cards.prompt: State the six reflexes the week rewards.
cards.answer: Find the cause before calling it schizophrenia; count the digits before predicting the side effect; clear confusion before diagnosing psychosis; validate before you assess; report on suspicion under 16; read every scan by the mass effect it threatens.

cards.prompt: Name the three H's, all lethal through mass effect.
cards.answer: Herniation, hydrocephalus and haemorrhage.

cards.prompt: Which of these count as immunosuppression when weighing a headache?

cards.text: The six headache warning signs are {{red}} flags, not yellow: imaging is {{now}}, not later.

cards.prompt: Why does the radiation of a CT head matter relatively little?
cards.answer: The brain is relatively radio-insensitive because it is not rapidly dividing, and the injuries sought are severe.
