cards.prompt: Which modality carries the highest radiation of the five discussed?
Which vein is the prime target of a depressed fracture at the vertex?
cards.answer: The superior sagittal sinus.

cards.text: Clear post-traumatic nasal drip is {{CSF}} leaking through a fracture of the {{cribriform plate}}.

cards.prompt: Why is intracranial gas under a fracture a cue to choose antibiotics carefully?
cards.answer: The fracture is open and infection can emerge as meningitis days later; routine antibiotics may not cross the blood-brain barrier, so a penetrating agent is started early.

cards.prompt: What does crowding of the foramen magnum on CT signify?
cards.answer: The step just before cerebellar tonsillar herniation; it is the finding that gets neurosurgery called.

cards.prompt: Order the self-reinforcing loop by which mass effect worsens itself.
Tonsillar herniation kills by compressing which structure?
options: The medulla at the foramen magnum

guide.s: a coagulopathic patient can bleed without the bright sign

cards.text: Only {{clot}} is bright on CT, so a {{coagulopathic}} patient can bleed without the bright sign.

guide.s: Hypertensive bleeds sit centrally, in the basal ganglia

cards.prompt: Where do hypertensive intraparenchymal bleeds classically sit?
Why are hypertensive bleeds central rather than peripheral?
cards.answer: The fine feeder vessels of the basal ganglia arise close to the circle of Willis, where pressure is highest, and cannot take the load.

cards.prompt: Match each haemorrhage to its danger and treatability.
pairs: Kills fastest, most fixable: clip, coil or ligate the artery and evacuate the clot
Harder to control: many torn veins, no tamponade, recurrence, elderly or anticoagulated patient
Double injury: hydrocephalus to come plus an artery no longer perfusing the brain

cards.prompt: Why does an atrophic brain get subdurals after minor blows?
cards.answer: Atrophy leaves the brain in a pool of CSF, free to rotate; rotation tears the bridging veins even after a low-energy impact.

cards.prompt: Which haemorrhage do standard texts attach the lucid interval to, and which one also produces a talk-and-deteriorate course?
cards.answer: Standard texts: epidural (about 20–50% of cases). A subdural, a slow venous bleed after minor trauma in an older patient, can do the same; both are described.

cards.prompt: What is the examinable statement about subdural mortality?
cards.answer: Subdural carries a higher mortality than epidural, which kills faster but is more treatable. The 50% quoted in lecture was uncited; published series range from about 14–34% to about 60%.

guide.s: trauma is the commonest cause overall

cards.text: {{Trauma}} is the commonest cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage overall; a ruptured {{aneurysm}} accounts for about 85% of spontaneous cases.

guide.s: pneumocephalus is on the search pattern

cards.prompt: On a multicompartmental trauma CT, what does a small black focus beside the epidural represent?
cards.answer: Air: pneumocephalus, the equivalent of an open fracture, so infection risk joins the search pattern.

cards.prompt: Match the site of obstruction to the ventricles that dilate.

guide.s: Blood can cause both types at once

cards.prompt: How can one bleed cause both obstructive and non-obstructive hydrocephalus?
cards.answer: Clot in the ventricles blocks the pathway; blood products at the granulations block absorption. Both often coexist, and the mass effect is what matters.

cards.prompt: Which can block the arachnoid granulations and cause non-obstructive hydrocephalus?
Why is a non-contrast CT the wrong first order for a suspected tumour?
cards.answer: Tumours are soft-tissue density, and even very large ones can be invisible without contrast; order contrast CT or MRI.

cards.text: An extra-axial mass such as a {{meningioma}} is identified by the rind of {{CSF}} separating it from the brain.

cards.prompt: What is the standard explanation for the disproportionate oedema around a metastasis, and what alternative was proposed in lecture?
cards.answer: Standard: vasogenic oedema from leaky, barrier-deficient tumour vessels, while glioblastoma infiltrates instead. Immune recognition of foreign cells was proposed in lecture. Learn the sign: small lesion, large oedema.

cards.prompt: Order the brain-infection cascade from first to most serious.
Match each infection to the MRI appearance that shows it.
pairs: Bright rim of hyperintensity lining the ventricle on FLAIR
Thick ring of enhancement on T1 post-contrast with surrounding oedema
Thickened enhancing meninges on post-contrast imaging

cards.prompt: Ventriculitis is lethal chiefly through which mechanism?
options: Hydrocephalus, as infection proteins clog the villi

guides.title: Week 42 · 1 Psychosis and Schizophrenia: Phenomenology, Delusions and the History of the Concept
guides.html:
Wong L1 · AFP 2009 · patient panel

Psychosis and Schizophrenia: Phenomenology, Delusions and the History of the Concept

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What hallucinations and delusions are, why schizophrenia's voices are so specific, how delusions arise from a normal failure of causal inference, the types of delusion and mood congruence, Kraepelin and Bleuler, the schizophrenias as a diagnosis of exclusion, and the mental status examination of a psychotic patient.

What psychosis is

Psychosis has two core phenomena. A hallucination is a sensory perception in the absence of a stimulus. A delusion is a fixed false belief. The test that separates a hallucination from an ordinary disagreement about what was heard is physical: a spoken voice in a room is energy that a microphone can record and a screen can display as a waveform; the voice a psychotic patient hears leaves no trace on any instrument. It is not "I hear it and you don't"; it is not there.

Any sensory modality is possible, but in schizophrenia the typical hallucination is auditory, and specifically human voices: speech in a language the person understands, saying something meaningful to them. Not music, not machinery. The modality is a useful discriminator across causes of psychosis.

ConditionTypical hallucination
SchizophreniaAuditory: voices
Hallucinogens (psilocybin, LSD)Visual distortions and illusions
DeliriumVisual
Temporal lobe (complex partial) seizuresOlfactory
Schizophrenia is the prototypical psychotic illness. Its course is chronic and episodic: symptoms worsen, improve and remit, but never simply disappear. There are no objective tests: no scan, no imaging, no biochemistry. The diagnosis is defined purely by symptoms, and making it is subjective.

The defining feature is psychotic symptoms; earlier conceptions of the illness emphasised cognitive impairment; and there are also negative symptoms: social withdrawal and low motivation. Negative symptoms in the diagnostic criteria are affective flattening, alogia and avolition; DSM-5 words them as diminished emotional expression or avolition. Hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and disorganized behaviour are the positive symptoms. Low motivation is avolition, a negative symptom; thought insertion, a delusion of external control, is a positive one.

Categories and spectrums

Psychiatric diagnosis is not categorical in the way the rest of medicine is. Shortness of breath with chest pain has a differential of sarcoid, tuberculosis or COPD, and it is one of them, occasionally two; there is nothing in between TB and COPD. Psychiatric syndromes blend: a singer can be mostly pop with some country songs. Schizophrenia relates to its neighbours along three different spectrums: a severity spectrum (schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, schizotypal and schizoid personality disorder), an obsessionality spectrum (schizophrenia, schizophrenia with obsessions, OCD with poor insight, OCD, Tourette's), and an affective spectrum (schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, depression). The first two are spectrums of severity; the affective line is a spectrum of categorisation, and the mixed middle is called schizoaffective disorder. Delusions that are persistent enough can look like obsessions, and obsessions intense enough can look like delusions; there is no clear line.

The Cluster A personality disorders (schizotypal, schizoid, paranoid) are a less severe phenotype of the same thing: eccentric or odd beliefs that are not quite delusional, social dysfunction that overlaps with the autism spectrum, and a genetic relationship to schizophrenia. A Cluster A picture in a teenager who later develops schizophrenia was not one disorder turning into another; it was schizophrenia before its age of onset, in the way that a child with Duchenne muscular dystrophy is not noticed at eight months, when no one walks, but at two years, when walking fails.

Delusions

"Paranoid" has two incompatible meanings. In the older formal nosology paranoid delusions is the umbrella term, with subtypes: persecution (people or entities are trying to harm you: the FBI, the mafia, aliens, a religious group are following or watching you), reference (media of any type contains hidden messages meant for you that others cannot see), and external control (thoughts or body are being directly controlled). In everyday clinical use "paranoid" now means persecutory. Other specific types are grandiose delusions, which are common in mania and less common in schizophrenia, erotomanic delusions and delusional jealousy. Erotomanic delusions are often seen in isolation, which is what delusional disorder is: delusions without hallucinations, and therefore not schizophrenia.

A useful teaching split, not an official nosology: first-order delusions are basic misperceptions that need no story (reference: the street lights are sending a code; external control), while second-order delusions require constructing a narrative: who is after you, why, what they are doing. Persecutory delusions are second-order. Hearing a voice that comes from inside but is perceived as outside is conceptually the same error as believing the body is not under one's own control.

Mood congruence
The content of a delusion tracks the mood state in a mood disorder with psychotic features. A severely depressed patient's delusions are hyper-negative and self-referential: guilt, sin, rotting from within, having committed a crime. A manic patient believes they are exceptionally talented, attractive, rich or powerful. Delusional content that fits the mood points to a mood disorder with psychotic features; content orthogonal to mood, or present when mood is euthymic, points to a primary psychotic disorder.

What makes a belief false is a judgement of probability: plausible, unlikely, impossible. Humans solve probability problems with heuristics that work for natural tasks (fishing, throwing a ball, archery) and fail for artificial ones (stock markets, credit cards, building aeroplanes), and many delusions begin as an erroneous inference about causality. Two demonstrations make the point. In the birthday problem, the number of people needed for a 50% chance that two share a birthday is 23; most people guess 183. In the arthritis and weather study (Redelmeier and Tversky, PNAS 1996), 18 patients with rheumatoid arthritis were followed for more than a year, pain, joint tenderness and function recorded twice a month for 15 months and matched against barometric pressure, temperature and humidity. All but one believed their pain was weather-related and all but two believed the effect was strong. The mean correlation was 0.016, none significant, across nine time lags from two days forward to two days back; 97 college students perceived correlations in uncorrelated random sequences. People perceive patterns where none exist, insist on narratives that are hard to disprove, and at the far end of that normal tendency lies delusion.

History

Descriptions of madness are ancient, but most do not meet modern criteria, and schizophrenia is absent from ancient Greek and Arab texts, including Hippocrates, who described epilepsy and depression but not psychosis. The modern concept dates to the late 1800s and early 1900s with Kraepelin and Bleuler. Kraepelin's dementia praecox (1919), named for early-onset dementia as opposed to senile dementia, already contains the modern symptom set: a "peculiar destruction of the internal connections of the psychic personality"; loss of the inclination and ability to keep attention fixed; hallucinations of hearing, particularly voices; delusions of sin, persecution, reference, influence through external agents, exalted ideas; the feeling of one's thoughts being influenced; incoherence of the train of thought; stereotypy; diminished mental efficiency; emotional dullness and weakened volition; catatonic excitement, negativism, autism. The "destruction of the internal connections of the psychic personality" is the origin of the popular confusion between schizophrenia and multiple personality: an amateur translation of the German.

The four pillars Kraepelin's description supplies are attention (a cognitive problem), hallucinations, thought disorder and influence on thought, and diminished mental efficiency. Cognitive impairment was therefore in the concept from the start, and whether cognition or psychosis is the primary problem in schizophrenia is still debated. Bleuler's four A's and Schneider's first-rank symptoms are not part of this week's teaching, though the DSM-IV-TR "note" that once allowed a single bizarre delusion or a running-commentary voice to satisfy Criterion A was a Schneiderian idea; DSM-5 removed it.

The schizophrenias

Neurosyphilis, complex partial epilepsy, metachromatic leukodystrophy, mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and structural lesions would all once have been diagnosed as schizophrenia before their causes were known. Schizophrenia is a clinical syndrome, a diagnosis made on symptoms with many possible causes, and there is a strange paradox in psychiatry: as soon as the cause of the symptoms is found, the condition is no longer called by the old name. A muscle biopsy that shows a mitochondrial myopathy means the patient no longer has schizophrenia. The same logic applies to 22q11 deletion. Schizophrenia is a leftover diagnosis of exclusion, and "the schizophrenias" is a heterogeneous group of diseases with similar phenomenology and different aetiologies.

The mental status examination of a psychotic patient

The MSE is the psychiatric equivalent of the physical examination: it describes the present state with standardised descriptors so that a patient's mental state can be conveyed across time and treatment stages. Its components are appearance and general behaviour, motor activity, speech, mood and affect, thought process, thought content, perceptual disturbances, sensorium and cognition, insight, and judgment. Mood is subjective (the patient's own report, asked over the past few weeks, optionally rated 1 to 10); affect is objective (range broad or restricted, intensity blunted, flat or normal, stability, congruence with mood and appropriateness to the situation). Inappropriate affect, a persecuted patient who does not seem frightened, occurs in some patients with schizophrenia.

ComponentWhat points to psychosis
Appearance and behaviourDishevelled or unkempt; poor eye contact; guarded, withdrawn or hostile; provocative dress suggests mania instead
Motor activityPsychomotor retardation with negative symptoms; catatonia (immobility with rigidity, or excited forms); parkinsonism within weeks of starting or raising an antipsychotic
SpeechPaucity or poverty of speech (alogia); incoherence; form matters more than content here
Thought processRate (flight of ideas) and flow (goal-directed versus disorganized); logical, tangential, circumstantial, loosely associated; incoherence is a lack of coherent connection between thoughts
Thought contentDelusions, distinguished from obsessions because the obsessional patient recognises the intrusion as abnormal; suicidal and homicidal ideas, with intensity and specificity
Perceptual disturbancesHallucinations in any modality; patients may deny them, so note a patient responding to internal stimuli as if someone were speaking
Insight and judgmentAwareness of illness and need for treatment; patients with schizophrenia are often unaware of their illness and respond less well to treatment, and unawareness tracks with executive dysfunction

Bizarre delusions that persist over time suggest schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder; acute delusions are more consistent with alcohol or drug intoxication. Screening questions for delusions include whether people are stealing from the patient or talking behind their back, whether they have special powers, and whether they feel guilty as if they had committed a crime or feel like a bad person; the last two, if positive, may also suggest a psychotic depression, which is the mood-congruence principle again.

Lived experience

Two patient educators who have spoken to this class every year since 2017 described psychosis from the inside. Their message: psychosis is a state of detachment from reality that can be intensely distressing, with vivid internal experiences that feel true; people do die because of psychosis; recovery is a long game in which the short-term crisis is managed safely while the building blocks of a meaningful, dignified, self-determined life are put in place; and a label can determine how a person accepts and works with what they are given. One educator was told a doctor now thought her diagnosis might be schizoaffective rather than schizophrenia, fifteen years in, and described what that suggestion means for the rest of a life. For a relative who does not accept the diagnosis, the approach recommended was LEAP: listen, empathise, agree where you can, partner; the Hearing Voices movement reminds clinicians that some people feel lonely without their voices, so "taking away their voices" can be taking away a part of them.

Sources differ: the panel said "one in ten humans will experience psychosis"; the lecture gave a lifetime prevalence of 0.5% for schizophrenia. These are different constructs. In the WHO World Mental Health surveys about 6% of people report a lifetime psychotic experience and roughly 3% meet criteria for any psychotic disorder; schizophrenia itself is 0.3 to 0.7% in DSM-5-TR. Use 0.5 to 1% for schizophrenia on the exam; never 10% for any disorder.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Tinnitus after a loud concert has a physical cause and is not a hallucination; a nine-month belief of having been hired by the FBI is a delusion; a three-week fear of being followed after a real mugging is a plausible worry, not a delusion.
  • "Paranoid" in a stem almost always means persecutory; formally it is the umbrella under which persecution, reference and external control sit.
  • Grandiosity favours mania; erotomanic delusions in isolation favour delusional disorder; delusional disorder has no hallucinations.
  • Delusional content that fits the mood is a mood disorder with psychotic features.
  • Olfactory hallucinations point to temporal lobe seizures; visual hallucinations with fluctuating attention point to delirium.
  • Lack of insight is characteristic of schizophrenia and of frontotemporal dementia; mania has little insight, depression over-emphasises problems.
Psychosis is hallucinations plus delusions; schizophrenia is the prototypical psychotic illness, auditory voices in a meaningful language, defined by symptoms alone, chronic and episodic, a syndrome of exclusion with many possible causes, and a concept that dates only to Kraepelin and Bleuler. Delusions are extremes of a normal failure of causal inference, and mood congruence is the cleanest way to separate a psychotic mood disorder from a primary psychosis.

guides.title: Week 42 · 2 Schizophrenia: Diagnostic Criteria and the Differential of Psychosis
guides.html:
Wong L1 · AFP 2014 · PD workshop · WFQ

Schizophrenia: Diagnostic Criteria and the Differential of Psychosis

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The DSM criteria for schizophrenia and what DSM-5 changed, the durations and features that separate brief psychotic, schizophreniform, schizoaffective and delusional disorder and the Cluster A personality disorders, the medical and drug-induced mimics with their findings, and the first steps of assessment and emergency management.

The criteria

Schizophrenia requires signs and symptoms of at least six months, including at least one month of active-phase symptoms. The active-phase requirement is Criterion A; the rest of the criteria set the functional decline, the duration, and the exclusions.

CriterionContent
A. Characteristic symptomsTwo or more of: (1) delusions; (2) hallucinations; (3) disorganized speech (frequent derailment or incoherence); (4) grossly disorganized or catatonic behaviour; (5) negative symptoms (diminished emotional expression or avolition), each present for a significant portion of a one-month period (less if successfully treated). At least one must be (1), (2) or (3).
B. FunctionFor a significant portion of the time since onset, functioning in one or more major areas (work, interpersonal relations, self-care) is markedly below the level achieved before onset; with childhood or adolescent onset, failure to reach the expected level.
C. DurationContinuous signs for at least six months, including at least one month meeting Criterion A; the rest may be prodromal or residual, shown by negative symptoms only or by two or more Criterion A symptoms in attenuated form (odd beliefs, unusual perceptual experiences).
D. Mood exclusionSchizoaffective disorder and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features are ruled out because no major mood episodes occurred with the active-phase symptoms, or, if they did, they were present for a minority of the total duration of the active and residual periods.
E. Substance and medical exclusionNot attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (a drug of abuse, a medication) or another medical condition.
F. Autism and communication disordersWith a history of autism spectrum disorder or a childhood-onset communication disorder, schizophrenia is added only if prominent delusions or hallucinations are present for at least one month.
Sources differ: the lecture slide reproduces the DSM-IV-TR criteria, which allow a single Criterion A symptom if the delusion is bizarre or the hallucination is a running commentary or two voices conversing, and which word the negative symptoms as affective flattening, alogia or avolition. The assigned review reproduces DSM-5, which removed that one-symptom exception, requires at least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech, removed the five subtypes, and rewords negative symptoms as diminished emotional expression or avolition. DSM-5-TR is current. Expect DSM-5 on the exam: a single bizarre delusion with nothing else does not make the diagnosis.

The prodrome precedes the active phase: social withdrawal, loss of interest in work or school, deterioration of hygiene, angry outbursts, and behaviour out of character. It is easily mistaken for depression. The "two or more voices conversing" and "running commentary" phenomena remain characteristic; they simply no longer count for two symptoms.

The other psychotic disorders

The neighbours of schizophrenia are separated by duration and which symptoms are present.

DiagnosisDistinguishing features
Brief psychotic disorderDelusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech or behaviour lasting at least one day but less than one month
Schizophreniform disorderSame picture as schizophrenia with symptoms lasting at least one month but less than six months
SchizophreniaSix months or more, including one month of active symptoms
Schizoaffective disorderA mood episode concurrent with active-phase symptoms; mood symptoms present for a substantial portion of the illness; and delusions or hallucinations for two weeks without prominent mood symptoms
Depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic featuresPsychotic symptoms occur exclusively during periods of mood disturbance; the content is usually mood-congruent
Delusional disorderNonbizarre delusions with an absence of hallucinations, disorganized speech or behaviour, and negative symptoms; functioning is largely preserved apart from the delusion's direct impact
Schizotypal personality disorderSubthreshold symptoms tied to persistent personality features: unusual beliefs and illusions (shadows that might or might not be real), never full delusions or full hallucinations
Schizoid personality disorderNo positive symptoms at all; affective flattening and negative-type features resembling schizophrenia's
Obsessive-compulsive and body dysmorphic disorderProminent obsessions, compulsions, preoccupation with appearance or body odour, hoarding or body-focused repetitive behaviours; the patient recognises the intrusion as abnormal
Post-traumatic stress disorderA traumatic event; symptoms relate to reliving or reacting to it
Autism spectrum or communication disordersDeficits in social interaction with repetitive, restricted behaviours and cognitive or communication deficits

Schizophrenia is a constellation: full delusions (fixed false beliefs) and full hallucinations (usually auditory) together with more. Affective flattening alone is not sufficient for schizophrenia; it is what schizoid personality disorder looks like. Schizotypal personality disorder has the positive-symptom flavour without the full phenomena. Delusional disorder is the classic exam contrast: the key difference from schizophrenia is that it does not include hallucinations, and the person is not preceded by a prodromal decline, does not recover spontaneously, and is still treated pharmacologically.

Secondary psychosis

Every new psychosis is evaluated for an intrinsic cause before a primary diagnosis is made: delirium, a mood disorder with psychosis, Cushing syndrome, and drug use, illicit and prescribed. Ideally the patient is observed in a controlled setting for an extended time; in most situations the history comes from family. The physical examination finds the organic causes. The most common drugs producing psychosis today are methamphetamine, which produces it acutely, and cannabis, which does so less acutely; a medication started days before the onset, a corticosteroid in high dose being the classic example, is the diagnosis until proven otherwise.

Medical conditionDistinguishing featuresLaboratory or imaging
Substance useAbnormal vital signs, needle marks, poor nutritionElevated blood alcohol; positive urine drug screen
Thyroid disorderCoarse hair and skin, exophthalmos, goitre, pretibial myxedema, tachycardia or bradycardia, tremorAbnormal TSH; anaemia; hyponatraemia
Delirium caused by infectionAltered consciousness, fever, hypo- or hyperreflexia, hypotension, an infection sourceAbnormal leukocyte count; positive HIV or rapid plasma reagin
DementiaCognitive and memory deficits, abnormal MMSENone specific
Vitamin B12 deficiencyAtaxia, atrophic glossitis, memory impairment, muscle weaknessLow B12; macrocytic anaemia; elevated iron and indirect bilirubin
Systemic lupus erythematosusAlopecia, discoid or malar rash, fever, oral ulcers, phlebitis, pleural or pericardial rubAnaemia; elevated ANA; pleural effusion; proteinuria
Cushing syndromeAbdominal striae, buffalo hump, hirsutism, moon face, proximal weaknessElevated 24-hour urine cortisol
Temporal lobe epilepsyPostictal state, abnormal neurological findingsAbnormal EEG
Brain tumourFocal neurological deficitsLesion on CT or MRI
Wilson diseaseAtaxia, dysarthria, hepatomegaly, hyperreflexia, jaundice, Kayser-Fleischer rings in the corneaBasal ganglia lesions on MRI; Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia; elevated liver enzymes
PorphyriaProximal muscle weakness, tachycardiaElevated urine porphobilinogen; hyponatraemia

Two pictures recur in vignettes. A patient with lupus, on ramipril for years, develops pressured speech, irritability and voices within days of starting prednisone 50 mg: the timeline makes steroid-induced psychosis the most likely diagnosis, ahead of lupus psychosis or a new primary disorder. An elderly patient with Alzheimer's disease who begins swatting at things that are not there, worse in the evenings, and is drowsy and inattentive at interview has delirium until proven otherwise: the least appropriate action is to prescribe an antipsychotic and review in a month; the physical examination, urinalysis, blood count and electrolytes, and if needed an emergency assessment, come first. Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.

Referral, admission and the first steps

Patients presenting with psychosis or newly diagnosed with schizophrenia should be urgently referred for psychiatric evaluation. Not every acute psychosis needs a hospital bed, but admission is considered for those who may pose a danger to themselves or others. In the emergency department, agitation with psychosis is managed with an antipsychotic plus a benzodiazepine: loxapine with lorazepam, or haloperidol with lorazepam, by mouth or by injection. The de-escalation that accompanies it is casual, friendly, respectful and non-confrontational ("you're not in trouble, we're here to help"), finds common ground, listens actively, and does not argue with delusions but does not agree with or support them either.

The diagnostic manual is 100% reliable and 0% valid, as the joke goes; it exists so that clinicians know they are talking about the same thing. Adding a fourth and fifth diagnosis to the same patient does not add understanding: it is the same person, the same brain, the same problem, fitting more and more criteria. That is why criteria lists are examined: the judgement itself is hard to examine.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Durations: brief psychotic disorder one day to one month; schizophreniform one to six months; schizophrenia six months or more with one month active.
  • Schizoaffective disorder needs delusions or hallucinations for two weeks without prominent mood symptoms; if psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, it is a mood disorder with psychotic features.
  • Delusional disorder: nonbizarre delusions, no hallucinations, preserved functioning.
  • Under DSM-5, negative symptoms plus catatonic behaviour without delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech does not satisfy Criterion A.
  • New psychosis with a new drug: the drug is the diagnosis. New visual hallucinations with inattention in dementia: delirium, investigate.
  • Kayser-Fleischer rings in a young psychotic patient: Wilson disease. Malar rash and oral ulcers: lupus. Moon face and striae: Cushing syndrome.
Schizophrenia is six months of illness with one month of two active symptoms, at least one of them delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech, with functional decline and no mood, substance or medical explanation. Everything else in the differential is settled by duration, by which symptoms are present, and by the medical work-up that every new psychosis deserves.

guides.title: Week 42 · 3 Schizophrenia: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Genetics and Violence
guides.html:
Wong L1–L2 · AFP 2014 · WFQ

Schizophrenia: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Genetics and Violence

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Prevalence, onset and sex ratio with the sources reconciled, the risk factors and the maternal influenza study, heritability and the familial risk table, why there is no genetic test, the genetic overlap with bipolar disorder, behavioural genetics, violence and its forensic trajectories, and the suicide, mortality and cost figures.

The core numbers

ParameterValue
Lifetime prevalence0.5% (one in 200); the assigned review gives 0.3 to 0.7%
Peak onsetMales age 23; females 40; men present between 18 and 25, women in two peaks, 25 to the mid-30s and after 40
Cases by age 3080%
Male to female ratio2:1 overall; 1:1.9 after 40; 1:4 after 60
RaceNo large differences (with some unique populations)
Global variationLess than for most disorders, which argues for a mostly genetic illness

The onset curves from Danish register data show a sharp male peak in the early twenties, around 55 to 60 per 100,000 person-years, and a broad, shallow female plateau through the late twenties and thirties with a further rise at 40 to 45. That later female onset used to be called paraphrenia and is probably related to menopause, in the same aetiological bucket as postpartum psychosis. Prevalence is similar across cultures and ethnicities; in the United States, Black patients are diagnosed at a disproportionately higher rate than non-Hispanic whites, a finding that may reflect bias in the diagnosis of psychosis rather than a difference in the illness. Schizophrenia is the most common psychotic disease.

Sources differ: the lecture gives lifetime prevalence 0.5%, the assigned American Family Physician review gives 0.3 to 0.7%, older textbooks say about 1%, and the practice quiz keys "0.5 to 1%". DSM-5-TR puts it at 0.3 to 0.7%. Any answer inside 0.5 to 1% is defensible; expect the slide's 0.5% on a lecture-based item. On sex ratio the lecture gives 2:1 and the review says "a slight predominance in men"; meta-analyses of incidence give about 1.4:1. Expect 2:1 on a lecture-based item and "slightly more common in men" as the safer general answer.

Risk factors

Risk factorMagnitude
GeneticHeritability 80%
Maternal viral infectionRelative risk 7-fold for influenza in the first trimester
Urban versus rural birthRelative risk 2-fold; attributable risk 34%
Season of birthMarch versus June or December, relative risk 1.11
Migration, race, geographyListed without a figure
Other environmental factorsCannabis use, Toxoplasma gondii infection, obstetric complications, central nervous system infection in early childhood, advanced paternal age over 55

The influenza study is worth knowing as a design. Serum samples drawn from pregnant women about forty years earlier had been kept at minus 80 degrees; investigators traced the offspring, by then old enough to have declared a diagnosis, and found a sevenfold higher rate of schizophrenia when the mother was influenza-antibody positive. Sevenfold is large in epidemiology: for calibration, smoking and lung cancer in a 25 pack-year smoker carries a relative risk of about 30. Urbanicity and season of birth are probably proxies for the same maternal infection risk, weaker and more dilute. And the large relative risk is non-specific: maternal influenza also raises the risk of autism, learning disability and ADHD, which is why a big relative risk on a non-specific exposure does not make a screening test.

Genetics

Schizophrenia is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder with complex genetics like most common diseases: a combination of rare, large-effect mutations and common variants of individually small effect, most of them in non-coding regions of the genome (coding regions are less than 1% of it), exacerbated by other neurodevelopmental insults and gene-by-environment interaction. Historical theories that blamed family environment and psychodynamic factors are disproven. Inheritance is non-Mendelian, and the familial risks are absolute lifetime risks against a population baseline of 0.5%.

Relationship to an affected personLifetime risk
Monozygotic twin, or both parents affected40 to 50%
First-degree relative10 to 15%
Second-degree relative3%
Third-degree relative2%
General population0.5%

Heritability of about 80% places schizophrenia among the most heritable illnesses, more than height or heart disease, comparable to autism, well above depression at about 30 to 35%. The 80% applies to schizophrenia alone, not to the whole spectrum. Most patients nevertheless have no family history of psychosis, and relatives are also at raised risk of schizoaffective disorder, schizotypal personality disorder, bipolar disorder, depression and autism spectrum disorder.

Why there is no genetic test
Linkage studies in multiply affected families mapped about 10% of the genome, including the HLA region on chromosome 6 and loci such as neuregulin and dysbindin. On the allelic spectrum, the 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge or velocardiofacial syndrome) carries a genotype relative risk of about 20 and is almost certainly causal, but it is very rare and its carriers are usually not called schizophrenic once the deletion is known. Common GWAS variants carry relative risks of 1.05 to 1.1: a whole genome now costs a few hundred dollars, but knowing a common variant tells you virtually nothing about a person's trajectory. Family-study heritability far exceeds SNP-based heritability, the missing heritability problem.

SNP-based genetic correlations link almost all psychiatric diagnoses; the strongest is between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder at 0.70, and only anorexia and ADHD are uncorrelated (negatively, at minus 0.26). The clinical overlap and the genetic overlap together suggest that diagnosis is not tightly linked to biology, and that bipolar disorder and schizophrenia may be one disease process affecting different circuits, mood in one person and psychosis in another, as multiple sclerosis in the optic nerve differs from multiple sclerosis in the cord. Where the lesion is matters in the brain in a way it does not in the liver.

Behavioural genetics supports the same conclusion. Behavioural disorders are on average more heritable than common medical disorders; personality traits are 50 to 80% heritable; and many measures of "environment" (parenting, childhood accidents, classroom environment, life events, social support, drug exposure) themselves show genetic influence. In the Minnesota study of twins reared apart (45 monozygotic and 26 dizygotic pairs, mean separation over 30 years), the correlation between identical twins was the same whether they were reared apart or together for fingerprint ridge count (ratio 1.01, the negative control) and for personality questionnaires (1.02 and 0.98): genetics accounts for about 50% of the variation in personality, shared family environment for only 1 to 9%. The argument does not extend to IQ, where the ratio was 0.78. Two caveats travel with it: this is a long-standing unresolved debate, and it concerns families within the normal range, not abuse or neglect. And DNA is a recipe, not a blueprint: ingredients (protein-coding genes) need cooking instructions (gene regulation, epigenetics, chromatin); humans and chimpanzees share 98.77% of their sequence and about 23,000 genes each.

Violence

Substance use, Cluster B personality disorders and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders are associated with an increased risk of violence; the diagnosis-associated risk in the general population is comparable to that of age, sex, substance abuse, education level and a history of violence. Antisocial personality disorder is partly defined by violence, so its association is a tautology. Psychiatrists see people with psychotic symptoms and police see people who act violently; in those specific populations the relationship looks different because the Bayesian prior probability is different. The same logic governs ordering tests: a test ordered in a population with a high prior yields true positives; ordered for everyone, it yields more false positives than true positives and more morbidity than benefit. Forensic-population statistics must never be conflated with general-population statistics.

PredictorPoint
Substance useThe perpetrator is intoxicated with alcohol or more in 50% of homicides; substance use is a huge driver of violence, and of suicide
Personality and cognitive styleImpulse control, affect regulation, threatened narcissism and a paranoid cognitive style operate across diagnoses
Psychotic self-defenceParanoia focused on a specific threat, a persecutory delusion about a particular person (a neighbour, a boss, a parent) that the patient may feel bound to retaliate against, is the most dangerous scenario
Acute exacerbationPeriods of symptom exacerbation are more dangerous
StrangersRandom violence toward a stranger is rare; public perception of the risk is misplaced

Among forensic psychiatry patients, 85% have a psychotic illness, though psychosis itself is not a strong predictor of violence. Their life-course trajectories fall into three groups: early starters (about 40%), violent before the illness, with conduct disorder, adverse life experiences and drugs; late starters (about 40%), violent only at or after onset, with symptom-related violence; and late-late starters (about 15%), violent after years of illness, often treatment-resistant, with a single severe episode related to symptoms, often an intra-familial homicide. Violence driven by psychosis is treatable because the psychosis is treatable; antisocial violence is addressed by reducing other risk factors, mainly substance use. In first-episode psychosis, about 40% could have had criminal charges at first presentation, and one third of homicides by people with a primary psychotic illness occur in the first episode, when the diagnosis first becomes apparent. The confound is that peak onset falls in young men, who are also the peak group for violence generally.

Suicide, mortality and cost

Suicide risk is 13 times that of the general public, with a lifetime risk of about 5%; auditory hallucinations, delusions, substance abuse and a history of suicide attempts raise it further, and adequate treatment with screening for risk factors lowers it. Overall mortality is two to three times the general population, most deaths being cardiovascular and respiratory disease, stroke, cancer and thromboembolic events.

The economic burden exceeds what the prevalence would predict because of early onset, lifetime disability and high medical burden. Direct care in the United States in 1990 cost US$17.3 billion, 3% of health costs, while mood disorders, ten times more common, cost US$19.2 billion; in the United Kingdom schizophrenia cost £810 million, 5.37% of hospital costs, against £260 million for diabetes; Canadian direct costs in 1996 were CA$1.12 billion plus CA$1.23 billion in lost productivity. Schizophrenia is the fifth leading cause of disability in established market economies and ninth worldwide, because disability-adjusted life years accumulate from an early age: cancer and Alzheimer's are diseases of the old, schizophrenia is not, and unipolar depression is first in DALYs in high-income countries for the same reason.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • The familial risk table gives absolute lifetime risks, not relative risks: 40 to 50% for an identical co-twin against 0.5% is a relative risk near 100.
  • Heritability 80% applies to schizophrenia, not to the spectrum; the strongest genetic correlation is with bipolar disorder, 0.70.
  • A sevenfold relative risk from maternal influenza is large but non-specific and does not screen; soft neurological signs in childhood do not screen either.
  • Incidence is about 15 to 20 per 100,000 person-years, not one per 1,000; most cases begin before 30, not late in life.
  • The most dangerous delusion is a targeted persecutory one; stranger violence is rare; one third of homicides by psychotic patients happen in the first episode.
  • Suicide 13 times, lifetime 5%; mortality two to three times, mostly cardiovascular.
Half a percent of people, 80% heritable and non-Mendelian, onset in the early twenties in men and later and twice in women, driven by rare large-effect variants, common small-effect variants and non-specific early insults such as first-trimester influenza. The illness is expensive because it starts young and disables for life, kills by suicide (5%) and cardiovascular disease (mortality two to three times), and its violence is mostly symptom-driven and therefore treatable.

guides.title: Week 42 · 4 Schizophrenia Neurobiology: Neurodevelopment, Anatomy, Histology and the Dopamine Hypothesis
guides.html:
Wong L2

Schizophrenia Neurobiology: Neurodevelopment, Anatomy, Histology and the Dopamine Hypothesis

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Why every level of biology shows an abnormality, the discordant-twin MRIs, hippocampal and cortical findings, radial and tangential migration and inside-out lamination, soft neurological signs, the pharmacological foundation of the dopamine hypothesis, amphetamine-induced release, abnormal salience, catecholamines as meta-information, and NMDA-dependent plasticity.

Every level shows something

Behaviour is controlled at every level of organisation, and every biological tool applied to schizophrenia finds an abnormality: culture, drug use and prenatal infection at the level of the organism; cortical volume and hippocampal size on MRI; connectivity and hypofrontality in circuits; cortical inhibition in network simulations; cortical architecture in histology; dendritic spines, sensory gating and dopamine release at the synapse; 80% heritability and polygenic complexity at the gene. That is the problem rather than the answer: if it is everything, it does not say what causes schizophrenia. An atherosclerotic plaque has no such spectrum of origins. The debate among researchers is which level is most important, and the outcome side of the same matrix has three domains: psychosis, negative symptoms, and cognitive impairment.

The integrated model: developmental cortical abnormalities (genes plus environment) disrupt networks and learning, producing a working-memory deficit that drives generalised cognitive impairment; aberrant dopamine release assigns importance to spurious events, producing delusions; and dopamine's role in motivated behaviour is why its disturbance produces anhedonia and amotivation.

Gross anatomy and histology

Schizophrenia is a disorder of neurodevelopment: assembling the cerebral cortex is one of the most complicated developmental tasks, many higher functions depend on it (and on the striatum), and there are gross and histological abnormalities. The coarsest summary is bigger ventricles, smaller cortex. The classic demonstration is MRI of identical twins discordant for schizophrenia: coronal sections of a well twin beside an affected twin (35-year-old women, 28-year-old men) show increased ventricular volume and decreased brain volume in the affected twin, especially the hippocampus and frontal cortex. Because the twins are genetically identical, the difference cannot be attributed to genotype alone.

The hippocampus is smaller in schizophrenia, but also in depression and bipolar disorder: hippocampal atrophy is a psychiatric-illness finding, not a schizophrenia finding. The hippocampus holds place cells for spatial navigation (a place field is about six feet across), encodes short-term memory of under two weeks, and is one of the few regions of the adult brain with ongoing neurogenesis and cell death, with a neuronal half-life of about two weeks. That is why unrehearsed material is forgotten in about two weeks: the neurons that encoded it die unless a mirror network is consolidated elsewhere in cortex.

Histological findingDetail
Laminar disorganisationPyramidal neurons are less dense in the superficial layers and shifted toward deeper layers; the changes are subtle and not diagnostic
InterneuronsReduced expression of GABA interneuron markers: lower GAD67 and GAT-1 mRNA and GAT-1 immunoreactivity, reduced somal size, fewer dopaminergic and thalamic axon terminals
Dendritic spinesDecreased dendritic spine density

The histological detail is low yield; the point is that circuit formation is abnormal and this is probably what drives the symptoms.

Radial and tangential migration

The cortex is built inside-out. Excitatory pyramidal neurons migrate radially along a radial glial scaffold from the ventricular zone; the neurons born last travel farthest and end up in the most superficial layers, while the earliest-born stay deep, like a wall whose framing goes in first and whose paint goes on last, except that here the layer farthest from the origin is installed last. Interneurons migrate tangentially, sweeping in from the ganglionic eminences. The two populations must intersect at the right time and the right place, and that is why the process can go wrong. Inside-out lamination appeared with the teleost fishes; everything below zebrafish has outside-in lamination, in which the outer layer is laid first and the inner layers cannot expand, so the brain cannot grow. The innovation that let the cortex enlarge is the same one that makes its assembly fragile: tune a car to make it faster and it becomes less reliable.

The developmental signature can be seen years before psychosis. In Elaine Walker's study, paediatric neurologists blind to adult diagnosis rated childhood home movies and found subtle soft neurological signs, coordination deficits and impaired left-right dominance, in the children who later developed schizophrenia, ten to fifteen years before onset. These signs cannot be used to screen: they are non-specific and co-inherited with learning disability, just as maternal influenza raises the risk of autism, learning disability and ADHD as well as schizophrenia.

Dementia praecox and dementia
Kraepelin's name meant early-onset dementia as opposed to senile dementia. When an older person with Alzheimer's disease becomes psychotic, the illness is called a neurodegenerative disorder from which psychosis emerges; when a young person with cognitive impairment becomes psychotic, it is called a primary psychotic disorder. Whether the cognitive impairment or the psychosis is the primary problem in schizophrenia is still debated, and schizophrenia does not clearly predispose to dementia.

The dopamine hypothesis

The empirical foundation is pharmacological. Stimulants (cocaine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDMA) act on the dopamine transporter and increase dopamine signalling, and at high doses produce paranoia, dystonia and aggression; antipsychotics block dopamine receptors. Too much dopamine can cause psychotic symptoms; amphetamine and other stimulants increase synaptic dopamine; antipsychotics reduce psychotic symptoms by blocking dopamine receptors. Cocaine and amphetamine are to the dopamine transporter what an SSRI is to the serotonin transporter: they prolong the transmitter's time in the cleft. Methamphetamine is taken up by monoamine transporters including DAT, targets the vesicular monoamine transporter VMAT2 and raises synaptic dopamine; it resembles the monoamine transmitters in structure and is now the commonest cause of acute drug-induced psychosis presenting to emergency departments. Hallucinogens work differently: LSD and psilocybin are serotonergic; PCP and ketamine are NMDA channel blockers; cannabinoids cause psychosis less acutely.

The direct evidence is Abi-Dargham's 1998 study. Baseline striatal D2 receptor availability did not differ between patients and controls, but amphetamine-induced dopamine release was greater in schizophrenia: 13.8% versus 7.1% (p under 0.05). Something is wrong with the dopamine system, not the receptors or the molecule but the pattern of release, and why is still unknown. Aberrant dopamine release then leads to incorrect assignment of importance to events, abnormal salience, which connects to the cognitive biases of delusion formation: false causality and over-emphasis of coincidence.

Meta-information
Glutamate and GABA are more than 99% of the brain's transmitters and carry the basic message: move the leg, fall asleep. The catecholamines (dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline) and indolamines (serotonin, melatonin) are a pinch of transmitter from nuclei in the midbrain projecting to the forebrain, and they carry meta-information: when, where and how much, not what. They indicate a change in state, highlight salient information and encode the magnitude of an input. Dopamine's psychological function is reward expectancy: an unexpected reward produces a spike, an unexpected absence of reward a dip. Dopamine is also the precursor of noradrenaline and adrenaline: phenylalanine to tyrosine (phenylalanine hydroxylase), tyrosine to DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step), DOPA to dopamine (aromatic amino acid decarboxylase), dopamine to noradrenaline (dopamine beta-hydroxylase), noradrenaline to adrenaline (PNMT).

The historical direction of discovery matters: antipsychotics were found by accident, and the dopamine hypothesis was learned from them, not the other way round. Seeman's 1975 Science plot showed that the clinical dose of an antipsychotic is inversely proportional to its D2 receptor affinity across two dozen drugs, an inductive proof that D2 is the target. D2 antagonism is necessary and sufficient for antipsychotic effect, and until recently no antipsychotic with a new mechanism had appeared since chlorpromazine in the 1950s; the newest agents, described with treatment, are the exception.

Glutamate, plasticity and neural nets

The NMDA receptor is the signal for learning: Hebb's rule, neurons that fire together wire together. Lashley searched for the engram, the smallest unit of memory, by lesioning trained animals, and found no single location; the modern answer is the synapse. Strong pre- to postsynaptic excitation makes subsequent signals more likely to depolarise the postsynaptic cell, long-term potentiation, through recruitment of AMPA receptors instructed by NMDA; long-term depression internalises them. Dopamine modulates that synapse, encouraging the molecular pathways that potentiate it, which is how the meta-information signal shapes learning. Neural networks in software learn the same way, through a pruning function, and a simple neural-net simulation of speech recognition can be perturbed into hallucination, recognising a word it was never shown: simple changes in circuits can generate complex symptoms. PCP and ketamine, NMDA blockers that produce psychosis, supply the ingredients of a glutamate hypothesis, and reduced interneuron markers supply those of a GABA hypothesis, but neither is a formal rival to the dopamine hypothesis.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Enlarged ventricles and reduced hippocampal and frontal volume in the affected member of a discordant identical-twin pair show the change is not simply genetic.
  • Hippocampal atrophy is not specific to schizophrenia; it occurs in depression and bipolar disorder.
  • Pyramidal neurons migrate radially and inside-out; interneurons migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences; late-born neurons travel farthest.
  • Soft neurological signs precede psychosis by a decade but are non-specific and do not screen.
  • Abi-Dargham: baseline D2 availability equal; amphetamine-induced release 13.8% versus 7.1%.
  • LSD and psilocybin are serotonergic; PCP and ketamine block NMDA; stimulants act on the dopamine transporter; methamphetamine also targets VMAT2.
  • Dopamine carries meta-information (when, where, how much) and encodes reward expectancy; glutamate and GABA carry the message.
Schizophrenia is a disorder of cortical assembly: subtle laminar disorganisation, fewer interneuron markers and spines, bigger ventricles and smaller cortex, with soft signs visible a decade before psychosis. Its symptoms map onto dopamine as a salience and reward signal, released abnormally in response to amphetamine, modulating glutamatergic plasticity in circuits whose miswiring can, in even a simple network, produce hallucinations.

guides.title: Week 42 · 5 Antipsychotics: Dopamine Pathways, Receptor Affinity and Side Effects
guides.html:
Wong L2 · AFP 2014 · WFQ

Antipsychotics: Dopamine Pathways, Receptor Affinity and Side Effects

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The four dopamine pathways and what D2 blockade does in each, parkinsonism versus Parkinson's and the meaning of extrapyramidal, dopamine receptors as GPCRs, the dose-digit rule that maps D2 affinity to side effects, the typical and atypical generations and why the category does not hold up, and the extrapyramidal symptoms with their treatments.

The dopamine pathways

All antipsychotics in current use are dopamine D2 receptor antagonists, and their effects and side effects follow from where dopamine tracts run. Tracts are named for origin and terminus.

PathwayOrigin to terminusNormal functionConsequence of D2 blockade
NigrostriatalSubstantia nigra to striatumMovement and sensory stimuli; the unconscious motor subroutines; degenerates in Parkinson's diseaseExtrapyramidal symptoms: parkinsonism (tremor, rigidity, akinesia, postural change)
TuberoinfundibularHypothalamus to pituitaryDopamine tonically inhibits prolactin: more dopamine, less prolactinProlactin elevation
MesolimbicVentral tegmental area to nucleus accumbensPleasure and reward-seeking; addiction, emotion, perceptionFeeling bad, low motivation; negative symptoms produced or worsened
MesocorticalVentral tegmental area to cortexCognition, memory, attention, emotional behaviour, learningAntipsychotic effect and cognitive effects: the therapeutic tract
Sources differ: the lecture slide numbers three tracts, with mesolimbic and mesocortical combined, and the lecturer said "three main dopamine tracts"; the same deck's later slides and the standard pharmacology texts list four pathways, and the practice quiz keys the nigrostriatal pathway for neurological side effects. Answer "three tracts, four pathways" if pressed; on a question that names four, they are mesolimbic, mesocortical, nigrostriatal and tuberoinfundibular.

Blocking the nigrostriatal tract produces parkinsonism, not Parkinson's disease, but the symptoms are identical: whether the neurons die or their postsynaptic target is blocked, the net effect is the same. The corticospinal tract was called the pyramidal tract because it decussates at the pyramids, so motor inputs that are not part of it are extrapyramidal; the name has nothing to do with function. The striatum (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus) stores the unconscious motor programs learned by practice, which is why an over-blocked patient is not paralysed but loses the fluency of movement, like a child learning to skate. Acetylcholine in the striatum influences dopamine signalling (the cholinergic interneuron's M4 receptors sit on the dopaminergic terminal beside D2), so anticholinergics treat extrapyramidal side effects: benztropine (Cogentin), trihexyphenidyl, procyclidine. Dopamine's tonic inhibition of prolactin means D2 blockade raises prolactin, with galactorrhoea among the listed adverse effects of haloperidol and the phenothiazines.

Receptors

Transmembrane receptors are ionotropic (ion channels, such as the GABA-A receptor to which benzodiazepines bind) or metabotropic (G-protein-coupled receptors and receptor tyrosine kinases). Most receptors in psychiatry are GPCRs, and all five dopamine receptors, D1 to D5, are GPCRs, not ion channels; some serotonin receptors are ionotropic and some are not. D1-like receptors (D1, D5) raise adenylyl cyclase activity; D2-like receptors (D2, D3, D4) lower it. Dopamine receptors share homology with the receptors for histamine H1, adrenaline, serotonin and acetylcholine, which is precisely why drugs given in large amounts to block D2 also hit those four. A 2018 crystal structure of D2 bound to risperidone is the first time the target has been seen; for decades the field was flying blind.

Sources differ: the recording has the lecturer say benzodiazepines bind "GABA-B" receptors; benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the ionotropic GABA-A receptor, and GABA-B is the metabotropic receptor (any pharmacology text). Whether the slip was his or the captions', use GABA-A.

Potency determines side effects

Binding to D2 receptors is inversely proportional to the clinical dose required for an antipsychotic effect (Seeman's 1975 relationship). Low-dose drugs have high affinity: nearly all of the drug in the body is sitting on D2 receptors, so the side effects come from decreased dopamine signalling. High-dose drugs have low affinity: hundreds of milligrams are needed to reach the same D2 occupancy, and the excess floats around binding other receptors of the same GPCR family, so the side effects come from non-dopamine receptor binding. The number of digits in the daily dose therefore predicts the side-effect profile; the principle applies to beta blockers and many other drug classes.

Dose bandDrugs and daily dose rangesD2 affinityExpected side effects
Single digits to low teensHaloperidol 2 to 5 mg; risperidone 6 to 9; paliperidone 6 to 12; fluphenazine 5 to 10; flupenthixol 10HighExtrapyramidal symptoms; prolactin elevation
TensOlanzapine 20 to 30; loxapine 50 to 100IntermediateMixed
HundredsChlorpromazine 300 to 800; clozapine 300 to 600; quetiapine 600 to 900LowSedation (histamine H1); cardiac effects and hypotension (alpha-adrenergic); constipation (muscarinic); no EPS (muscarinic)

The corollary is "no EPS": a low-potency drug's own antimuscarinic activity self-treats the parkinsonism its D2 blockade would produce, like giving benztropine with every dose, a built-in side-effect pill. The rule is a heuristic with edges: paliperidone's range crosses into two digits, and clozapine's overlaps quetiapine's. Off-target effects also include dry mouth and dry eyes from muscarinic blockade and orthostatic hypotension from alpha blockade.

Sources differ: the slide prints dose ranges; the lecturer quoted single figures aloud (clozapine 500, quetiapine 600, olanzapine 20, loxapine 50), and the assigned review lists licensed ranges that overlap but do not coincide (haloperidol 5 to 20, risperidone 2 to 8, paliperidone 3 to 12, olanzapine 10 to 30, clozapine 150 to 600, quetiapine 300 to 800 mg/day). None is wrong: they answer different questions (typical maintenance for the potency argument versus the licensed range). Expect the digit pattern, ones, tens, hundreds, on a lecture-based item; answer a specific range in the terms of whichever source the stem quotes.

Typical and atypical

First-generation (typical) agents such as chlorpromazine, haloperidol, perphenazine and thiothixene most commonly cause extrapyramidal symptoms; second-generation (atypical) agents most commonly cause weight gain and metabolic change. There is no difference in effectiveness between the two generations and quality of life is similar at one year; the difference is the adverse-effect profile, and prior response and prior adverse effects guide the choice. Laboratory monitoring is not needed for first-generation drugs. Every antipsychotic carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.

The typical/atypical category does not hold up. The proposed criteria for atypicality have been less EPS or tardive dyskinesia, better efficacy for negative symptoms, better tolerance, compliance and outcome, and a 5-HT2 to D2 affinity ratio; these features are not consistently associated with atypicality, and clozapine is the only truly atypical antipsychotic, because it works when other antipsychotics have failed. Older or newer, high or low potency, there is no clear pattern in efficacy for psychotic symptoms across the class. The digit rule organises the side effects better than the generation label does.

DrugDose (mg/day)Common adverse effectsSerious adverse effects and notes
Chlorpromazine300 to 1,000Drowsiness, dry mouth, prolactin elevation, EPS, glucose intolerance, postural hypotension, weight gainNMS, tardive dyskinesia; the first antipsychotic
Haloperidol5 to 20Drowsiness, dry mouth, EPS, galactorrhoea, hypotension, tachycardiaNMS, QT prolongation, tardive dyskinesia; more effective for positive symptoms but a high risk of EPS
Aripiprazole10 to 30Anxiety, constipation, dizziness, headache, insomnia, metabolic change, nauseaAgranulocytosis, NMS, TD; smaller effect on lipids
Clozapine150 to 600Constipation, dizziness, headache, metabolic effects, salivation, sedation, tachycardia, weight gainAgranulocytosis, myocarditis, seizures, TD; reserved for severe refractory illness
Olanzapine10 to 30Akathisia, constipation, dizziness, hyperprolactinaemia, metabolic change, postural hypotension, weight gainAgranulocytosis, NMS, TD; more weight gain than older second-generation drugs but a lower discontinuation rate
Paliperidone3 to 12Hyperprolactinaemia, metabolic change, orthostatic hypotension, priapism, somnolence, weight gainNMS, QT prolongation, TD; the active metabolite of risperidone
Quetiapine300 to 800Agitation, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, metabolic change, postural hypotension, somnolence, weight gainAgranulocytosis, NMS, TD; high discontinuation rate
Risperidone2 to 8Anxiety, hyperprolactinaemia, hypotension, insomnia, metabolic change, nausea, weight gainAgranulocytosis, NMS, TD; more EPS and prolactin elevation than other second-generation drugs
Ziprasidone120 to 200Agitation, hypotension, metabolic change, nausea, somnolence, tachycardiaAgranulocytosis, NMS, TD; the least weight gain
Lurasidone40 to 160Akathisia, hyperprolactinaemia, metabolic change, nausea, parkinsonism, somnolenceNMS, TD; more adverse effects at higher doses

Extrapyramidal symptoms and their treatment

The extrapyramidal symptoms are pseudoparkinsonism, akathisia (a sensation of inner restlessness and inability to be still) and dystonia; they are associated most with first-generation drugs, and the patient is kept on the lowest effective dose. Drugs used to treat them are propranolol, lorazepam, amantadine, benztropine and diphenhydramine. Tardive dyskinesia involves the facial muscles after prolonged treatment, with puffing of the cheeks, protrusion of the tongue, chewing motions and pursing of the lips; it is typically irreversible, though symptoms may lessen after the drug is stopped. A young man on a new antipsychotic who cannot sit still, has involuntary muscle contractions, tremor, stiffness and involuntary facial movements is showing the whole family at once, and the drug most likely to have caused it in its usual dose range is the single-digit, high-affinity one: haloperidol rather than loxapine, olanzapine or clozapine.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Neurological side effects come from the nigrostriatal pathway; prolactin from the tuberoinfundibular; the antipsychotic effect itself from the mesocortical (and mesolimbic) tract.
  • Quetiapine sedates because of histamine H1 affinity, not because it blocks dopamine more strongly than haloperidol.
  • Low-potency drugs cause little EPS because their antimuscarinic action is built in; high-potency drugs cause EPS and prolactin elevation.
  • Antipsychotics cause parkinsonism, not Parkinson's disease; anticholinergics treat it, and propranolol is the choice for akathisia.
  • Typical and atypical drugs are equally effective; typicals give EPS, atypicals give metabolic effects; clozapine is the only drug that is different.
  • Dopamine receptors are GPCRs; D1-like raise cAMP and D2-like lower it; benzodiazepines act at GABA-A.
Count the digits in the daily dose. Ones (haloperidol, risperidone, paliperidone) means high D2 affinity: extrapyramidal symptoms and raised prolactin. Hundreds (chlorpromazine, clozapine, quetiapine) means low affinity: sedation, hypotension, constipation, and no EPS because the drug's own antimuscarinic effect is a built-in side-effect pill. The pathways explain the rest: nigrostriatal for parkinsonism, tuberoinfundibular for prolactin, mesolimbic for feeling bad, mesocortical for the therapeutic effect.

guides.title: Week 42 · 6 Schizophrenia: Treatment and Course
guides.html:
Wong L2 · AFP 2014 · NICE

Schizophrenia: Treatment and Course

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Treatment principles and the NICE points, the four-week rule and the refractory algorithm ending in clozapine and ECT, why clozapine and depots work best, clozapine's blood-count schedule, the efficacy and weight-gain rankings side by side, metabolic monitoring, the three named psychosocial treatments, the outcome statistics, and the two new non-D2 mechanisms.

Principles of treatment

Psychotic symptoms need urgent psychiatric referral; hospitalisation is for those who may pose a danger to themselves or others, not for every acute psychosis. The most effective treatment is multidisciplinary: medication, psychological treatment and social support. The goal is remission, defined as six months with no symptoms or mild symptoms that do not interfere with behaviour. Antipsychotics are first-line and should be started as soon as psychotic symptoms are recognised or the diagnosis is made; the initial choice is individualised by cost, adverse-effect profile, dosing regimen and patient preference, since the generations do not differ in effectiveness. Antipsychotics beat placebo for overall symptoms and relapse prevention; patients report better quality of life but more weight gain, sedation and movement disorders, and everyone who responds should be offered maintenance.

Response in the first two to four weeks is highly predictive of long-term response, though the maximal effect may take several months; an adequate trial is at least four weeks at a therapeutic dose before stopping or switching. For refractory illness the algorithm has four steps.

Little or no improvement after four weeks: switch antipsychotic and repeat the trial for four to six weeks. No response: clozapine. No response: consider electroconvulsive therapy. Two failed adequate trials is the operational definition of treatment resistance, and clozapine is its treatment.
NICE guideline pointDetail
ReferralAll persons presenting with psychotic symptoms are urgently referred to mental health services; a first presentation is not started on an antipsychotic in primary care unless in consultation with a psychiatrist
StartingOffer an antipsychotic at diagnosis; discuss risks and benefits; weigh potential adverse effects in the choice
NeverNo combination of antipsychotics; no loading dose
FormulationOral antipsychotics for acute exacerbations or recurrences
RelapsePatients are told of the high risk of relapse if therapy is discontinued within one to two years
Physical healthPhysical examination and cardiovascular risk assessment at least annually, shared with the psychiatrist
PsychologyCBT is offered to all persons with schizophrenia
Shared careStable responders may return to their family physician; re-refer for poor response, nonadherence, intolerable adverse effects, comorbid substance use, or threat to self or others

Choosing Wisely adds the same two prohibitions: no antipsychotic for any indication without initial evaluation and ongoing monitoring, and no routine prescribing of two or more antipsychotics at once.

Clozapine and depots work best

Clozapine and depot antipsychotics work best. A Finnish within-individual cohort of psychiatric rehospitalisation during monotherapy, compared with no antipsychotic, produced a forest plot of twenty formulations; the three best were long-acting injectable paliperidone (hazard ratio 0.51), long-acting zuclopenthixol (0.53) and oral clozapine (0.53). Every long-acting injectable beat its own oral form where both appeared (paliperidone, zuclopenthixol, olanzapine, risperidone, haloperidol, flupentixol); oral quetiapine (0.91) and oral flupentixol (0.92) sat at the bottom. The outcome is rehospitalisation, not symptom score, which is why the ranking is an adherence argument in numbers.

Depots are not superior pharmacology. A drug does not work if it is not in the body; an injection every two weeks, every month or, for the longest, every three months means the patient is medicated every day, whereas pills may not be taken. Across medicine, only about one third of patients take medication as prescribed; two thirds do not, or take a few doses and forget. That is probably why depots work: they are in there.

Clozapine is reserved for the patient who has not responded to other antipsychotics, and it is the only drug that is genuinely different. Its cost is monitoring for agranulocytosis: so a complete blood count weekly for six months, every two weeks for the next six months, then monthly; it is prescribed only by a psychiatrist. Its serious adverse effects also include myocarditis and seizures, with sedation, salivation, constipation, tachycardia and weight gain among the common ones. Two combinations are named for the emergency department when psychosis comes with agitation, always an antipsychotic plus a benzodiazepine: loxapine with lorazepam, or haloperidol with lorazepam, oral or by injection. De-escalation comes first: casual, respectful, non-confrontational; "you're not in trouble, we're here to help"; find common ground; do not argue with delusions but do not agree with or support them either; listen actively.

Choosing among the drugs: efficacy against weight

A 2019 network meta-analysis of 32 antipsychotics ranks them on two facing forest plots. For overall symptom change, clozapine (standardised mean difference −0.89) and amisulpride (−0.73) lead; olanzapine (−0.56), risperidone (−0.55), paliperidone (−0.49) and haloperidol (−0.47) sit in the middle; the weakest active drugs reach only about −0.2 against placebo at 0. For positive symptoms amisulpride (−0.69), clozapine (−0.64) and risperidone (−0.61) lead. Every antipsychotic beats placebo, by very different margins.

Sources differ: the lecturer said that older or newer, high or low potency, there is no clear pattern in efficacy; the slide behind him ranks 32 drugs with non-overlapping intervals at the extremes. Both are true at their own resolution: within the broad middle the drugs are interchangeable, but clozapine and amisulpride stand apart at the top, as the published meta-analysis (Huhn and colleagues, The Lancet 2019) shows. On an exam, clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic.

The facing plot is weight gain, the side effect with the greatest influence on overall health and mortality, because metabolic disease with hypertension and cardiovascular disease is the largest lifestyle-related illness group and antipsychotics contribute direct metabolic derangements.

DrugWeight change versus placebo (kg)
Ziprasidone−0.16, the only negative, interval crossing zero
Lurasidone+0.32
Aripiprazole+0.48
Haloperidol+0.54
Amisulpride+0.84
Risperidone+1.44
Paliperidone+1.49
Clozapine+1.89
Quetiapine+1.94
Olanzapine+2.78
Zotepine+3.21

The pairing is the point: clozapine, the most effective drug, is mid-table for weight; olanzapine, the second-generation workhorse, gains the most; ziprasidone gains nothing. Second-generation metabolic effects (weight, insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, lipid abnormalities) vary by drug, are not dose-dependent, and the weight gain is usually rapid in the first few weeks and then plateaus but can continue for a year or more.

Metabolic screening on a second-generation drugBaseline6 weeks12 weeksQuarterlyAnnually
Blood pressure, BMI, lifestyle counsellingYesYesYesYesYes
Fasting glucose, fasting lipidsYesYesYesYes
Medical history, waist circumferenceYesYes

Psychosocial treatment and optimal care

Three interventions are named with an indication each: family psychoeducation and support for relapse prevention; assertive community treatment teams to reduce relapse and hospitalisation in the severely ill; cognitive behavioural therapy for symptom reduction or relapse prevention, though it is uncommon. Housing and community supports remain a major problem, the tension being deinstitutionalisation against paternalism. The review adds social skills training and family interventions as adjuncts; CBT is the most used, but a Cochrane review found no clear evidence it is superior to other talking therapies. Combined psychosocial treatment and medication reduced discontinuation and relapse with absolute risk reductions of 14% and 8%, numbers needed to treat of 7 and 12. Comorbid anxiety, panic, PTSD and OCD are common; SSRIs and anxiolytics help those but do not treat schizophrenia itself.

Optimal treatment
Antipsychotic medication with stable and consistent adherence, chosen for the patient by side effects against target symptoms, with a depot considered and a clozapine trial if other antipsychotics fail. Social and functional supports: help with poor executive function and cognition, family or community treatment teams, psychoeducation, and practical assistance with housing, income and structured activities, individualised to the patient.

Course and outcome

Antipsychotics work for psychotic symptoms but do not change the overall functional outcome: the psychosis is treated and the patient's life is not made much better. Three numbers go with it.

  • Only 25% of patients stay on an antipsychotic for 18 months.
  • In chronic schizophrenia, under 10% reach symptomatic and functional remission after 18 months of treatment.
  • In first-episode schizophrenia, under 15% are in remission at five-year follow-up.
  • Antipsychotics do reduce relapse and hospitalisation.

Functional outcomes remain poor: unemployment and social isolation, with cognitive and negative symptoms greatly impairing employment and economic status in a modern information economy; homelessness, bad housing, marginalisation, poor physical health and few supports form a vicious cycle. The famous finding of better outcomes in low- and middle-income countries is named and doubted as likely an artefact of measurement biased toward higher-income countries. Course: about 20% can expect a positive outcome; despite adequate treatment one third remain symptomatic; most need some support but most live independently; predictors are not understood. Tolerance is real: a patient stable for years can relapse without ever stopping the drug, and constitutively blocking a receptor for years is, on first principles, not a great idea; intermittent dosing has been tried and the data are unclear.

Since chlorpromazine in the 1950s the number of mechanistically distinct antipsychotics has stayed at about three, while heart disease went from three or four to about fifteen; virtually all the new drugs are variations on old themes. Two genuinely new mechanisms exist. Xanomeline-trospium (KarXT): xanomeline is an orthosteric agonist of muscarinic M1 and M4 receptors that reduces ventral tegmental dopamine firing, the rationale being that clozapine's metabolite norclozapine is an M1 agonist; alone it causes intolerable diarrhoea, sweating and drooling, so it is paired with trospium, a peripheral anticholinergic. Ulotaront (SEP-363856): an agonist at trace amine-associated receptor 1 and serotonin 5-HT1A, a receptor family identified in 2001 that binds methamphetamine and the endogenous trace amines, published as a non-D2-binding drug for schizophrenia; ralmitaront is the second TAAR1 agonist. Both separated from placebo on PANSS totals in their trials.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Four weeks without improvement means switch, not add; NICE and Choosing Wisely both forbid antipsychotic combinations and loading doses.
  • Clozapine is indicated after two failed adequate trials; its monitoring is a weekly CBC for six months, fortnightly for six, then monthly.
  • Depots work through adherence, not potency; about one third of patients take medication as prescribed.
  • Most effective drug: clozapine. Most weight gain among common drugs: olanzapine. Least: ziprasidone. Metabolic effects are not dose-dependent.
