  • First-generation drugs need no laboratory monitoring; second-generation drugs need glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks, then annually.
  • Family psychoeducation prevents relapse; ACT reduces hospitalisation in the severely ill; CBT is offered to all but is uncommon in practice.
  • 25% stay on treatment at 18 months; under 10% chronic remission; under 15% first-episode remission at five years.
Start an antipsychotic at diagnosis, give it four weeks, switch once, then clozapine, then ECT. What keeps patients out of hospital is the drug being in the body, so depots and clozapine top the rehospitalisation ranking. Weigh clozapine's efficacy and the CBC schedule against olanzapine's kilograms, monitor metabolic parameters at 6 and 12 weeks then yearly, add family psychoeducation, ACT and CBT, and remember that only a quarter of patients are still taking the drug at 18 months.

guides.title: Week 42 · 7 Adverse Drug Reactions: Serotonin Syndrome and NMS
guides.html:
SLM01 · Lake · Vanessa's Law

Adverse Drug Reactions: Serotonin Syndrome and NMS

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The WHO and Gell and Coombs classifications and how they nest, the four management strategies, the four-tier severity scale and the reporting rules, safe prescription writing, the one-tablet serotonin-syndrome case, the toxicity spectrum and mechanisms, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and the comparison table that separates the two by history, clock and reflexes.

Adverse drug reactions: the numbers and the two systems

In the general population adverse drug reactions complicate 5 to 15% of all drug management. Rates in psychiatry are similar, but the risk with antipsychotics is about three times that of other drugs. Everyone is at risk, more so at the extremes of age, with impairment, and with polypharmacy. In the past 25 years 10% of drugs have been withdrawn from the market or given a black-box warning, which is why identifying an adverse reaction matters: it is an underestimated harm. The first triage question is whether the reaction is immune-mediated. Non-immune reactions go to the WHO classification, Types A to F; immune reactions go to the Gell and Coombs classification, Types I to IV. The two systems nest: every Gell and Coombs reaction is non-dose-related, unexpected and host-dependent, which is the definition of WHO Type B.

WHO typeNameDefining featuresExample
AAugmentedDose-related; expected. The most common typeSerotonin syndrome; neuroleptic malignant syndrome; a tenfold dosing error
BBizarreNon-dose-related; unexpected; host-dependent; pharmacological plus immunologicIdiosyncratic and hypersensitivity reactions; all Gell and Coombs types
CChronicDose-related and time-related, the only type with bothTardive dyskinesia after prolonged antipsychotic exposure
DDelayedTime-related; harm appears long after exposureTeratogenesis; secondary malignancy
EEnd of useWithdrawal symptoms on stoppingSSRI discontinuation syndrome; benzodiazepine withdrawal
FFailure of therapyAbsence of the intended effectOral contraceptive failure with an enzyme inducer such as St. John's Wort

The examples for Types C to F are the conventional ones. The traps are D against E (harm after a latency versus harm on stopping: a discontinuation syndrome is Type E) and remembering that F counts as an adverse reaction at all.

Gell and CoombsOnsetReactantAlso known asSignature
Type IMinutesIgE, mast cell activationAnaphylaxisHives, urticaria, bronchoconstriction, hypotension, shock
Type IIMinutes to hoursIgG against a cell-surface antigenCytotoxicHaemolytic anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia
Type IIIHoursIgG in soluble immune complexesImmune complexSerum sickness, fever, rash, arthralgia, urticaria, glomerulonephritis, vasculitis
Type IVDaysT-helper cellsDelayed hypersensitivityAllergic contact dermatitis, maculopapular rash

Onset time is the fastest discriminator. Types I to III are antibody-mediated and IV is cell-mediated, which is why only IV takes days. II and III both use IgG: II attacks a cell, III deposits a clump.

Managing, grading and reporting a reaction

There are four strategies, in order from least to most disruptive: (1) watch and wait; (2) change the dose and monitor, decreasing for a dose-related reaction and increasing for a withdrawal reaction; (3) discontinue the drug, which raises the question of which drug is the offender; (4) continue the drug and add another to treat the symptoms of the reaction. Classification dictates the direction of the dose change: call a Type E reaction Type A and you move the dose the wrong way.

SeverityCriteriaMatching strategyReport?
MildNo antidote or treatment; no medical attention neededWatch and waitNo
ModerateChange in treatment but not discontinuation; specific treatment may be required; medical attention may or may not be neededChange the dose, or continue and addNo
SevereRequires discontinuation, specific treatment of the reaction, and medical attentionDiscontinuePriority
LethalContributed directly or indirectly to deathThe outcome to preventPriority

Reporting to Health Canada is counterintuitive. A hospital reports under Vanessa's Law; the individual practitioner does not report a well-documented reaction to an older medication, because nothing is learned. Individual reports are prioritised for new drugs (under five years on the market), bizarre reactions, and severe or lethal reactions: report what is new, weird or catastrophic. The reporting decision therefore depends on having classified (Type B) and graded (severe) the reaction first.

Prescription writing is the same Type A lesson from the prescriber's side. Never a trailing zero (20.0 mg reads as 200 mg), always a leading zero (.5 reads as 5), never OD, QD, QOD or U (OD reads as right eye; QD as QID), always state the route, and order by dose rather than by fraction of a tablet. Of four orders, the correct one is "citalopram 20 mg po daily".

The case: one tablet, three serotonergic drugs

A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her sister at 1 a.m., agitated and disoriented, "like she was really drunk". She moved to the city three days ago, has been depressed for months with poor sleep and hyperphagia, and was started on citalopram 20 mg daily today by a new family doctor. Her sister adds that she had been avoiding the antidepressant and using natural products: St. John's Wort three times daily and L-tryptophan 1 g at bedtime for more than two months. No alcohol, drugs, cannabis or allergies. Only one tablet is missing from the citalopram vial. Vitals: heart rate 115, blood pressure 150/100, respiratory rate 26, temperature 39 °C, diaphoretic, oriented to person only; no rapid speech, logical thought, no hallucinations, no suicidal ideation. Labs and toxicology are pending and are never reported. A video shows the physical finding: hyperreflexia.

The pill count is the most important object in the case, and it works by a negative finding: one 20 mg tablet is a standard starting dose, so this is not an overdose and not a toxicity of citalopram alone. It must be an interaction with what was already on board. The timeline makes the single changed variable visible: two serotonergic agents ran for months without symptoms, a third was added today, and symptoms began the same day. The clean thought-form examination shows the altered mental status is toxidrome-driven, not psychiatric.

Three agents, three mechanisms: citalopram decreases serotonin reuptake; St. John's Wort decreases serotonin reuptake; L-tryptophan is a serotonin precursor. Diagnosis: serotonin syndrome. Type A, augmented, by a pharmacodynamic interaction, because two or more drugs have similar effects at the target site and the reaction is predictable, simply too much serotonin. The "dose" is the cumulative serotonergic burden, so a Type A reaction can occur at a normal dose of every individual drug. Severity: severe. Management: acutely stop all three drugs, since there is no single offender.
Sources differ: the poll asks which physical finding the video showed, and the module's timeline names hyperreflexia among the four presenting symptoms, but its severity table also stars myoclonus as one of her features. Hyperreflexia is the keyed answer, since the clip demonstrates an elicited reflex sign and hyperreflexia with clonus is the discriminator the module builds the syndrome around (Hunter criteria: clonus, hyperreflexia). Clonus is rhythmic and reflex-induced; myoclonus is spontaneous and arrhythmic. Lead-pipe rigidity would mean NMS; akathisia is a subjective symptom of dopamine blockade and cannot be elicited with a hammer.

Serotonin syndrome

It is a clinical diagnosis requiring a thorough medication review and physical examination; serum serotonin levels are unreliable and do not correlate with the presentation. The presentation is a triad of neuromuscular excitation, altered mental status and autonomic dysfunction, with onset within one hour in about 28% of patients and within six hours in 61%.

SeverityNeuromuscular excitationAltered mental statusAutonomic dysfunction
MildHyperreflexia, tremor, myoclonusAnxiety, restlessness, insomniaDiaphoresis, mydriasis, tachycardia
ModerateOpsoclonus; spontaneous or inducible clonusAgitationHypertension; hyperthermia under 40 °C; hyperactive bowel sounds; diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting
SevereRigidity, respiratory failure, tonic-clonic seizureComa, delirium, confusionSevere hyperthermia at or above 40 °C; dynamic blood pressure

The patient's eight findings (hyperreflexia, myoclonus, diaphoresis, tachycardia, agitation, hypertension, hyperthermia at 39 °C, confusion) straddle all three tiers: toxicity is a continuum and a patient is graded by her worst feature. Note what she lacks: no documented clonus, no rigidity, no seizure, no coma, no diarrhoea. The five mechanisms by which drugs raise serotonin are the map for any medication list.

MechanismAgents
Decrease serotonin uptakeSSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics; opioids (methadone, buprenorphine, tramadol, dextromethorphan); antiepileptics (carbamazepine, valproate); St. John's Wort
Decrease serotonin breakdownMAO inhibitors; linezolid
Increase serotonin releaseAmphetamines
Increase serotonin precursorsTryptophan; lithium, fentanyl and LSD are listed under the same heading, though strictly only tryptophan is a precursor
Prevent breakdown of drugsPharmacokinetic contributors that impair metabolism or elimination of a serotonergic drug

The non-obvious offenders are the examinable ones: tramadol, dextromethorphan in cough syrup, methadone, buprenorphine, fentanyl, linezolid, carbamazepine, valproate, lithium, St. John's Wort. Prevention has three principles: a complete medication history including over-the-counter and natural products before prescribing; education, telling patients to check with the pharmacist before self-selecting products; and safe washout periods when switching, most concerning with MAO inhibitors (conventionally two weeks off an MAOI, five weeks after fluoxetine). Management beyond stopping the drugs is supportive: benzodiazepines for agitation, active cooling, cyproheptadine in moderate to severe cases, sedation and intubation for the severest; antipyretics do not work because the heat is muscular, and restraints worsen it.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Incidence 0.01 to 0.2%, rare. It usually starts with mental status changes, then muscle rigidity, autonomic instability and hyperthermia: a patient who becomes confused after an antipsychotic dose increase is the earliest warning. It is Type A, linked directly to the drug's effects, fatal in 6 to 10% if untreated; 30% get rhabdomyolysis and 30% progress to acute kidney injury, the chain being rigidity, muscle breakdown, myoglobinuria, kidney injury. Creatine kinase is the key investigation; management is stopping the dopamine antagonist, aggressive intravenous fluids, cooling, benzodiazepines, dantrolene for severe rigidity and hyperthermia, bromocriptine or amantadine, and ECT when refractory; restart a lower-potency agent no sooner than two weeks after resolution.

Sources differ: the module's NMS slide says the mechanism is associated with increased central dopamine, while its own comparison table says NMS is precipitated by dopamine antagonists. The slide is in error: NMS is acute central D2 hypoactivity from antagonism, or from abrupt withdrawal of a dopamine agonist such as levodopa (StatPearls, Medscape). Answer decreased dopamine, D2 blockade. Both of the module's headline emergencies are Type A: predictable extensions of the drug's own pharmacology.
Serotonin syndromeNeuroleptic malignant syndrome
Precipitated bySerotonergic agentsDopamine antagonists
OnsetUnder 12 hours, abrupt1 to 3 days, gradual
Vital signs (identical)Hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hyperthermia over 40 °CThe same
Mucosa (identical)HypersalivationHypersalivation
Skin (overlapping)DiaphoresisDiaphoresis, pallor
Mental status (overlapping)Variable: agitation, comaVariable: stupor, coma, alert
Muscles (overlapping)Increased tone, especially lower extremitiesLead-pipe rigidity in all muscle groups
Reflexes (distinct)Hyperreflexia; clonus unless masked by toneHyporeflexia
Pupils (distinct)DilatedNormal
Bowel sounds (distinct)HyperactiveNormal or decreased

Work the table top-down. The history decides it: serotonergic agent or dopamine antagonist. Then the clock: hours versus days. Then the reflex hammer: serotonin excites, dopamine blockade stiffens and silences. Then pupils and bowel sounds. Never the vitals, which the table labels identical. In severe serotonin toxicity rigidity can mask the clonus, so absent clonus does not exclude it. Malignant hyperthermia is the operating-room cousin, a ryanodine-receptor reaction to volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine with masseter spasm and rising end-tidal carbon dioxide; extrapyramidal symptoms are D2 blockade without fever or autonomic instability. Lithium toxicity also gives ataxia and hyperreflexia and lithium sits on the serotonin mechanism figure; the lithium level and a precipitant (a new NSAID, ACE inhibitor or thiazide, or a diarrhoeal illness) separate it. Same vitals, opposite reflexes, different drugs, different clock.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Type A is dose-related and expected and is the most common; Type B is host-dependent and contains every Gell and Coombs reaction; Type C alone is both dose- and time-related.
  • A withdrawal reaction is Type E and is managed by increasing the dose; a delayed reaction is Type D.
  • Serotonin syndrome and NMS are both Type A; a Type A reaction can occur at a normal dose of each drug when the burden is cumulative.
  • Serum serotonin is useless; the diagnosis is medication history plus examination, and 61% present within six hours.
  • Hospitals report under Vanessa's Law; individuals report new drugs, bizarre reactions and severe or lethal reactions.
  • Hyperreflexia, clonus, dilated pupils and hyperactive bowel sounds mean serotonin; lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia and normal pupils mean NMS.
  • NMS begins with mental status change; 6 to 10% mortality untreated; 30% rhabdomyolysis.
Classify first, because classification drives the dose direction and the reporting decision. Serotonin syndrome is a clinical triad after a serotonergic agent, abrupt within hours, hyperreflexic with clonus, dilated pupils and hyperactive bowels; NMS follows a dopamine antagonist over one to three days, begins with confusion, and is lead-pipe rigid and hyporeflexic with normal pupils. The vitals are identical; the drug history and the reflex hammer decide it. In the case, one tablet plus two hidden natural products made a severe Type A reaction, and the treatment was to stop all three.

guides.title: Week 42 · 8 Personality Disorders and Validation
guides.html:
PD workshop · CAMH BPD Clinic · DBT

Personality Disorders and Validation

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What the exam wants from personality disorders, why they are neither a separate axis nor mild, the categorical-versus-dimensional debate, schizoid against schizotypal against schizophrenia, and the DBT skill of validation: its definition and effect, what it is not, the five levels with worked lines, validating the emotion and not the belief, the and-statement, and disappointment after self-harm.

What the examiners want from personality disorders

The Friday hour was a flipped classroom run by two CAMH psychiatrists, one from the Borderline Personality Disorder clinic and an expert in dialectical behaviour therapy. The didactic content lives in the five personality-disorder self-learning modules, four of which are about borderline personality disorder; the contact hour was a question-and-answer session followed by one clinical skill, validation. Their guidance on scope is the closest thing the week has to a statement of what the questions will look like.

  • Not every criterion for every personality disorder is needed. The other disorders are examined by gestalt, with obvious prompts, and the two most often asked are narcissistic personality disorder and borderline personality disorder.
  • The only criteria to memorise are the borderline criteria, for practice, for the exam, for an OSCE station and for the licensing examination. Two acronyms exist for them, in the way MSIGECAPS serves depression and GSTPAID serves bipolar disorder. A multiple-choice item is unlikely to be that complicated; an OSCE-format encounter is where the criteria matter.
  • Personality disorders are ordinary DSM disorders. Older editions put them on a separate axis with what is now intellectual disability, as lifelong conditions; that separation is gone.
  • They are not less pathological. Patients with borderline personality disorder function at levels comparable to schizophrenia, and life expectancy is reduced by an estimated 12 to 20 years depending on the study.
  • The categorical-versus-dimensional debate concerns personality disorders in general more than borderline disorder in particular. The ICD has moved to dimensional diagnosis for the other personality disorders but kept borderline personality disorder as a category, because it is well studied with established treatments; the DSM has not changed. The diagnoses still exist and still need to be known.
  • Self-diagnosing during the psychiatry block is normal: psychiatric conditions stem from evolutionarily adaptive traits gone awry, and what makes a disorder is severity and effect on functioning.
Cluster A against schizophrenia
Schizophrenia has full delusions (fixed false beliefs) and full hallucinations, usually auditory, in a constellation of symptom types; affective flattening alone is not sufficient. Schizotypal personality disorder has sub-syndromal positive symptoms only: unusual beliefs and illusions, seeing shadows the person can question, never full hallucinations. Schizoid personality disorder has no positive symptoms at all, only negative-type symptoms such as affective flattening. The same holds from the schizophrenia side: Cluster A is genetically related to schizophrenia and sits below the psychotic threshold, and a person with a Cluster A diagnosis who later develops schizophrenia had schizophrenia all along, before the age of onset.

Two further points from the questions. Relationship instability in borderline personality disorder need not run across every relationship: romantic only, family only, or across the board all satisfy the criterion. The internet's "favourite person" idea has no evidence base yet, may have more to do with autism than with borderline disorder (the two co-occur), and is not going to be on the exam.

Validation

Validation is expressing an understanding of what makes sense about what is going on for someone else, and receiving validation decreases emotional arousal. It is the tool for the patient who is yelling or who has had bad encounters with clinicians before. It matters in borderline personality disorder because the disorder develops in part from emotional invalidation, so these patients are more sensitive to it; validation is the clinical corollary of the invalidating-environment half of the biosocial model, in which an emotionally vulnerable temperament meets an invalidating environment. It is not a soft skill that is merely nice: it makes assessment faster and more effective. A patient admitted for suicidal thoughts, vomiting in the back of the emergency department and too distressed to be examined, settled once the clinician said this must be so hard, here for a mental-health crisis and now a stomach problem too, and the medical assessment could proceed.

Validation is notBecause
Praise, agreement or reinforcementOne can totally disagree with someone, or watch them do something unhelpful, and still validate their perspective
Asking questionsIn dialectical behaviour therapy a question is a change strategy, pushing for change, and can make a dysregulated person more dysregulated; the shut-down patient cannot handle questions in that moment
Problem-solvingPeople often cannot engage in problem-solving until they have first been validated; opening with validation gets the person's brain back online

The levels get more validating up the list. The live teaching used one running patient statement: "You started me on this medication and now my vision's all messed up and no one's taking me seriously."

LevelWhat it isWorked line
1 Appearing interestedNot something said: facial expression, posture, full attention. With electronic records and phones, medicine is distracted; with a dysregulating patient, do the note afterwards, which may save time in the long run. Make eye contact, do not look bored, do not look at your computerNon-verbal
2 Simple reflectionReflect back a chunk of exactly what the person said, choosing the part that is understandable, then leave it there without jumping to questions or solutions. Feels uncomfortable at first; practise it"Oh, wow, your vision's off. Oh my."
3 Mind readingGuess at something the person has not said; often underneath anger is fear. More validating but riskier: a wrong guess is invalidating, so be tentative ("I'm guessing you must be worried", never "you're really worried") and back off if wrong"Oh my God, you must be really worried. That sounds scary."
4 Makes sense for this person given their contextTheir history. Validate only what is valid: not "I am not taking you seriously" when that is untrue, but "it makes sense you'd be worried I won't""You've told me medical professionals have missed things before. I can see why you'd worry I won't take this seriously."
5 Makes sense for anyoneThe most validating level. Prefer 5 over 4 when both apply: "that makes sense, you've had a lot of breakups" is less validating than "of course you're upset, anyone would be", because a level-4 statement can itself invalidate"I can see why you're so worried about your vision. Anyone would be."
Sources differ: the module slide reproduced in the workshop deck lists six ways to be validating, the sixth being "be genuine, authentic, cheerleading", while the live teaching presented five levels and never mentioned the sixth. The five map onto the slide's first five items. Answer the slide's six if asked to list the module; answer the five levels, with level five the most validating, if asked how they are ranked. In Linehan's own hierarchy the sixth level, radical genuineness, treating the patient as an equal rather than as fragile, is the highest.

Emotions are always valid. When nothing else fits, validate that the emotion makes sense. With a patient with schizophrenia, the delusion is not validated, but "I can see how scared you are" is. When the emotion is out of proportion there is always a grain of truth: validate the emotion, not its size. Not "it makes sense you're so angry you're throwing chairs", but "I can see how angry you are right now, and it seems it's because I'm going on vacation". With a delusion, "it makes sense to be scared if you think people are poisoning the food": the emotion given the belief, without the belief. The intensity, amplitude, duration and threshold may all be off; the emotion itself is valid.

Say "and", never "but". Pair validation with an and-statement to add the clinician's own view: "it makes sense to me that you want to be admitted, and at the same time I don't think that's going to be helpful for you." Something about English makes "but" dismiss all the validation that came before it.

After self-harm, warmth can reinforce the behaviour, and validation is not the only useful thing: a little genuine disappointment is also useful. In clinic, "oh, shoot, that's too bad, I'm sorry to hear that", then an and-statement: "I know you've been working on this really hard, and let's see what we can do." In the emergency department, "ouch, that sounds really ineffective for you", calling a spade a spade rather than moving in with "poor thing".

The demonstration

A surgeon at ankle-surgery follow-up meets a patient with a written list, worried the wound is infected, who talks over the surgeon. In the first take the surgeon interrupts: "we only have fifteen minutes"; the patient protests that she has not got through the list. In the second take: "I can totally see why you'd want to make sure we cover everything and nothing gets missed, and it's great you've been so diligent taking notes. At the same time, if we go through the whole list at once I might not remember every item, so could we take each point one at a time?" The patient agrees. The ankle shows oedema, not infection; she stopped her diuretic because she kept forgetting doses and gave up. "I can see how you want to take the medication properly as indicated. At the same time it's important to treat the swelling. Would you be willing to start again, even if you sometimes forget a dose?" The lesson: weave a validating statement in before anything else, then use the and-statement to be helpful; some doses beat none.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Memorise the borderline criteria; recognise the rest by gestalt; expect narcissistic and borderline disorder to be the ones asked.
  • Borderline personality disorder is not mild: functioning comparable to schizophrenia and 12 to 20 years of lost life expectancy.
  • Validation lowers arousal; it is not praise, not a question, not a solution.
  • Level 3 is the risky one: tentative wording, and back off if wrong. Level 5 beats level 4.
  • Validate the emotion given the belief, never the belief; validate the emotion, never its size.
  • "And", not "but"; disappointment, not warmth, after self-harm.
  • Schizotypal: odd beliefs and illusions. Schizoid: negative symptoms only. Schizophrenia: full delusions and hallucinations in a constellation.
Validation says what makes sense in the other person's experience and brings arousal down so assessment can happen. Appear interested, reflect, guess tentatively, make sense of it in their history, or best of all say anyone would feel this; when nothing else works, the emotion is always valid. Then the clinician's own view follows with "and". For the exam, know the borderline criteria, treat the other personality disorders as gestalt, and separate schizoid, schizotypal and schizophrenia by the presence and completeness of positive symptoms.

guides.title: Week 42 · 9 Assessing Children and Adolescents, and Ontario Law
guides.html:
Klein · child psychiatry · HCCA and CYFSA

Assessing Children and Adolescents, and Ontario Law

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Why child psychiatry matters in numbers, the four-part interview and developmentally phrased safety questions, the history template with strengths and HEADSS, the milestone list, the youth mental status examination with parent-child interaction, the impression template and management framework, the biopsychosocio-cultural model and the four Ps, and Ontario's rules on confidentiality, consent, capacity and mandatory reporting.

Why child psychiatry

20% of children experience a mental health disorder, and 70% of adults with psychiatric disorders report symptom onset before 18: the entire justification for the specialty. Before 2018 youth emergency visits and hospitalisations for mental health rose; from 2022 to 2025 care shifted toward the community (physicians and agencies) with fewer emergency and inpatient contacts, while mood and anxiety medication use by youth rose across 2015 to 2024. Mental health accounts for about a fifth of all youth hospital admissions, and only one in five Canadian children receive appropriate mental health services. The peak age of onset of mental illness is 15, with up to 75% of onset by 25; adult disorders are often chronic with multiple relapses; mental illness is the largest and most rapidly growing cause of disability; and youth are less likely than any other age group to access services, blocked by stigma, low mental health literacy, poor access and inadequate system structure. Early intervention is integral to basic healthcare: early psychosis intervention, parenting programmes (Triple P and SNAP), and mood and anxiety programmes.

Children are not little adults

Assessment, language and diagnostic thresholds must be developmentally calibrated; every paediatric modification in the week (irritable mood in depression, one-year dysthymia, generalised anxiety needing only one of six symptoms) follows from this. The interview has a fixed order: start together, child and parents, to set the frame and observe the parent-child interaction; the child separately for confidential material; the parents separately for collateral, developmental and family history; then come back together for summary and feedback. Rapport comes from age-appropriate plain language without jargon, play and drawing, a break, water or a snack, a friendly introduction ("I am a doctor who helps kids and teens with big feelings"), and structure.

StageAgeTechnique
Infant and preschool0 to 6Play, games, art, drawing
Latency, school age7 to 11Play remains important but the child is more capable of dialogue
Adolescence12 to 18Interview with and without parents
Safety is asked in developmental language. To a 9-year-old: "do you ever think about not wanting to be alive?" To a 15-year-old: "do you ever have suicidal thoughts?" Same question, translated.

The history template: identifying data (age, family, school, activities, school supports and IEP, parental employment and finances); strengths, a named standalone section; reason for referral (commonly low mood, anxiety, suicidal ideation or behaviour, self-harm); history of presenting illness, listening for at least the first five minutes, then enquiring about each symptom category (mood, anxiety, OCD, substances, mania and psychosis) and safety: suicidal ideation with plan and intent, homicidal ideation, self-harm past and present; past psychiatric history (hospitalisations, emergency visits, therapy, medication trials, attempts, self-harm); past medical history (asthma, seizures, traumatic brain injury); family psychiatric history including medications and suicide; medications including over-the-counter and natural products; allergies and the reaction; past personal history (pregnancy, delivery, temperament, sleep, feeding; milestones in language, social, gross and fine motor, cognitive; friends); family; school; gender, sexual orientation and sexuality; trauma; and "three wishes, hopes for the future". The psychosocial mnemonic is HEADSS: home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide and self-harm.

MilestoneAge
Smile6 weeks
Roll over3 months
Sit6 months
Crawl6 to 9 months
Walk, first words12 to 18 months
Two words together2 years
Tricycle3 years

A child who talked at two and a half, against a norm of 12 to 18 months for first words, had a speech delay. That is the only milestone list of the week.

The mental status examination in youth

Appearance (as stated age, kempt, dishevelled, malodorous); behaviour (calm, cooperative, agitated, movements); speech (rate, rhythm, volume, pressured, latency); eye contact; mood in the patient's own words; affect (euthymic, dysthymic, elevated; full versus restricted; congruent versus incongruent); safety (suicidal ideation, self-harm, homicidal ideation, plan and intent); thought form (goal-directed, tangential, circumstantial, thought blocking, loose associations); thought content (delusions: paranoid, grandiose, somatic); perceptual disturbances (auditory and visual hallucinations); cognition (oriented to time, person and place, grossly intact though not formally assessed); insight and judgement (good, partial, limited, poor); and the paediatric extra, parent-child interaction, observed in the together-at-the-start segment. It is the domain an adult-trained examiner forgets, and therefore the one examined.

The impression, as a template
Age plus duration plus core symptoms, then pertinent negatives about safety, then the precipitating context, then family history, then the diagnostic statement with a severity specifier. "A 15-year-old youth who presents with 8 weeks of significantly low mood with anhedonia, poor sleep, low appetite and energy, social isolation, poor academic performance and attendance. No suicidal ideation, no plan or intent. This comes in the context of a friend-group rupture. There is a family history of bipolar disorder, anxiety and depression. Her presentation is most in keeping with major depressive disorder, moderate." The diagnosis line lists the differential and rule-outs: "MDD, rule out GAD."

The management framework, numbered with one number missing: (1) safety: a safety plan including coping strategies, the emergency department if acutely unsafe, crisis lines, walk-in clinics, community resources; (2) investigations: collateral first, then psychometric scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7, SNAP-IV), then bloodwork (CBC, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, liver and lipid profiles, ferritin, TSH, B12 and folate); (4) psychopharmacology (SSRIs, psychostimulants); (5) psychotherapy (individual, group, family, parent coaching); (6) school: psychoeducational assessment and recommended accommodations; (7) community, such as cultural and social groups; (8) other: bibliotherapy, apps, websites. School is a management modality, the paediatric-specific move. The scales map to their targets: PHQ-9 for depression, GAD-7 for anxiety, SNAP-IV for ADHD with parent and teacher versions, which is how the two-settings criterion is evidenced.

Formulation uses a three-circle biopsychosocio-cultural model: biological (physical health, disabilities, genetic predisposition, neurochemistry, immune response), psychological (beliefs, behaviour, personality, self-esteem, coping, emotions, social skills), and social, cultural and environmental (peers, family circumstances, cultural traditions, social support, education, poverty). The bridging items are placed deliberately: drug effects between biological and social, temperament between biological and psychological, family relationships and life events between social and psychological, and mental health alone at the centre. Three circles, not four; culture is folded into the social circle. The four Ps organise the case: predisposing (family history, ADHD and a learning disability, sensitive temperament), precipitating (the proximate trigger, such as friends dropping her ten weeks before an eight-week low mood), perpetuating (a protective activity lost, such as swimming stopped a year earlier), and protective. Searching self-harm online is a consequence, not a cause.

Ontario law: confidentiality, consent, reporting

Confidentiality balances autonomy and protection; the high-risk behaviours are substance use, sexual behaviour and suicidality. Be clear at the start: everything discussed is private and goes into a report to the family doctor, and the only limits are concern about safety: harm to yourself, harm to others, safety of young children under 16, and driving safety. What the youth shares alone stays private from parents as long as it is not unsafe. The two limits people forget, children under 16 and driving, are the two that get tested.

Consent and capacityRule
StatuteHealth Care Consent Act, 1996
Minimum ageThere is no fixed minimum age for consenting to medical treatment in Ontario
CapacityUnderstand the treatment and appreciate the consequences of treatment versus no treatment; both limbs required
DefaultPresumption of capacity; the mature minor doctrine; capacity is decision-specific

A capable 15-year-old, not her parents, consents to disclosing the impression to the family. Mandatory reporting falls under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. A physician with reasonable grounds to suspect that a child under 16 has experienced or is at risk of abuse or neglect must immediately and directly report to a Children's Aid Society, must not rely on anyone else to report on their behalf, and must file a further report on new grounds. For a child aged 16 or 17, reporting is permitted but not required. The threshold is suspicion, not proof; the duty is personal and non-delegable, so telling a supervisor or the school does not discharge it; and it is ongoing. The under-16 threshold matches the confidentiality script.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • 70% of adult psychiatric illness begins before 18; peak onset 15; 75% by 25; one in five children get appropriate care.
  • Interview order: together, child alone, parents alone, together again. Strengths and parent-child interaction are the paediatric additions to history and mental status examination.
  • First words at 12 to 18 months; two words at 2; tricycle at 3.
  • Management: safety, then collateral before bloodwork, then medication, therapy, school, community, other.
  • Confidentiality has four limits; consent has no minimum age; capacity is understand plus appreciate, presumed.
  • Under 16: must report on suspicion, personally, immediately, and again on new grounds. 16 or 17: may report.
  • Precipitating means proximate; a family history predisposes; an online search for self-harm is a symptom.
Calibrate everything to development: interview together, then apart, then together; ask a 9-year-old about not wanting to be alive and a 15-year-old about suicidal thoughts; add strengths to the history and parent-child interaction to the mental status examination; manage safety first and school as a modality. In Ontario there is no age of consent, capacity is understand and appreciate and is presumed, confidentiality has four limits, and a suspicion about a child under 16 must be reported to the Children's Aid Society by you, now, and again if new grounds arise.

guides.title: Week 42 · 10 Youth Anxiety and Depression
guides.html:
Klein · child psychiatry · CBT first

Youth Anxiety and Depression

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Anxiety as the most common youth disorder and its four-step developmental sequence, the individual disorders with their paediatric clues and the one-of-six rule for generalised anxiety, the two paediatric modifications to major depression, the epidemiology and survey data, the organic mimics and baseline panel, and management with CBT as gold standard, off-label SSRIs and the black-box warning to age 24.

Anxiety: the most common disorder in youth

Anxiety disorders are the most common psychiatric disorder in youth. At any time nearly 7% of youth globally have one; 6 to 10% of children, with a median onset at 11; lifetime prevalence 20 to 30%, female more than male after puberty; comorbidity with other anxiety disorders, depression and ADHD is high. The four most common disorders are also a developmental sequence, and the order is the likeliest single question from the block.

OrderDisorderTypical age of emergence
1Separation anxietyEarly childhood
2Specific phobiaEarly school age
3Social anxietyLate school age, early teens
4Generalised anxietyMid to late teens

Anxiety moves outward across development: from the caregiver, to a specific object, to the peer group, to abstract future events.

DisorderCore featurePrevalence and onsetPaediatric clues
Separation anxiety disorderDevelopmentally inappropriate, excessive fear of separation from an attachment figure12-month prevalence 4% in children, 1.6% in adolescents; lifetime 8%
Social anxiety disorderMarked fear of social settings and others' scrutiny7% (9% in the US); median onset 13Crying, tantrums, freezing, clinging, shrinking in peer settings; trouble with presentations, ordering food, eating in public, using the phone
Generalised anxiety disorderExcessive anxiety, difficult to control, over 6 months, plus only 1 of 6: restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance1 to 2% of adolescentsWorries about performance, school, sports, somatic symptoms, reassurance seeking, perfectionism, difficulty with transitions
Specific phobiaMarked fear of a specific situation5% of children, 16% of adolescents; lifetime 20%Spiders, needles, dogs, the dark, vomiting
Selective mutismConsistent failure to speak where speaking is expected, despite speaking elsewhere, over 1 monthRare, 0.03 to 2%
Panic disorder2% of teens; rare before puberty
Agoraphobia2% of teens
School avoidanceClinically common but not a DSM diagnosis: name the underlying disorder
Sources differ: the slide's generalised anxiety criterion for youth requires only one of the six associated symptoms, whereas the adult criterion requires three. Both are correct: the DSM-5-TR itself states that only one item is required in children. Expect "one of six" for a child and "three of six" for an adult.

Depression in youth

The criteria are the same as adult major depressive disorder (mood, sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicide) with two paediatric modifications: the mood can be irritable instead of low, and persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) needs only one year rather than the adult two. The youth phenotype has more irritability, labile mood, loss of energy, somatic symptoms, appetite and sleep change, as against the adult's anhedonia and low mood; children show more somatic concern, anxiety and psychomotor agitation, adolescents more hypersomnia and mood reactivity. More than 60% of youth with major depression have a comorbid diagnosis. Onset before adulthood predicts greater adult severity (more episodes, admissions, self-harm and suicide attempts) and worse physical health (obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease) and social and occupational outcomes.

MeasureFigure
Lifetime prevalence11% (severe 3%)
One-year prevalence7.5% (severe 2.3%)
Cumulative incidence by 1820%
Recurrence by 2160%
Later anxietyTwice the risk
Self-reported suicidal ideation5.5% of males, 10.7% of females
Self-reported suicide attempt4.3%
Pandemic global adolescent depression and anxiety25% and 20%
Canadian 15- to 24-year-olds with depression11%; the highest rates of mood and anxiety disorders of any age group
Poor or fair mental health, 15 to 1720%, female more than male
Unmet mental health need, ages 2 to 17, 202436%, greater for girls
What it looks like in the office
A 15-year-old in grade 10 with ADHD and a reading disability is brought by her parents with eight weeks of low mood. She spends all day in bed, cannot sleep at night and sleeps by day, will not come to meals and is losing weight, has no energy and "feels heavy", showers once a week despite encouragement, has not attended school for six weeks and says she "can't do it", and has stopped the crocheting and painting she loved. Her friends dropped her ten weeks ago and blocked her. She will not talk to her parents and is always on her device; they found searches about self-harm and panicked because of the family history. Mood, sleep, interest, energy, appetite, psychomotor slowing and hygiene are all there, in the youth pattern of somatic complaint and withdrawal rather than stated sadness; the friend-group rupture is the precipitant; the self-harm searches are the safety question that must be asked directly.

Self-reported positive mental health fell over six years; by 2023 about a fifth of youth who had reported good mental health in 2019 reported it as fair or poor, with the biggest declines in girls, older teens and transitional-aged youth. Youth often do not share their parents' opinion of their mental health, which is the clinical reason the interview separates child and parents: self-report and collateral disagree, and both are needed.

PresentationOrganic mimics to rule out
AnxietyHyperthyroidism, sympathomimetics, diabetes, hypoglycaemia, substance use, phaeochromocytoma, caffeine
DepressionHypothyroidism, anaemia, vitamin deficiencies, brain injury, viral illness, chronic pain

The baseline panel is the same for both: CBC, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, liver and lipid profiles, ferritin, TSH, B12 and folate. Anxiety points to hyperthyroidism, depression to hypothyroidism.

Management

Psychosocial: psychoeducation; lifestyle, "sleeping enough, eating enough and moving enough"; safety planning; supportive management; school and family involvement; community supports. Psychotherapy: CBT is the gold standard, with interpersonal psychotherapy for adolescents the named alternative for depression. Pharmacology: SSRIs are used clinically for moderate to severe anxiety and depression, but no SSRI is approved by Health Canada for these paediatric indications, so all such prescribing is off-label and belongs in the consent discussion. Medication is added for high impairment, limited progress with CBT, or to increase CBT's effectiveness. Side effects: gastrointestinal, headache, insomnia or sedation, dry mouth, blurred vision; rare and serious: suicidal ideation, mania, serotonin syndrome.

FDA black-box warning, 2004: close observation for the emergence of suicidality, up to age 24. The number is 24, not 18; the monitoring window runs past the paediatric range into transitional-aged youth. Health Canada's non-approval and the FDA's boxed warning are two different regulators saying two different things; do not conflate them.
Sources differ: the slide pairs a US regulator's warning with a Canadian regulator's approval status. Both are correct and distinct: the FDA boxed warning on antidepressants and suicidality dates from 2004 and was extended to age 24 in 2007, and Health Canada has approved no SSRI for paediatric depression or anxiety (fluoxetine is FDA-approved for paediatric depression but not Health Canada-approved). Answer "up to 24" for monitoring and "no Health Canada approval" as printed.

The case resolution follows the framework: the 15-year-old shares alone, consents to a joint discussion, the family accepts the diagnosis of major depressive disorder and is open to individual and family therapy, medication is considered, follow-up is in two weeks (the black-box observation), and a safety plan is in place: the emergency department if acutely unsafe, distraction, and asking for help.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Separation, phobia, social, generalised: the four most common anxiety disorders in the order they emerge.
  • Youth generalised anxiety needs one of six symptoms; selective mutism needs one month; generalised anxiety needs six months.
  • School refusal is a presentation, not a diagnosis.
  • Irritable mood counts; youth dysthymia is one year; over 60% of depressed youth have a comorbidity.
  • Lifetime depression 11%, cumulative 20% by 18, recurrence 60% by 21.
  • Anxiety: rule out hyperthyroidism. Depression: rule out hypothyroidism. Ferritin, TSH, B12 are on the panel.
  • CBT first; SSRIs off-label in Canada; watch for suicidality to age 24.
Anxiety is the commonest youth disorder and emerges outward, from separation to phobia to social to generalised, with the child needing only one associated symptom for generalised anxiety. Depression keeps the adult criteria but allows irritable mood and one-year dysthymia, comes with comorbidity in most cases, and recurs in 60% by 21. Rule out thyroid disease in both directions, treat with CBT first, add an SSRI off-label for impairment or poor progress, and observe for suicidality to age 24.

guides.title: Week 42 · 11 ADHD: Presentation and Assessment
guides.html:
SLM02 · Richards-Bentley · Klein

ADHD: Presentation and Assessment

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Executive functioning and its nine domains, the seven categories behind executive dysfunction, the ADHD criteria with both symptom lists, why adult ADHD is missed through internalisation, intelligence and transitions, the comorbidity map for depression, anxiety, emotion dysregulation and substance use, and adult screening with the self-report scale and the CADDRA checklist.

Executive functioning

Executive functioning is the set of processes for managing ourselves and our internal resources in order to achieve a goal. It runs on distributed neural networks rather than one location: the prefrontal cortex is the mainframe (working memory, planning, motivation, impulse control, avoiding distraction); the parietal cortex decides what should hold attention, holds visuospatial working memory and interprets sensory input so plans stay effective; the basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum complete the network, and disorders may involve the networks, the white matter connecting them or the transmitters they use. Nine domains are defined, each with a clinical example.

DomainDefinitionClinical example
InhibitionStopping ourselves from acting on impulse; redirecting thoughtsNot checking the phone during rounds
ShiftingMoving freely between situations; thinking flexibly as circumstances changeManaging several patients' acuity at once in the emergency department
Emotional controlBringing thought to bear on feelingsSharing a poor prognosis
InitiationStarting a task in a timely manner; generating ideas and strategies independentlyKeeping track of time while history-taking and knowing when to shift topic
Working memoryHolding information in mind to complete a taskRemembering the history until you can chart
Planning and organisationBreaking a task into a step-by-step series of actionsOrganising an approach to a licensing exam
Task monitoringAssessing progress toward a goal and adjusting plan or paceSpotting holes in a history and going after them
Organisation of materialsManaging our "stuff": work, play and storage spacesKeeping track of the stethoscope on the wards
Self-monitoringMonitoring our own emotions and behaviour against what is expectedBehaving professionally with patients

Executive dysfunction is not itself a diagnosis, and it is non-specific: the same complaint belongs to seven categories, neurodevelopmental (ADHD, autism), anxiety (generalised anxiety), psychosis (schizophrenia), substance (cannabis use disorder), mood (major depression), neurocognitive (Alzheimer's disease) and other medical (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency). Some people have extreme executive dysfunction with no psychiatric diagnosis, and when disorders co-occur their effects compound. That list is the differential for adult ADHD.

The disorder and its criteria

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder that leads to difficulties with inattention, with hyperactivity and impulsivity, or with both. Prevalence is 5 to 8% of youth and 2 to 4% of adults, similar across cultures and stable for thirty years. The framing criteria: symptoms occur often, for at least 6 months, in 2 or more settings, with several present before age 12, causing impairment, and not better explained by another disorder; 6 or more of 9 symptoms in a domain, or 5 or more at age 17 and older. Presentations are predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined. Significant comorbidity with mood and anxiety disorders; the rating scale is the SNAP-IV, in parent and teacher versions, which is how two settings are evidenced.

Inattention (9)Hyperactivity and impulsivity (9)
Poor attention to detail, careless mistakesFidgets or squirms
Difficulty sustaining attentionLeaves seat when sitting is expected
Does not seem to listen when spoken toRuns or climbs; in adults, feeling restless
Does not follow through on instructions, fails to finish workUnable to play or do fun things quietly
Difficulty organising tasks and activitiesAlways on the go, driven by a motor
Avoids tasks requiring sustained mental effortTalks excessively
Loses things needed for tasksBlurts out answers before the question is finished
Easily distracted by extraneous stimuliDifficulty awaiting turn
Forgetful in daily activitiesInterrupts or intrudes on others
Sources differ: the two Week 42 decks each print only eight inattention items, and different ones: the child psychiatry slide omits "easily distracted by extraneous stimuli" and the adult module's list omits "does not follow through and fails to finish work", both beside a printed threshold of six. The CADDRA checklist, and DSM-5-TR, list nine in each domain. Expect "6 of 9", and "5 for age 17 and older". The hyperactivity items are translated for adults: running and climbing becomes feeling restless.

Why adult ADHD is missed

  • Symptoms change across the lifespan. Hyperactivity and impulsivity become more internalised with age: the fidgety child becomes the adult who works hard to suppress an internal need to move. The majority with childhood ADHD remain symptomatic and impaired into adulthood, though it is less likely to be recognised. Female and gender-diverse patients have more internalised symptoms that are harder to spot or are attributed to other diagnoses.
  • Doing well in school does not rule it out. People with ADHD can hyperfocus when interested, stimulated or under pressure, and IQ compensates for the impairments and forestalls diagnosis: higher IQ correlates with later diagnosis, sometimes delaying treatment. "How did you do in school?" does not exclude ADHD in a medical student.
  • ADHD presents at transitions, ranked: abrupt loss of structure first, then rising demands for self-regulation, then more available distraction and immediate reward. The university student moving into residence loses the structure of parents and teachers, must now regulate bed, meals and class attendance, and faces screens beside the textbook and parties down the hall; early parenthood is the same model.
  • Academics: lower GPA in all years, lower graduation and more probation, worse timed-test performance, missed deadlines, and lower writing quality even after controlling for impulsive mistakes. Compared with learning disabilities, ADHD brings worse time management, concentration, selection of main ideas and test-taking, and less support in secondary school. Students with inattentive symptoms report lower academic adjustment, lower career-decision self-efficacy, and a sense that they must work harder for the same result.

Comorbidity and confounders

ConditionOverlap and discriminator
Major depressionRestlessness, motivation and concentration belong to both; ADHD adds difficulty shutting off an active mind at bedtime, irregular fatigue, chronic demoralisation and poor self-esteem. Assess for episodic disturbance: look for distinct depressive episodes with wellness between, and ask whether the ADHD signs persisted during the well periods; check for mood factors such as a new academic year or parenthood.
AnxietyCorrelates with ADHD, especially in girls and women, and with more frequent trauma and harder recovery, since a scattered mind struggles to build a coherent narrative. Treating the ADHD mitigates ADHD-related anxiety. Distractibility can masquerade as social anxiety; the difficulty tolerating the boredom of switching off and initiating sleep can masquerade as generalised anxiety.
Emotion dysregulationCommon and self-rated as extreme: 55% of adults with ADHD score in the 95th percentile. When a patient presents with emotion dysregulation, ask whether untreated ADHD is a factor.
Substance useGreater risk of misuse even controlling for amount used. Ask for the pattern underlying the use: cannabis at the end of the day to calm a scattered mind, stimulants to overcome task inertia, attempts to microdose; that reveals untreated ADHD and opens motivational interviewing. Caffeine antagonises adenosine, an inhibitory transmitter, so it raises dopamine and glutamate; look for extensive use without a use disorder, a minimal response, or a paradoxical one. Cannabis: some perceive short-term improvement and almost as many worsening, and most of both groups eventually report amotivation. Stimulant challenge tests are not part of assessment and a positive response is not diagnostic; in a 2019 survey of over 55,000 Canadian post-secondary students, 4.5% had taken a stimulant not prescribed to them.
Menstrual cycleIn the follicular phase rising oestrogen and testosterone bring motivation, confidence and focus; premenstrually falling oestrogen and progesterone bring poor focus and dysregulated mood. Ask for the time course; some patients need a dose change across the cycle.
SSRIsRaised serotonin can lower dopamine, producing serotonergic fogging or serotonin amotivation: cognitive flatness on an SSRI; given the dopamine hypothesis of ADHD, those with ADHD may be more vulnerable. Emotional blunting or poor concentration on an SSRI is a cue to assess for ADHD.

Screening and diagnosis in adults

Screening is based on a physician interview, review of collateral and mental status examination. There is no perfect questionnaire, and questionnaires are age-specific; put past and present symptoms on the same form; ask for specific examples; collateral means report cards and a parent or partner completing a screener. The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale has 18 items rated never to very often over the past six months; items 1 to 6 are Part A, and 4 or more positive on Part A is a positive screen. It has a higher negative than positive predictive value: better at ruling out than ruling in, with a high false-positive rate, and no substitute for a thorough history. A positive screen leads to the CADDRA ADHD checklist, the DSM criteria rated 0 to 3 with columns for retrospective childhood symptoms and current symptoms; rating both on one form is how onset before 12 is confirmed. The worked example scored 6 of 9 for attention and 2 of 9 for hyperactivity: a predominantly inattentive presentation whose hyperactive symptoms had improved entering adulthood while inattentive ones worsened. Where difficulty is minimal, ask what strategy is in use; where symptoms worsened entering adulthood, ask what structure or strategy was lost. The Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults structures the assessment.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Executive dysfunction is a sign, not a diagnosis, with seven categories of cause.
  • Often, 6 months, 2 settings, before 12, 6 of 9 (5 at 17 and older); 5 to 8% of youth, 2 to 4% of adults.
  • Good grades and high IQ delay diagnosis; women internalise; transitions unmask.
  • Depression is episodic, ADHD continuous; treating ADHD reduces its anxiety; over half sit in the top 5% for emotion dysregulation.
  • Screener first (4 of 6 on Part A; good at ruling out), then the checklist with childhood and current columns.
ADHD is a continuous neurodevelopmental disorder, present before 12, in two settings, for six months, with six of nine symptoms (five in adults). It is missed in adults because hyperactivity turns inward, because intelligence and hyperfocus compensate until a transition strips away structure, and because it hides inside depression, anxiety, emotion dysregulation and substance use. Screen with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, confirm with the CADDRA checklist rating childhood and current symptoms together, and always ask for examples and collateral.

guides.title: Week 42 · 12 ADHD: Treatment
guides.html:
SLM02 · CADDRA October 2024

ADHD: Treatment

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Psychoeducation as the first intervention and the grief that follows diagnosis, the strategies that treatment builds on from exercise and body doubling to Pomodoro and the Eisenhower matrix, the CBT evidence, the CADDRA first- and second-line drug table with doses, the four mechanisms, the four points to share before starting a stimulant, and SMART goals as the medication yardstick.

Treatment starts with psychoeducation

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition with symptoms along a continuum from mild to severe, occurring across the lifespan. Treatment is multimodal, combining education, medication, and behavioural modification, motivational interviewing or psychotherapy, collaborative among physician, patient and family, and targeted to goals that change over time. Psychoeducation is the first intervention. Its twelve moves: discover what they know; demystify the myths and the diagnostic process; instil hope, since evidence-based treatments exist and work; educate on combining pharmacological and psychosocial care; empathise with discouragement, grief and frustration; encourage with more positive than negative comments; recognise goals achieved; be sensitive to ethnic, cultural and gender framing; motivate by nurturing strengths; promote regular exercise, consistent sleep hygiene and a healthy nutrition routine; use humour; give resources. Psychosocial interventions, cognitive or behavioural, reduce impairment at school, work and home and in relationships: schedule communication and schedule fun, use relaxation and mindfulness, and validate strengths. Referrals range from psychologist and tutor to occupational therapist, ADHD coach and vocational coach.

Grieving the diagnosis
Diagnosis is often a positive moment, but it can be stigmatising, there is mourning for the struggles of the past, and there are challenges in working out the "true self" and what role ADHD plays. Suffering does not correlate with functional impairment; each developmental task (Erikson's stages, from trust versus mistrust through identity versus role confusion to intimacy versus isolation) sets different priorities; and grief risks being under-addressed in the office. Three questions guide treatment: what has the diagnosis meant to them; what do they believe about themselves, unreliable, unmotivated and incapable, or creative, spontaneous and flexible; and what are they good at, what is not needing treatment.

Effective treatment starts with strategies

StrategyWhat to do
MotivationAsk what is motivating them now: negative self-talk (raises motivation briefly, worsens self-concept), procrastination that builds pressure (overcomes inertia, lowers quality), caffeine and other stimulants, cannabis to switch off, and exercise, where one hour of effective exercise may buy up to four hours of improved concentration and reduced hyperactivity and impulsivity. Can motivation be made healthier?
Body doubling and accountabilityWorking alongside another person builds motivation through the dopaminergic system; searches for it rose sharply during the pandemic. Accountability: say the goal aloud to yourself or a friend, or write it, and make it very specific ("I'll arrive twenty minutes early and start my homework in the waiting room").
GamificationTurn the mundane into something interesting so the goal becomes salient; patients with ADHD often have higher motivation than others when stimulated. Streak charts, time trials.
DistractionsChain-analyse the physical symptoms, thoughts, moods and behaviours behind a distraction (restlessness, "I'll recharge my focus with my phone"); schedule movement breaks; keep a memory pad for intruding tasks; sit at the front of the lecture hall. Increase the distance between the student and the distraction (noise-cancelling headphones, coping cards) and decrease the distance to the reward.
MultitaskingThe idea is efficiency and one task as a break from another; the reality is risk of derailing with every task switch, less efficiency than we think, tasks started and not finished, and further guilt.
PomodoroSet a specific goal; 25 minutes of work, 5 of break, typically four cycles before a longer 30-minute break; make breaks safer by standing, stretching or fetching water rather than screens. Small tasks become easier to start; it builds insight into symptoms and progress; it flags the best time of day for each task and flags medication wear-off. If pages read improve on medication but fall away by late afternoon, consider a different time of day or a divided dose.
Goal setting and the Eisenhower matrixWell intentioned but disorganised: the neurology is "right now" versus "non-existent", exceptional at putting out fires while other tasks are discarded, feeding a negative self-concept. The matrix sharpens focus on the most appropriate task at the most appropriate time: urgent and important; important but not urgent (exams, taxes, neglected until they become crises); urgent but not important; neither. Circle the most avoided task to make it salient, break it down if it still cannot be started, and keep the matrix visual on a whiteboard updated each evening, because visual working memory is less prone to distraction by negative self-talk.
RemindersMany reminders are unrealistic guilt reminders ("I should be in bed by now"); move to sequential reminders: 9 p.m. "Have I had dinner?"; 10 p.m. "Bedtime in an hour, is what I'm doing aligned with that?" Ask where the reminder is, whether it can be more salient, and when the student gets derailed.
MemoryAnxiety distracts the auditory-verbal working memory; methylphenidate may improve auditory working memory, but with less effect when anxiety is comorbid. Use visual strategies instead of verbal, which anxious rumination interferes with less.

CBT for adult ADHD has evidence in individual and group forms, as does group mindfulness and individual coaching; adolescents have less evidence for individual CBT and more for school- and family-based interventions. With comorbid depression and anxiety, the effect size is larger when CBT is added to a stimulant and gains persist at 6 and 12 months. CBT beat relaxation and educational support (67% versus 33% response) and supportive therapy of validation and peer normalisation without strategies (53% versus 28%), with group CBT giving the higher response in ADHD symptoms. Higher baseline severity predicted more response to CBT, not to supportive therapy, and response was independent of medication status.

Pharmacotherapy

The Canadian ADHD Resource Alliance table of October 2024 makes long-acting stimulants first line and everything else second line. Effect sizes for stimulants targeting ADHD are high, and some patients take a stimulant paired with a non-stimulant.

LineProductDurationStarting doseTitration and maximum
1stMixed amphetamine salts XR (Adderall XR), 5 to 30 mg capsules, sprinkleableAbout 12 h5 to 10 mg once in the morningUp 5 to 10 mg weekly; max 30 mg children, 20 to 30 mg adolescents and adults
1stLisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse), 10 to 70 mg; a prodrugAbout 13 to 14 h20 to 30 mg once in the morningUp 10 to 20 mg weekly; max 60 mg all ages
2ndDextroamphetamine (Dexedrine) tablets and spansules4 h tablets, 6 to 8 h spansules2.5 to 5 mg twice daily; spansule 10 mgMax 20 to 30 mg youth, 50 mg adults
1stMethylphenidate Biphentin, 10 to 80 mg, sprinkleableAbout 10 to 12 h10 to 20 mg once in the morningUp 10 mg weekly; max 60 mg youth, 80 mg adults
1stMethylphenidate OROS (Concerta), 18, 27, 36, 54 mgAbout 12 h18 mg once in the morningUp 18 mg weekly; max 54 mg youth, 72 mg adults
1stMethylphenidate Foquest, 25 to 100 mgAbout 13 to 16 h25 mgMax 70 mg youth, 100 mg adults
1stMethylphenidate Quillivant ER chewables and suspension8 to 12 h20 mgMax 60 mg; suspension and chewables not interchangeable
2ndMethylphenidate short-acting (Ritalin) and SR3 to 4 h; 8 h SR5 mg two to three times dailyMax 60 mg all ages
2ndAtomoxetine, 10 to 100 mg, swallow wholeUp to 24 h0.5 mg/kg/day in youth; 40 mg daily in adults for 7 to 14 daysHold 7 to 14 days between steps: 0.8 then 1.2 mg/kg; adults 60 then 80 mg; max 1.4 mg/kg or 100 mg
2ndGuanfacine XR (Intuniv XR), 1 to 4 mg, swallow wholeUp to 24 h1 mg morning or eveningUp to 1 mg weekly; max 4 mg at 6 to 12, 7 mg at 13 to 17; 4 mg as adjunct to a stimulant
Sources differ: the child psychiatry part of the week carried a generic pharmacology table with a lisdexamfetamine maximum of 70 mg and a Concerta range to 72 mg without age banding; the CADDRA 2024 chart prints lisdexamfetamine's maximum as 60 mg at all ages, Concerta's as 54 mg in youth and 72 mg in adults, and Biphentin's as 80 mg in adults. The CADDRA chart (October 2024, caddra.ca) is the source for every dose it covers.
ClassMechanism
Amphetamine-basedBind monoamine transporters, enter the terminal and inhibit VMAT2, reducing vesicular storage; the monoamine build-up makes the transporters run in reverse, releasing noradrenaline and dopamine into the cleft; may also inhibit monoamine oxidase and compete for reuptake. The same mechanism by which methamphetamine causes psychosis.
Methylphenidate-basedInhibits reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline, increasing prefrontal activity; also acts on serotonergic and adrenergic pathways.
AtomoxetineInhibits noradrenaline reuptake; unlike stimulants, the goal is 24-hour coverage at steady state, like a once-daily antidepressant.
Guanfacine XRBinds postsynaptic alpha-2A adrenergic receptors in the prefrontal cortex, contributing to behavioural inhibition and reduced impulsivity; 24-hour coverage; may help emotion regulation.
Stimulant treatment can easily backfire: appetite suppression means the patient forgets to eat, and poor intake produces poor concentration and irritability at wear-off in the late afternoon. Four points before starting: take it sufficiently early to protect the day-night schedule; take it after food, with easy high-calorie healthy options coached; remember lunch with an alarm, because hunger can no longer be the only cue to eat; and watch substances: caffeine compounds side effects, alcohol feels more potent, cannabis reduces stimulant effectiveness.

A stimulant should build on strategies. Goals are SMART: specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, time-based. "I want to be better with my readings and get better grades" becomes "four Pomodoro cycles of reading", monitored in 25-minute blocks by pages read, whether a page had to be reread for mind-wandering, note-taking afterwards and general attentiveness. The Pomodoro block is the medication-response yardstick and its wear-off flag is the dose-timing tool. Neither deck gives a stimulant adverse-effect list or monitoring schedule; standard practice adds height, weight, heart rate and blood pressure at each visit, sleep, appetite, mood, tics and psychotic symptoms, with a cardiac history and family history of sudden death before starting. Resources: the Centre for ADHD Awareness, Canada, with peer-led groups (including for ADHD with substance use disorder), webinars on trauma, relationships and perimenopause, a resource navigator and reading list; and eConsult, which answers within seven days. A strategy that works in one environment can fail in another and ADHD bites hardest at transitions, so connect the patient to supports that outlast your episode of care.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Psychoeducation first; treatment multimodal and collaborative; ask what is not needing treatment.
  • One hour of exercise, up to four hours of focus; body doubling works on dopamine; multitasking derails at every switch.
  • Pomodoro 25 and 5 flags the best time of day and medication wear-off; keep the Eisenhower matrix visual.
  • CBT 67 versus 33 over relaxation, 53 versus 28 over support; severity predicts response; medication status does not.
  • First line: long-acting stimulants. Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug, max 60 mg. Concerta max 72 mg in adults. Atomoxetine and guanfacine give 24-hour coverage.
  • Amphetamine reverses the transporter via VMAT2; methylphenidate blocks reuptake; guanfacine is alpha-2A.
  • Take it early, after food, set a lunch alarm, watch caffeine, alcohol and cannabis.
Educate first, then build strategies (exercise, body doubling, gamification, distance from distractions, Pomodoro, a visual Eisenhower matrix, sequential reminders, visual memory aids, CBT), and only then add a long-acting stimulant that builds on those strategies, chosen from the CADDRA first-line list, started early in the day after food with a lunch alarm and a substance warning, and measured against SMART goals in 25-minute blocks so that wear-off sets the dose timing.

guides.title: Week 42 · 13 Attachment, Adverse Childhood Experiences and Social Media
guides.html:
Klein · Bowlby · Felitti

Attachment, Adverse Childhood Experiences and Social Media

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Bowlby's definition and Ainsworth's Strange Situation, the two-axis attachment grid and its application to the week's case, the social determinants that bridge into adverse childhood experiences, Felitti's seven categories and the CDC's ten items, the ACE pyramid and the toxic-stress curve, and the evidence on social media use, harms, benefits and the trials that limit it.

Attachment

Attachment is the deep emotional bond that connects one person to another across time and space (Bowlby, 1958). It is shaped in early childhood through interactions with primary caregivers and may influence future interpersonal relationships throughout life. Ainsworth's Strange Situation of the 1970s classifies infant attachment by how the infant reacts during separations and reunions and behaves when the caregiver is absent and returns; the manipulated elements are caregiver presence, a stranger, and an exit, and the classification comes from the reunion, not the separation.

Low anxietyHigh anxiety
Low avoidanceSecureInsecure-anxious (preoccupied)
High avoidanceInsecure-avoidant (dismissive)Disorganised

Insecurity is dimensional along two orthogonal axes, anxiety about abandonment and avoidance of closeness. Secure is low on both; disorganised is high on both and is the pattern most associated with frightening or frightened caregiver behaviour, maltreatment and later psychopathology. In the week's case, a mother who wants her daughter to "come to her" and reacts and instructs when she does loads the anxiety axis; a father with occasional loud outbursts and parents who avoid talking about emotions when calm load the avoidance axis; an eight-week stay with grandparents at age five after a sibling's birth is a discrete disruption; and the internal working model that results is "does not trust them, feels like a burden". A sibling relationship is not an attachment relationship, because the definition is a bond with primary caregivers: of five family facts, not being close to a brother is the one least related to attachment.

Social determinants and adverse childhood experiences

Social determinants of health are the social and economic factors that influence people's health and well-being: income and social status, social supports and coping, biology and genetics, gender, access to health services, physical environments, employment and working conditions, culture, education and literacy, childhood experiences, race and racism, and healthy behaviours, with housing, food insecurity, Aboriginal status and sexual orientation also named. Childhood experiences and racism appearing as determinants is the bridge into adverse childhood experiences, and poverty is printed inside the psychiatric formulation model itself.

Adverse childhood experiences are potentially stressful events or environments before 18: abuse (physical, emotional, sexual), neglect (physical, emotional), household dysfunction (parental separation, incarceration of a household member, mental illness in a household member), and other stress such as bullying, famine and war. The Felitti study of 1998 mailed a questionnaire to 13,494 adults at a large health maintenance organisation, of whom 9,508 (70.5%) responded, and studied seven categories: psychological, physical or sexual abuse; violence against the mother; and living with household members who were substance abusers, mentally ill or suicidal, or ever imprisoned. The number of categories, not any single event, was compared with adult risk. The finding is dose-response.

Abuse (3)Neglect (2)Household challenges (5)
PhysicalPhysicalMental illness
EmotionalEmotionalDivorce
SexualParent treated violently
Incarcerated relative
Substance abuse
Sources differ: the original study counted seven categories of adversity; the CDC checklist shown on the next slide counts ten items in three domains. Both appear in the week. Use seven for Felitti's study and ten (3 plus 2 plus 5) for the CDC list, and the dose-response principle for both: the count predicts adult risk (Felitti et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine 1998; CDC ACEs resources).
The ACE pyramid, bottom to top: historical trauma and intergenerational adversity, then (through neurodevelopment and epigenetic influences) adverse childhood experiences, then disrupted social, emotional and cognitive functioning, then (through adaptations) health-risk behaviours, then disease, disability and social problems, then early death. Health-risk behaviours are framed as adaptations to adversity, not moral failings.

Stress and performance form an inverted U. Low stress brings boredom, inactivity and demotivation; optimal stress brings productivity, motivation, creativity and focus; high stress brings burnout, anxiety, overwhelm, exhaustion and breakdown, and toxic stress sits at the far right where performance collapses. Some stress enhances performance; toxic stress is the bridge from the pyramid to functional impairment.

Social media and youth mental health

Up to 95% of 13- to 17-year-olds use social media, and almost a third use it "almost constantly"; nearly 40% of 8- to 12-year-olds use it despite 13 being the usual minimum age, for about 1.5 hours a day, mostly TikTok and YouTube. Youth are particularly vulnerable because self-regulation is still developing, platforms are constantly accessible and immersive, and ages 10 to 19 are a critical, highly sensitive period of brain development. High, frequent use is linked to psychiatric disorders. By platform category, youth online activity is social networking 42.86%, video-sharing 28.57%, instant messaging 17.86%, and games and blogs 3.57% each: gaming is a small fraction of youth online activity. Outcomes depend on time spent, type of content, activities and interactions, and essential activities displaced, such as sleep and physical activity.

BenefitsRisks and harms
Positive community with others who share identities, abilities and interestsMore than 3 hours a day doubles the risk of mental health outcomes including anxiety and depression
Online friendships and social connectionsA new platform in a natural experiment among US college students raised depression by 9% and anxiety by 12% over baseline, with 300,000 new cases of depression
Access to important informationGreater use predicted poor sleep, online harassment, poor body image, low self-esteem and more depressive symptoms, especially in teenage girls
Space for self-expressionCyberbullying-related depression, body image and disordered eating, poor sleep quality
Interactions with diverse peer groups
Social support online, especially for marginalised groups
