Limiting use helps, especially for transitional-aged youth and adults with more severe problems: a randomised trial limiting social media to 30 minutes a day for three weeks significantly improved depression severity, and another deactivating it for four weeks improved subjective well-being. The take-home: higher relative concern of harm in adolescent girls and those already experiencing poor mental health. Social media is not simply bad; the outcome is dose- and content-dependent, which makes it a screening question (how much, on what, and is it displacing sleep?) and a specific intervention (cap it at 30 minutes a day). Of the claims that 75% of adolescents use it, that gaming equals social media time, that there are almost no benefits, and that time spent does not correlate with impact, all are false; that girls are more negatively affected than boys is true.

Take-home
A general approach to assessing children and adolescents; anxiety is the most common mental health presentation in youth; depression and anxiety are highly comorbid, as is ADHD; adverse childhood experiences negatively affect health and mental health throughout life; early intervention is key, because the peak age of onset is 15, up to 75% of illness begins by 25, and youth access services less than any other age group; and social media can be both positive and negative, particularly negative for youth with heavy use and existing mental health challenges. Early intervention is modifiable and integral to basic healthcare: early psychosis intervention, the Triple P and SNAP parenting programmes, and mood and anxiety programmes.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Attachment is a bond with primary caregivers; a sibling relationship is not one. Classification comes from the reunion.
  • Two axes, anxiety and avoidance; disorganised is high on both.
  • Felitti: 7 categories, 9,508 respondents, dose-response. CDC: 10 items, 3 plus 2 plus 5.
  • Pyramid mechanisms: neurodevelopment and epigenetics between intergenerational adversity and ACEs; adaptations between functioning and health-risk behaviours.
  • Toxic stress is the right-hand tail of the inverted U.
  • 95% of teens use social media; over 3 hours a day doubles risk; 30 minutes a day for three weeks improves depression; girls and those already unwell are most at risk.
Attachment is built with primary caregivers and read off the reunion, along axes of anxiety and avoidance. Adversity in childhood is counted, not weighed: the number of categories predicts adult disease and early death through a pyramid whose health-risk behaviours are adaptations, with toxic stress as the point where performance collapses. Social media is nearly universal, dose- and content-dependent, doubly harmful past three hours a day, improvable by capping it, and most dangerous to adolescent girls who are already struggling.

guides.title: Week 42 · 14 Skull, Meninges and Dural Venous Sinuses
guides.html:
Lisk · Lab 10 · MAPS

Skull, Meninges and Dural Venous Sinuses

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The eight bones, sutures and landmarks with the pterion and middle meningeal artery, the three fossae and the three arterial entry foramina, the internal landmarks and the paediatric fracture cases, the three meningeal layers and their real and potential spaces, the dural partitions and the tentorial compartments, the three venous drainage chains, the cavernous sinus and the danger triangle.

The skull

The skull divides into the calvaria (the roof), the cranial base (the floor) and the facial skeleton, most bones united by fibrous sutures. Sutures are not fused at birth so that the fetal skull can mould during delivery and the brain can grow afterwards; the neonatal skull shows an anterior fontanelle at the future bregma and a posterior fontanelle at the future lambda. Eight bones form the calvaria and cranial base: frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid. The whole skull's colour key adds lacrimal, mandible, maxilla, nasal, vomer, zygomatic and sutural (wormian) bones.

Suture or landmarkBetween
Coronal sutureFrontal and parietal bones
Sagittal sutureThe two parietal bones, in the midline
Lambdoid sutureParietal bones and occipital bone
Squamous sutureParietal bone and squamous temporal
BregmaCoronal meets sagittal; site of the anterior fontanelle
LambdaSagittal meets lambdoid; site of the posterior fontanelle
PterionFrontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of sphenoid; the thinnest part of the vault
The pterion overlies the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery. Trauma to the temple fractures the pterion, lacerates the artery, and arterial blood strips the periosteal dura off the inner table: a lens-shaped epidural haematoma. The artery's route: external carotid, maxillary, middle meningeal, through the foramen spinosum in the greater wing of the sphenoid, travelling in the periosteal layer of the dura and grooving the parietal bone.

The cranial cavity's roof is the calvaria and its floor is divided into three fossae. The anterior cranial fossa (frontal, ethmoid, lesser wing of sphenoid) holds the frontal lobes, with the crista galli and cribriform plate at the midline; the middle cranial fossa (sphenoid body and greater wings, temporal) holds the temporal lobes and, in the sella turcica's hypophyseal fossa, the pituitary; the posterior cranial fossa (occipital, petrous temporal) holds the cerebellum, pons and medulla. The anterior fossa floor sits highest and the posterior lowest, so one axial CT slice cuts all three. Three arteries enter through three openings: the internal carotid through the carotid canal, the vertebral arteries through the foramen magnum, and the middle meningeal through the foramen spinosum. The brain is supplied by the internal carotid and vertebral systems; the dura by the external carotid system, which is why an epidural bleed is an extracerebral, external-carotid-territory bleed. The sphenoid floors the middle fossa and carries the foramen rotundum, ovale and spinosum and the superior orbital fissure; the parietal has grooves for the middle meningeal artery and granular foveolae, pits made by arachnoid granulations, but no foramina.

Internal landmarks of the base: frontal crest and crista galli (falx attachment), anterior and posterior clinoid processes, sella turcica with the hypophyseal fossa, the petrous ridge of the temporal bone (tentorium attachment, with the superior petrosal sinus along its crest), the clivus, the grooves for the transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and the internal occipital protuberance at the confluence of sinuses. Several bones contain air spaces: the frontal, ethmoidal, maxillary and sphenoidal sinuses, of which the sphenoidal matters most here, for its relation to the cavernous sinus.

Sources differ: the pre-lab quiz calls the cranial base seen from above with the calvaria removed the "interior, superior view", while the lab manual captions the same view "internal, inferior view" and reserves "internal, superior view" for the vault seen from inside. Gray's names the view for the part shown and the quiz for the direction of gaze. Learn both labels and match the examiner's vocabulary.

Two paediatric cases. A young child with head trauma and no intracranial bleed has a long linear branching fracture of the right parietal bone ending at the lambdoid and squamosal sutures; a fracture is distinguished from a suture by being sharper, straighter, non-serrated and in the wrong place, and the child's skull shows open sutures, patent fontanelles, tooth buds, a thin diploë and a large vault relative to the face. A 6-year-old with a skull fracture and a haematoma has a non-serrated fracture line crossing the parietal bone between the coronal and lambdoid sutures with an ipsilateral biconvex extradural collection; acute fractures are best assessed by non-contrast CT with bone windows and 3D reconstruction, since MRI is poor for cortical bone. An 85-year-old with bleeding from the ear and confusion after trauma has a temporal bone fracture, because the external acoustic meatus and middle ear are housed in it; think CSF otorrhoea, Battle's sign, facial and vestibulocochlear nerve injury and middle meningeal injury.

The meninges and their spaces

The cranial meninges protect the brain, support blood vessels and enclose the subarachnoid space, and potential spaces exist above and below the cranial dura. The dura mater is the external layer and consists of two layers, periosteal and meningeal; the arachnoid mater is a thin avascular membrane lining the meningeal dura, with trabeculae extending to the pia, which bridges over sulci and strips easily; the pia mater is the innermost membrane, adherent to the brain, dipping into every sulcus, and cannot be peeled off. The periosteal dura is continuous with the pericranium through the sutures, which is why epidural blood stops at sutures; the layers from outside in are scalp, pericranium, external table, diploë, internal table, periosteal dura, meningeal dura.

SpaceBetweenStatusContents
EpiduralPeriosteal dura and inner tablePotential cranially; real in the spine, with fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus, where epidural anaesthesia goesPathological arterial blood from a torn meningeal artery
SubduralMeningeal dura and arachnoidPotentialPathological venous blood from torn bridging veins
SubarachnoidArachnoid and piaRealCSF, arteries and veins on the surface of the brain, crossed by trabeculae
Sources differ: the lecture's meninges slide reproduces a spinal-cord cross-section whose annotation reads "epidural space, real space". That is true of the spine; cranially the epidural space is only a potential space created by arterial bleeding (Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy). Read the annotation with its context: cranial epidural potential, spinal epidural real, subdural potential, subarachnoid real.

Dural reflections and the venous sinuses

The meningeal layer peels away from the periosteal layer and folds back on itself in specific locations to form dural partitions and dural venous sinuses, the sinus being the space created between the separated layers, endothelium-lined, valveless and held open by dura. The falx cerebri separates the hemispheres and sits in the longitudinal fissure, attached anteriorly at the crista galli, with the superior sagittal sinus in its upper margin and the inferior sagittal sinus in its free margin. The tentorium cerebelli overlies the cerebellum and sits in the transverse fissure, separating the occipital lobes from the cerebellum; its anterior attachment is the petrous ridge of the temporal bone and its posterior attachment the occipital bone along the transverse sinus grooves, with the attached margin ending at the posterior clinoids and the free margin at the anterior clinoids. The tentorial notch is its anterior opening, through which the midbrain passes: the site of uncal herniation, compressing the midbrain and the oculomotor nerve. The diaphragma sellae roofs the sella turcica and stabilises the pituitary, pierced by the infundibulum. The falx cerebelli separates the cerebellar hemispheres and is named only in the lab.

The tentorium divides the cranial cavity into two compartments. Supratentorial: the cerebral hemispheres, the diencephalon and the intracranial parts of cranial nerves I and II, which are forebrain outgrowths. Infratentorial: the brainstem, the cerebellum and cranial nerves III to XII, which arise from the brainstem.

Cerebral veins coalesce in the subarachnoid space and cross the arachnoid and meningeal dura to empty into the sinuses; the bridging veins, unsupported across the subdural interval, are the source of subdural bleeding, and cerebral atrophy in the elderly stretches them. CSF is extruded into venous blood across the arachnoid granulations, which project into the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral venous lacunae and leave the granular foveolae on the skull. Venous sinuses drain the brain mainly to the left and right internal jugular veins.

RouteChain
SuperficialCerebral veins, superior sagittal sinus, confluence of sinuses, transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, jugular foramen, internal jugular vein
DeepGreat cerebral vein and inferior sagittal sinus, straight sinus (at the junction of falx and tentorium), confluence, transverse, sigmoid, internal jugular
CavernousOphthalmic veins from the orbit and infratemporal fossa, cavernous sinus, then either the superior petrosal sinus to the transverse-sigmoid junction or the inferior petrosal sinus directly to the internal jugular

The sigmoid sinus makes the deep S-shaped groove behind the petrous and mastoid temporal, heading for the jugular foramen; the transverse sinus grooves the internal occipital squama; the confluence sits at the internal occipital protuberance. The cavernous sinus is a named learning outcome. In its lateral wall, from superior to inferior: oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic, maxillary; inside the lumen: the internal carotid artery with the abducens nerve immediately lateral to it. The abducens is therefore the most vulnerable nerve in cavernous sinus disease, and an isolated failure of abduction is often the first sign. The optic nerve and chiasm lie above the pituitary, so a macroadenoma growing up produces bitemporal hemianopia and growing laterally produces ophthalmoplegia with ophthalmic and maxillary sensory loss; the sphenoidal sinus below is the trans-sphenoidal surgical corridor. The facial vein's tributaries drain the danger triangle, from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose, and anastomose without valves through the ophthalmic veins and through the pterygoid plexus and deep facial vein into the cavernous sinus, which is why facial infection can produce septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Eight bones; parietal and temporal paired. Coronal is frontal-parietal; bregma is anterior fontanelle, lambda posterior.
  • Pterion: four bones, thinnest vault, middle meningeal beneath, foramen spinosum, epidural bleed.
  • Internal carotid via carotid canal, vertebral via foramen magnum, middle meningeal via foramen spinosum.
  • Cranial epidural potential, spinal epidural real; subarachnoid real and CSF-filled.
  • Four dural partitions: falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, diaphragma sellae, and the easily forgotten falx cerebelli.
  • Tentorium anterior attachment: petrous ridge, not the clinoids; the midbrain passes through the notch.
  • Cavernous sinus wall: III, IV, V1, V2; lumen: carotid and VI.
  • Sigmoid, not transverse, makes the groove behind the petrous bone; the internal jugular exits at the jugular foramen.
Eight bones and four sutures meet at the pterion over the middle meningeal artery; the periosteal dura is glued to the skull at the sutures, so arterial blood beneath it makes a lens; the meningeal dura folds into falx, tentorium and diaphragma and splits from the periosteal layer to make the sinuses, which carry CSF from the arachnoid granulations and blood from the bridging veins down through the confluence, transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the jugular foramen. The tentorium hangs from the petrous ridge, the midbrain threads its notch, and the cavernous sinus holds the carotid and the abducens in its lumen with the other four nerves in its wall.

guides.title: Week 42 · 15 Brain Surface, White Matter and Ventricles
guides.html:
Lisk · Lab 10 · MAPS

Brain Surface, White Matter and Ventricles

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The three primary vesicles and their adult derivatives, the two longitudinal axes, the sulci and lobes with the hidden insula and the limbic ring, the two functional gyri and lateralisation, grey and white matter in cord and forebrain, the three fibre classes with the corpus callosum and internal capsule, the ventricular system and the full CSF chain with its four eponyms, the cisterns, and obstructive against communicating hydrocephalus.

From neural tube to adult brain

The central nervous system begins as a hollow tube that grows at different rates in different regions. By the fourth week there are three primary brain vesicles that give rise to every part of the adult brain, and by the fifth week five secondary vesicles.

Primary vesicle (4 weeks)Secondary vesicle (5 weeks)Adult derivative
Prosencephalon (forebrain)TelencephalonCerebral hemispheres
DiencephalonThalamus, hypothalamus, subthalamus
Mesencephalon (midbrain)MesencephalonMidbrain, part of the brainstem
Rhombencephalon (hindbrain)MetencephalonPons and cerebellum
MyelencephalonMedulla oblongata
Sources differ: the lecture's developmental diagram groups pons and cerebellum together as metencephalon derivatives, but a later slide labels the cerebellum "(myelencephalon)". The cited textbooks, Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy and Gray's Anatomy for Students, assign the cerebellum to the metencephalon; the later label is a slide typo. Answer metencephalon, and recognise a question written from the typo.

Adult groupings: forebrain is hemispheres plus diencephalon; hindbrain is brainstem plus cerebellum; the brainstem is midbrain, pons and medulla. The human nervous system has two longitudinal axes bent at the midbrain, so rostral and caudal, dorsal and ventral each mean different things above and below the bend: dorsal is superior in the forebrain and posterior in the brainstem and cord; superior, inferior, anterior and posterior are absolute. Two fissures pair with two dural partitions: the longitudinal fissure holds the falx cerebri, and the transverse fissure, between occipital lobes and cerebellum, holds the tentorium cerebelli.

Lobes, sulci and gyri

A cerebral hemisphere consists of cerebral cortex (grey matter), subcortical white matter and basal nuclei (grey matter). Three sulci divide the lateral surface: the central sulcus separates frontal from parietal; the lateral (Sylvian) fissure separates temporal from frontal and parietal; the parieto-occipital sulcus separates parietal from occipital. The insular lobe lies deep to the lateral fissure and is not visible on an intact lateral view. On the medial surface four sulci are named, the cingulate sulcus arching above the cingulate gyrus, the central sulcus reaching the vertex, the parieto-occipital sulcus, and the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe, on whose banks the primary visual cortex lies. The limbic lobe is not a discrete lobe; it is formed by the cingulate gyrus, the parahippocampal gyrus and the uncus, the last being the structure that herniates through the tentorial notch.

Sources differ: the lecture's learning outcome says five cerebral lobes and its slide says the limbic lobe is not a discrete lobe, while the lab manual lists six lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, insula and limbic. Standard texts describe four classical lobes plus the insula, with the limbic lobe as a functional sixth in many neuroanatomy texts (Gray's Anatomy for Students; Moore). Answer six including insula and limbic on a lab-based question, and five with the limbic lobe described separately on a lecture-based one.

Only two functional areas are named: the precentral gyrus, primary motor area, immediately anterior to the central sulcus, and the postcentral gyrus, primary somatosensory area, immediately posterior; the leg and foot representation runs over the paracentral lobule on the medial surface. The hemispheres are anatomically similar but functionally different; the dominant hemisphere controls language, the left in most people; and each hemisphere controls voluntary movement of, and receives sensation from, the contralateral side of the body, so a right precentral lesion weakens the left side and a left-hemisphere lesion usually adds a language deficit.

Grey and white matter, and the subcortical fibres

Grey matter in the spinal cord is organised into horns; grey matter in the forebrain is organised into a cerebral cortex and deep nuclei. The arrangement is inverted: forebrain grey is superficial (cortex) plus deep nuclei with white matter deep; spinal grey is deep and central, the butterfly of horns, with white matter superficial in columns or funiculi. Neither is exclusively nuclear and neither is grey-superficial in both.

White matter tracts carry information toward or away from the neuronal cell bodies of the cortex, in three classes. Commissural fibres connect homologous regions of the two hemispheres: the corpus callosum and the anterior commissure. Projection fibres connect cortex to subcortical structures, brainstem and cord, ascending and descending: the corona radiata fanning down into the internal capsule. Association fibres connect regions within one hemisphere; no named bundle is given.

The corpus callosum has U-shaped fibres connecting similar regions, left premotor to right premotor. Its parts on a sagittal view are the genu in front, the body, and the splenium behind; on a transverse section the forceps minor sweeps from the genu into the frontal lobes and the forceps major from the splenium into the occipital lobes. The internal capsule has an anterior limb, a genu and a posterior limb, traced as a V pointing medially on an axial section with the lentiform nucleus in its angle: the anterior limb lies between the head of the caudate medially and the lentiform laterally, the posterior limb between the thalamus medially and the lentiform laterally. The posterior limb carries the corticospinal tract and somatosensory thalamocortical fibres, which is why a small lacunar infarct there produces a dense contralateral hemiparesis out of proportion to its size; the genu carries corticobulbar fibres. The basal nuclei are treated collectively here, and the thalamus as a whole; their components belong to later weeks.

Ventricles and cerebrospinal fluid

The ventricles develop from the lumen of the neural tube and are continuous with one another and with the central canal of the cord. They are filled with cerebrospinal fluid produced by the choroid plexus, which supports and cushions the brain, transports nutrients to and waste from it, and exchanges continuously with the parenchyma. The two lateral ventricles, separated by the septum pellucidum, each have an anterior horn, body, trigone (atrium), posterior horn and inferior horn; the interventricular foramen (of Monro), one each side, leads to the third ventricle, surrounded by the thalamus; the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) runs through the midbrain to the fourth ventricle, which is continuous with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture (foramen of Magendie), one in the midline, and the lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka), paired.

The chain: choroid plexus of the lateral ventricles, lateral ventricles, foramina of Monro, third ventricle, aqueduct of Sylvius, fourth ventricle, foramen of Magendie and foramina of Luschka, subarachnoid space and cisterns, arachnoid granulations, superior sagittal sinus, internal jugular veins. A side branch runs from the fourth ventricle down the central canal. The last three steps are the first three of the venous drainage chain: CSF and venous blood are one circuit joined at the granulations.
Sources differ: the ventricles slide names both the median aperture, which it prints as "medial", and the lateral apertures, while the summary flowchart routes CSF out of the fourth ventricle through the lateral foramina only and ends at the dural venous sinuses. The standard term is median aperture, foramen of Magendie, one in the midline (Gray's); the ventricles slide is the fuller account. Write "median", and know that the flowchart omits it.

Subarachnoid cisterns are expanded subarachnoid spaces over irregular contours of the brain: the interpeduncular cistern between the cerebral peduncles in front of the midbrain, the ambient cistern around the midbrain, the superior (quadrigeminal) cistern behind the midbrain beneath the splenium, and the cisterna magna between cerebellum and medulla below the fourth ventricle, the target of suboccipital puncture. Aneurysmal subarachnoid blood pools in the suprasellar and interpeduncular cisterns in a star shape. Obstructive hydrocephalus is a block within the ventricular system, classically at the aqueduct: the ventricles upstream dilate and those downstream do not, so aqueductal stenosis dilates the lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth. In communicating hydrocephalus CSF leaves the ventricles normally but absorption at the arachnoid granulations fails, after subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis, and all ventricles dilate.

Lab specimens and the wet brain

On the models and the whole wet brain, find the longitudinal fissure and hemispheres, the central sulcus with the precentral and postcentral gyri, the lateral fissure, the parieto-occipital, calcarine and cingulate sulci, the transverse fissure, and six lobes. The arachnoid is a thin, avascular, translucent membrane that bridges over sulci and strips off easily; the pia is intimately adherent, dips into every sulcus and cannot be peeled. The space deep to the arachnoid is the subarachnoid space, filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The falx cerebri separates the hemispheres; the tentorium separates the occipital lobes from the cerebellum, with the midbrain passing through the tentorial notch; the falx cerebelli separates the cerebellar hemispheres. The cranial meninges dissection exposes the dura, arachnoid and pia in sequence, the superior sagittal sinus opened, the lateral venous lacunae, the arachnoid granulations and the branches of the middle meningeal artery.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Three primary vesicles at four weeks; cerebellum from the metencephalon with the pons; medulla from the myelencephalon.
  • Central sulcus: frontal from parietal. Lateral fissure: temporal from the rest. Insula deep to the lateral fissure. Limbic lobe: cingulate, parahippocampal, uncus.
  • Precentral motor, postcentral sensory; language left in most; contralateral control.
  • Horns in the cord, cortex plus nuclei in the forebrain.
  • Commissural, projection, association; genu, body, splenium; forceps minor frontal, major occipital; internal capsule limbs with the corticospinal tract posterior.
  • Monro, Sylvius, Magendie, Luschka; the third ventricle is surrounded by the thalamus; the aqueduct runs through the midbrain.
  • Lateral and third dilated with a normal fourth means aqueductal stenosis.
Three vesicles become five and then the adult brain; the hemisphere is cortex, white matter and basal nuclei, carved by the central sulcus, lateral fissure and parieto-occipital sulcus, with the insula hidden and the limbic lobe a ring rather than a lobe. Grey matter sits outside in the forebrain and inside in the cord. Fibres cross the midline, project up and down through the internal capsule, or associate within a hemisphere. CSF is made in the ventricles, leaves the fourth by three apertures, bathes the cisterns and returns to blood at the granulations, and a block in the aqueduct swells only what lies upstream.

guides.title: Week 42 · 16 Neuroimaging: Haemorrhage, Herniation and Hydrocephalus
guides.html:
Moreland · medical imaging · MAPS

Neuroimaging: Haemorrhage, Herniation and Hydrocephalus

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The Monro-Kellie relationship and why mass effect is the concern in every intracranial pathology, the modalities and the CT-first rule, skull fractures and pressure in both directions, the six headache red flags, the herniation routes, the four haemorrhages by space, shape and vessel, obstructive against non-obstructive hydrocephalus, intra- and extra-axial masses with oedema as the metastasis clue, and the four infections and the ring-enhancing trap.

Why the brain is different

The brain is entirely encased by bone, which restricts the imaging modalities available (ultrasound is blocked by cortical bone and is useful only in the neonate, through the fontanelle) and makes intracranial pathology more serious, because the skull cannot expand and mass effect can rapidly injure or kill. The Monro-Kellie hypothesis describes the dynamic equilibrium among the non-compressible components inside the rigid skull: brain tissue, blood within vessels, CSF, and "other", the fourth being whatever pathology is added. Hydrocephalus, the haemorrhages, neoplasms, abscess, depressed skull fractures and parenchymal oedema all throw off that relationship; rapid detection and treatment is the key to survival. The three H's, herniation, hydrocephalus and haemorrhage, all kill through mass effect, and a shifting brain crushes veins, infarcts, swells and shifts further: a self-reinforcing loop.

Regardless of the underlying abnormality, the primary concern is the resulting mass effect in the confined space of the skull. The various forms of herniation are rapidly lethal and require emergent intervention.
ModalityProsCons
RadiographyAccessible, quick, low cost, low radiation, good for bonePoor soft-tissue visibility; insensitive to infection and inflammation
UltrasoundReal time, excellent resolution, no radiation, low cost, good for vesselsOperator dependent; cannot see cortical bone or past bone or air
CTGreat three-dimensional resolution; best for bone; good soft tissueHigh radiation, limited availability, cost, skill to interpret
MRIExcellent soft-tissue contrast, good resolution, no radiationVery limited availability, cost, contraindicated in some patients, poor for cortical bone, skill to read
Nuclear medicine (PET)Problem-solving; functional rather than anatomic; separates chronic change from active tumourThe highest radiation of the five, very limited availability, slow, poor resolution

The brain is relatively radio-insensitive, not rapidly dividing, so a CT head's radiation matters little against the injuries sought; MRI's main contraindication is free metal in the patient.

CT is the primary initial tool for brain imaging despite limited sensitivity for some pathologies; MRI visualises parenchyma better and is the problem-solving tool; with either, contrast is used to examine vasculature and to improve the visibility of inflammation or lesions. Skull fractures are caused by high-energy trauma and the concern is their impact: direct brain injury, haemorrhage and herniation, infection, and CSF leakage; the primary tool is CT with bony reconstructions, and a CT head does not include the facial bones, which must be requested separately. A depressed fracture immediately raises intracranial pressure, risks parenchymal injury from the sharp fragments and needs emergent neurosurgical repair; the vein running under a depressed vertex fracture is the superior sagittal sinus, and intracranial gas means an open fracture; meningitis can declare itself days later, and routine antibiotics may not cross the blood-brain barrier, so the gas is the cue to start a penetrating agent early. A fracture through the cribriform plate presents as clear post-traumatic nasal drip, which is CSF rhinorrhoea, not a cold. A fracture that tears the dura lowers pressure as CSF leaks, producing sagging of the brain and downward cerebellar tonsillar descent: tonsillar descent appears with both high pressure (a posterior fossa mass) and low.

Headache red flagNote
ThunderclapSudden, severe, "worst of their life": subarachnoid haemorrhage
New neurological deficitWeakness, numbness, vision change, seizure
Fever and neck stiffnessMeningitis or encephalitis
Recent head trauma
ImmunosuppressionAbscess or opportunistic infection
Advanced ageNew severe headache over 50

Any of the six requires emergent head imaging: they are red flags, not yellow, and the imaging is now, not later. Immunosuppression includes steroid use, HIV, inherited immunodeficiency, a recent bone-marrow or organ transplant, and systemic illness such as cancer.

Herniation

Depending on the site of mass effect there are different forms of herniation, and in all the parenchyma is damaged by direct compression or by vascular compromise when supplying vessels are crushed. Six routes are labelled on the diagram: cingulate (subfalcine) beneath the falx, seen on CT as midline shift with displacement of the ventricles; central (transtentorial) straight down through the incisura; uncal, the medial temporal lobe over the tentorial edge; transcalvarial, brain extruding through a skull defect; upward cerebellar through the incisura; and downward cerebellar (tonsillar) through the foramen magnum. A relatively small posterior fossa bleed is disproportionately dangerous because the compartment is small and the brainstem sits at its outlet; on CT, crowding of the foramen magnum is the step just before the tonsils herniate, and the finding that gets neurosurgery called.

Sources differ: the lecture credited the cerebellum with breathing and heart rate; those are medullary functions (standard neuroanatomy), and what kills in tonsillar herniation is compression of the medulla at the foramen magnum. The conclusion, that a posterior fossa bleed is among the most lethal, stands.
Sources differ: the lecture's diagram labels the downward route "central (trans-tentorial)" and "uncal", while its CT case one slide later captions a hemisphere pushed down under the tentorium "infratentorial herniation". Standard terminology is descending transtentorial or uncal herniation (Radiopaedia). Answer in the lecturer's vocabulary where the item is his, and know the standard term.

The four haemorrhages

There are four basic types: intraparenchymal, subarachnoid, subdural and epidural. In trauma more than one is often present at once; on CT haemorrhage is bright, because clot is denser than brain: flowing blood in a vessel is not bright, and neither is the bleed of a patient who cannot form a clot, so a coagulopathic patient can bleed without the bright sign; and blood shows up in different potential spaces depending on the injury, so localising the site tells you the cause. From outside in, the layers are the superior sagittal sinus, the outer and inner dura, the arachnoid, the subarachnoid space and the pia.

TypeVessel and mechanismShape and suturesSetting
EpiduralArterial, classically the middle meningeal artery; higher pressure, expands rapidlyLens-shaped, biconvex; does not cross suturesTrauma, often with a skull fracture
SubduralStretching and tearing of bridging cortical veins crossing to a dural sinus; venous, low pressure, so slow and insidious; also leakage from a parenchymal bleedCrescentic; crosses suturesThe elderly, whose atrophy leaves the brain in a pool of CSF, free to rotate and tear the veins even after a low-energy impact
SubarachnoidBetween arachnoid and pia; trauma or ruptured aneurysm; angiography finds the sourceSerpiginous, layering in the sulci along the gyriThunderclap headache
IntraparenchymalWithin the brain substance: hypertension, trauma, infarct, tumour, cerebral amyloid angiopathyRound hyperdense lesion in parenchymaHypertensive bleeds sit centrally, in the basal ganglia: their fine feeder vessels arise close to the circle of Willis, where pressure is highest, and cannot take the load. Can cause cerebellar herniation from the posterior fossa
Sources differ: the imaging deck's summary slides print "biconcave" beneath the epidural image, while the lab manual and standard texts say biconvex or lentiform, and the deck's own picture is unmistakably a lens bulging inward. Extradural haematoma is biconvex (Radiopaedia; Radiology Masterclass); the deck's word is a wording error. Answer "biconvex, lens-shaped", and recognise that an item written from the deck saying "biconcave" means the same lesion.

Epidural against subdural. When a fracture shears the middle meningeal artery, the arterial bleed strips the dura off the bone and expands fast. It kills fastest and is the most fixable: the artery can be clipped, coiled or ligated and the clot evacuated. A subdural is harder: dozens of torn veins, no tamponade, recurrence, an elderly or anticoagulated patient. Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is a double injury: hydrocephalus to come, plus an artery no longer perfusing the brain.

Sources differ: Dr. Moreland told the classic “talk, go home, go to bed, die” story about a subdural haematoma, a slow venous bleed after a minor blow. Standard texts attach the lucid interval to epidural haematoma (roughly 20–50% of cases; UChicago Medicine), though it is also described in acute subdurals (JAMA). Expect “lucid interval → epidural” on a standard item; on a Moreland-written item, the elderly patient with a low-energy injury who deteriorates hours later has a subdural.
Sources differ: in the question period Dr. Moreland put subdural mortality at 50%, a figure given from memory without a citation. Published acute-subdural mortality runs from about 14–34% in recent series to about 60% in older ones (Wilberger 1991; J Trauma 2012). No single number is examinable; expect “subdural carries a higher mortality than epidural, which kills faster but is more treatable”.
Sources differ: the slides give trauma or ruptured aneurysm as the causes of subarachnoid haemorrhage; Dr. Moreland added that trauma is probably the more common. That is correct: trauma is the commonest cause overall, and a ruptured aneurysm accounts for about 85% of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage (MSD Manual). Answer “aneurysm” for a thunderclap or spontaneous stem, “trauma” for the commonest cause overall; an aneurysm must be occluded or it keeps bleeding.

The memory hook: the dura is stuck to the skull at the sutures, so epidural blood is trapped between sutures as a lens, while subdural blood spreads freely under the dura across sutures as a crescent. A single trauma CT can carry all four: epidural along a convexity, subarachnoid blood in the sylvian and basal cisterns, a subdural crescent along the tentorium, and parenchymal contusions in the temporal lobe; a black focus beside the epidural is air, so pneumocephalus is on the search pattern too. Practise the one-liner: lens and suture-bounded, epidural; crescent following the inner table, subdural; blood in sulci, fissures and cisterns, subarachnoid; blood inside the brain, intraparenchymal. Intraventricular haemorrhage is not one of the four categories. In the lab's case, a 72-year-old three days after a fall, with a gradually worsening headache, intermittent confusion, imbalance, drowsiness and mild left-sided weakness, has a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over the right hemisphere: a subdural haematoma compressing the right precentral gyrus and internal capsule.

Hydrocephalus, neoplasm and infection

Hydrocephalus is an increase in the volume of CSF causing distension of the ventricles, which produces mass effect and can lead to herniation. CSF is absorbed primarily into the venous system through the arachnoid villi and granulations. It is caused either by mechanically blocking flow before the site of absorption (obstructive), when only the part of the ventricular system upstream of the block dilates and treatment removes the obstruction or places a ventricular drain, or by a process preventing absorption (non-obstructive), when proteinaceous material, blood products, diffuse metastasis or infection block the granulations and all ventricles enlarge. Aqueductal stenosis enlarges the lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth; a central neurocytoma at the foramen of Monro obstructs; diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage blocks reabsorption. Look at which ventricles are big: the obstruction sits between the last dilated and the first normal ventricle. Block the third ventricle and the laterals expand; block the fourth and the laterals and third expand. Tuberculosis joins blood, protein and diffuse metastasis among the non-obstructive causes. Blood can cause both types at once: it clots inside the ventricles and it clogs the granulations, and which mechanism dominates matters less than the mass effect. The chain that links four objectives: ruptured aneurysm, subarachnoid haemorrhage, blocked granulations, non-obstructive hydrocephalus, mass effect, herniation.

Brain neoplasms are primary benign, primary malignant or metastatic; whatever the type, the first concern is that mass effect is not causing herniation, hydrocephalus or haemorrhage. Most are soft-tissue density and hard to characterise on non-contrast CT, so contrast CT or MRI is usually required, and often only pathology determines the type. Very large tumours can be invisible on a non-contrast CT, so a suspected tumour is imaged with contrast from the start; tumours also bleed, adding a second mass effect. The first question about any mass is intra-axial (within the parenchyma) or extra-axial (outside it, seen pushing the brain away, buckling the cortex inward). The classic extra-axial mass is a meningioma, marked by the rind of CSF separating it from brain. Metastases create far more oedema and mass effect than a primary lesion of the same size, so a small lesion with disproportionate oedema favours metastasis; primary tumours vary in enhancement with relatively little inflammation unless they become necrotic or bleed.

Sources differ: Dr. Moreland explained the extra oedema around a metastasis as the immune system recognising foreign cells, renal cells in the brain, that a primary tumour's related cells do not provoke. The observation is correct (JCPSP 2022), but the standard mechanism is vasogenic oedema from leaky, barrier-deficient tumour vessels, with glioblastoma infiltrating the surrounding brain instead (Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience 2022). Learn the sign, small lesion with disproportionate oedema, rather than the immune explanation.

The blood-brain barrier and the skull protect against infection; violating them, by trauma or by advanced superficial infection such as sinusitis or mastoiditis, is the common route of spread. Four entities, and they form a cascade, usually in this order and progressively more serious: meningitis (thickened enhancing meninges on post-contrast MRI), cerebritis (hazy parenchymal signal without a rim), ventriculitis (a bright rim lining the ventricle on FLAIR; its proteins clog the villi, so it kills through hydrocephalus) and brain abscess (a thick ring of enhancement on T1 post-contrast with surrounding oedema; if it breaches, infection floods the brain). Treatment is difficult because many drugs cannot cross the barrier.

Metastasis, abscess and glioblastoma can all appear as a ring-enhancing intra-axial mass with surrounding oedema, and even with MRI they can look very similar. The correct answer to such an image may be that they cannot be reliably distinguished on imaging: correlate clinically and proceed to biopsy or aspiration.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Four Monro-Kellie components; CT first, MRI to solve problems, contrast for vessels, inflammation and lesions.
  • Depressed fracture raises pressure; dural tear with CSF leak lowers it; both can drop the tonsils. Gas means an open fracture.
  • Six red flags mandate emergent imaging; the facial bones need their own CT.
  • Epidural: arterial, lens, stops at sutures, fracture. Subdural: venous, crescent, crosses sutures, elderly. Subarachnoid: sulci and cisterns, aneurysm. Parenchymal: five causes.
  • Obstructive dilates upstream only; non-obstructive dilates all. Lateral and third big, fourth normal: the aqueduct.
  • Small lesion, huge oedema: metastasis. Ring-enhancing lesions may be indistinguishable.
  • Bright blood means clot: a coagulopathic patient may bleed isodense. Hypertensive bleeds are central. Epidural kills fastest; subdural is hardest to stop.
  • Gas under a fracture: open, barrier-crossing antibiotics. Clear nasal drip: CSF via the cribriform plate. Vertex fracture: the superior sagittal sinus. Cascade: meningitis, cerebritis, ventriculitis, abscess.
Everything in the skull competes for a fixed volume, so every pathology is read by the mass effect it causes and the herniation it threatens. CT finds bone and acute blood first, MRI answers the harder questions, and contrast shows vessels, inflammation and lesions. Name the haemorrhage by its space and shape, name the hydrocephalus by which ventricles are big, ask whether a mass is inside or outside the brain and whether its oedema fits its size, and admit when a ring-enhancing lesion cannot be named without tissue.

guides.title: Week 42 · 17 Critical Appraisal and the Psychiatric Interview
guides.html:
HSR · CASP · ICE clinical skills

Critical Appraisal and the Psychiatric Interview

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The definition of critical appraisal, evidence-informed practice and the filtered-unfiltered pyramid, the CASP three-question spine and its section mapping for cohort and RCT, the two papers and the four cases they are mapped onto, the limitations taught, then the psychiatric interview: the hierarchy, the technique items, the history template and screening scripts, the twelve-heading mental status examination, the six risk domains and the suicide script, and the Taylor formulation.

Critical appraisal: becoming a consumer of research

Critical appraisal is the process that allows us to evaluate medical evidence to decide whether a research article is useful for informed decisions about care that is unique, and relevant to the individual patient we are caring for. In evidence-informed practice, research evidence has equal footing with health care resources, clinical state and circumstances, and patient preferences and actions; clinical expertise ties them together. The evidence pyramid shown has filtered information at the top (systematic reviews, then critically appraised topics such as evidence syntheses and guidelines, then critically appraised individual articles) and unfiltered information below (randomised controlled trials, cohort studies, then case-control studies, case series and reports), with background information and expert opinion at the base. The two starred tiers, RCTs and cohorts, are the designs appraised this week.

CASP, the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme, is a set of ten checklists, one per study design. The spine is three questions: is the article valid; what are the results; are they relevant to the specific cases. The cohort checklist answers them in sections A, B and C; the RCT checklist in sections A and B for validity, C for results and D for relevance.
Cohort studyRandomised controlled trial
PaperReal-world effectiveness of antipsychotic treatments in a nationwide cohort of 29,823 patients with schizophrenia, Tiihonen and colleagues, JAMA Psychiatry 2017Effectiveness of antipsychotic drugs in patients with chronic schizophrenia, Lieberman and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine 2005, the CATIE trial
What it isA Finnish register cohort using within-individual comparison; its rehospitalisation ranking is the "clozapine and depots work best" slideA fixed-duration trial whose defining finding was high discontinuation: only a quarter of patients stayed on treatment at 18 months
Validity sectionsAA and B
Results and relevanceB, then C with the specifics of the caseC, then D with the specifics of the case

Both papers are mapped, choose all that apply, onto the four cases of the week: a 23-year-old university student with months of withdrawal, persecutory beliefs about his devices and a reply to a commanding voice, whose father has schizophrenia (first psychosis); a 33-year-old brought by police in January in one shoe, screaming that people want to murder her, talking to the walls, known to improve after a single dose and positive for cannabis and methamphetamine (substance-induced psychosis); a 54-year-old with hypertension and dyslipidaemia, remitted on long-acting paliperidone after voices and cameras in the apartment, 30 pounds heavier and puckering and chewing without awareness (chronic schizophrenia in family practice, with tardive dyskinesia); and a 33-year-old game designer eight years in remission on risperidone 2 mg who wants to stop because of erectile dysfunction and anorgasmia before his wedding (side effects and long-term treatment). The discriminating variable is population match: both papers studied chronic schizophrenia on maintenance treatment, so the family-practice case fits best and the substance-induced case fits worst; the discontinuation question is one a real-world cohort answers better than a fixed-duration trial. "Not sure" is an allowed validity verdict.

The only limitations taught are four bullets under two headings. Are the articles outdated? The doses used, and newer antipsychotics not included. Are they generalisable? Different health care systems, and applicability to only one point in time. A Finnish register is not the Canadian system, and a 2005 trial does not reflect current agents. The appraisal habits that matter in psychiatry: state the PICO before opening the checklist; for a cohort ask what confounder would explain the result and whether it was measured, since confounding by indication (sicker patients get the newer drug) and immortal time are the central threats in register cohorts of treatment; for an RCT ask whether the analysis was intention-to-treat and how much attrition there was; and remember that psychiatry trials have large placebo responses, rating-scale outcomes whose statistical significance may be clinically trivial, blinding that fails when a drug sedates or causes weight gain, and comparisons of depot against oral drug that confound pharmacology with adherence.

The psychiatric interview

Psychiatric interviewing relies on "looking, listening, wondering about the meaning of the things you see and hear, and thinking about their connection to what you know". Slow down. The only requirements are interest, attention, a willingness to practise, and experience. Do not confuse the order of the presentation with the sequence of information-gathering: "forget the idea of interviewing from a checklist", which makes the interviewer sound more interested in an agenda than in the patient, but use a checklist towards the end or afterwards to make sense of what has been gathered. The history and the mental status examination cover the same five domains, asked about and then observed: behaviour and adaptive functioning against overt behaviour; physical manifestations against appearance; emotions against mood and affect; consciousness, orientation, memory and intellect against sensorium and memory; speech, thinking, perception and self-experience against speech, thought process, thought content and perception.

The diagnostic hierarchy, top down
Physical and drug-induced conditions, hallmark confusion, are recognised most reliably, are most open to specific and sometimes life-saving treatment, and may feature every sign of the conditions below. The psychoses, hallmark impaired reality-testing with delusions and hallucinations, are disabling and sometimes dangerous, with good evidence for drug treatment, and may show the features of the conditions below them. Depression and anxiety, affective symptoms without confusion or impaired reality-testing, are very common, often situational, treated with medication and psychological, environmental and behavioural approaches, with a less sinister prognosis. Higher rungs feature lower-rung symptoms; lower rungs rarely show higher-rung signs. Exclude organic causes first, then psychosis, then mood. The five appraisal questions: how dangerous, how impaired, what context, what physical factors, who is the person.

Technique is learnable and the group ticks it live. Start by greeting the patient, giving one's name and student status, asking the patient's understanding of the interview, saying how much time there is, and opening with open questions. Elicit the spontaneous account: listen, let statements finish, leave silence, ask whether there is anything more, notice and respond to verbal hints and non-verbal clues, encourage feelings and thoughts. Get more: continue open questions while productive, then move to closed questions to resolve ambiguities, encourage precise dated and quantified information, ask one concise question at a time, avoid leading questions and jargon, and show calm interest in emotionally loaded material (suicide, abuse, money, sex, death), raising it unprompted when clues appear. Say "die by suicide" or "complete suicide", not "commit suicide"; "drug use", not "drug abuse". Manage time, avoid repetition, stay flexibly on task, redirect tactfully. Close by not leaving sensitive topics to the end, summarising briefly, and thanking the patient. Key phrases: "help me to understand"; "let's work together to"; "you're doing well, let's keep going"; "in the interest of time, I may ask questions more quickly"; "I apologise if I interrupt you"; "what you're talking about is important". Convey at the end an understanding of the concerns, validation, and where appropriate hope.

The history opens with name and role, purpose, circumstances, the limits of confidentiality, and thanks. Identifying data include living situation, relationship status and partner's gender, children, income and occupation, and inpatient or outpatient with voluntary or involuntary status. The chief concern is asked as "please tell me about the concerns that you've had recently"; the history of present concern covers context (events, stressors, losses, precipitants), symptoms with onset, duration, progression, intensity and fluctuation, probed with "describe for me what that's like; how do you experience it?", impact on functioning, supports and coping, similar past experiences and longitudinal course, last period of wellness, changes to usual personality when unwell, reason for seeking help and expectations, a review of systems for mood, anxiety and psychosis, and risk. Past psychiatric history quantifies attempts by number, severity, medical intervention and most recent. Substance use covers type (including gambling and online use), first, typical and last use, periods of abstinence, withdrawal, treatment and impact. Past medical history singles out endocrine and neurological conditions, seizures and head injuries; medications include contraceptives and over-the-counter and herbal products. The developmental history runs prenatal, early childhood, school age, sexuality, adulthood, and looks for emotional development, major themes, recurring patterns, identity, failure and loss, and the impact of experiences on beliefs and trust; at this stage the priority is the presenting problem, its biopsychosocial context and its impact.

ScreenScripted question
Depression"Have you ever had 2 weeks or more when you felt sad or low, for most of the day, nearly every day?" and the same for loss of interest; then anchor an episode and ask about suicidal ideation, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, sleep
Mania"Have you had an unusually high mood for many days in a row? How many days?" "Did you have increased energy during this time? Were you more active?"
AnxietyGeneralised: regular worry about multiple things, hard to control. Panic: intense physical anxiety all of a sudden. Agoraphobia: avoiding public situations. Social: fear of performance or judgement. Phobia: specific feared things
Obsessive-compulsive and post-traumaticIntrusive thoughts that keep coming back; behaviours done over and over that are hard to resist. Something horrific causing intense fear; recurrent dreams, nightmares or flashbacks
DelusionsEach begins "Has it ever seemed that": "people are after you" (persecutory); "some outside force is controlling your actions or thoughts" (control); "others know what you think" (mind reading); "you have special traits or abilities" (grandiosity); "things happen because of you, or people are talking about you" (reference); "thoughts are put into or taken out of your head by some outside force" (insertion, withdrawal); "something has changed in your body" (somatic). In psychotic depression delusions are mood-congruent: nihilistic, somatic, guilty
Auditory hallucinationsScreen: "Do you ever hear things that others don't hear, like a voice speaking to you?" Quality: conscience, inside or outside the head. Number and recognisability. Commentary: "are the voices commenting on your actions?" Command: "are the voices telling you what to do? Are they telling you to hurt yourself or others?" Then ask about concurrent substance use and the intensity of symptoms when abstinent

The mental status examination and risk

The mental status examination is the physical examination of psychiatry: pressured speech, distractibility and affect lability point to mania; dysphoria, delayed thought processing and poverty of speech to depression. The write-up order is appearance, attitude, behaviour, level of alertness, speech and thought form, cognition, mood, affect, thought content, perception, insight, judgement. Appearance and behaviour record apparent against chronological age, grooming, dress, habitus, eye contact, attitude (polite, collaborative, guarded, evasive, hostile), reliability, and motor findings including psychomotor change, tics, tremor, tardive dyskinesia, dystonia and catatonia. Speech has nine axes: rate, rhythm, volume, tone, quantity, spontaneity, latency, fluency, articulation. Mood is subjective, in the patient's words, rated 0 to 10 with 0 worst and 10 well, the reverse of most scales. Affect is objective, on four axes: quality and intensity (euthymic, depressed, elevated, anxious, irritable), range (full, restricted, flat, blunted), stability (fixed to labile), and congruence with mood and thought content. Thought process runs organised and goal-directed through circumstantial, tangential, loosening of associations, word salad, plus flight of ideas, thought blocking and repetition. Thought content covers themes, over-valued ideas, delusions, obsessions, and suicidal or homicidal ideation with intent and plan. Perception records hallucinations reported in four modalities (visual, auditory, olfactory, tactile) and the observed sign of responding to internal stimuli. Cognition covers level of consciousness, orientation to name, place and time, attention, memory, intellect, and a formal screen if applicable. Insight is realising one has a mental health concern and appreciating its implications, two parts; judgement is recent behaviour as it relates to safety, social functioning and treatment decisions; both are graded none, partial, or intact.

Risk has six domains, not one: suicide; other deliberate self-harm; violence to others; inability to look after oneself; self-neglect; neglect of dependents; plus safe driving and cooking. The suicide script, in order: "Has life seemed so stressful that you think about death or suicide?" "Are you thinking about ways that you would end your life?" "Have you prepared or acquired the means for suicide?" "How would you describe your level of intent?" "Have you attempted suicide in the past? When?" Then classify acute against chronic, and active (plans for suicide) against passive (thoughts of death), and end on protective factors: "What are some reasons for staying alive?"

Formulation follows the Taylor triad: classify the illness (the symptoms and signs the patient brings), discern the predicament (the context in which they are understood), and discover the disease (the pathophysiology) if possible. The management plan is biopsychosocial, covering medication, therapy and lifestyle change, and must be feasible and mitigate any safety concerns. The case is presented as history, mental status examination, a two- to three-sentence summary of the most pertinent historical and mental state findings, a diagnostic impression, and the plan; the mark rewards data collection that captures the individual's psychosocial context, terms applied in the appropriate categories (an affect word never in the mood line), an accurate description of the illness, and synthesis rather than transcription.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Valid, results, relevant: cohort A, B, C; RCT A and B, C, D. Ten CASP checklists.
  • Filtered above unfiltered on the pyramid; the two starred tiers are RCT and cohort.
  • Outdated (doses, newer drugs) and generalisable (systems, one point in time) are the only limitations taught.
  • Gather organically, present conventionally, checklist at the end.
  • Confusion tops the hierarchy; clear it first.
  • Mood 0 is worst; affect has four axes; insight has two parts; judgement is recent behaviour.
  • The suicide script ends on reasons for living; "die by suicide", never "commit".
Appraise a paper by asking whether it is valid, what it found and whether it applies to this patient, then say honestly that a 2005 trial and a Finnish register may be outdated or ungeneralisable. Interview by looking, listening and wondering before asking, clear the organic rung first, script the screens for mood, mania, delusions and voices, walk the suicide ladder to its protective end, and write the mental status examination in its twelve headings with mood as the patient's word and affect as the clinician's observation.

guides.title: Week 42 · 18 Integrated Review and Formative Quiz Walkthrough
guides.html:
Week 42 · WFQ · cross-cutting

Integrated Review and Formative Quiz Walkthrough

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The week in one page, the thirteen places where the sources disagree and what to answer, all eleven formative quiz questions walked through with their traps, the patient-educator panel's messages, and nine applied cases that cross the week's lectures.

The week in one page

Psychosis week joins five threads. Schizophrenia: a hallucination is a perception without a stimulus and a delusion a fixed false belief; the criteria need two of five symptoms for a month within six months of disturbance and functional decline, with schizophreniform under six months, delusional disorder without hallucinations, and any found cause moving the case out of the schizophrenias. Prevalence 0.5 to 1%, peak male onset in the early twenties, heritability about 80%, forensic patients 85% psychotic and the targeted persecutory delusion the most dangerous. Ventricles bigger and cortex smaller, radial and tangential migration that must meet, dopamine released abnormally to amphetamine and mis-assigning salience. Antipsychotics are D2 antagonists whose side effects follow the pathway and the dose digits: single-digit drugs give parkinsonism and prolactin, three-digit drugs give sedation, hypotension and constipation with no EPS, and clozapine is the only truly atypical drug. Four weeks, switch, clozapine, ECT; depots and clozapine keep people out of hospital; only a quarter are still on treatment at 18 months. Adverse reactions: Type A for the predictable, Type B for the bizarre, serotonin syndrome fast and hyperreflexic, neuroleptic malignant syndrome slow and rigid. Personality and development: memorise the borderline criteria, validate before anything else, interview children together and apart, report suspected abuse under 16, know anxiety's four-step sequence and depression's two paediatric modifications, screen adults for ADHD with the self-report scale and treat with education, strategies and a long-acting stimulant. Neuroanatomy: eight bones meeting at the pterion over the middle meningeal artery, three meninges and their potential spaces, the tentorium hung from the petrous ridge with the midbrain in its notch, sinuses draining to the jugular foramen, CSF from choroid plexus to granulations, and on CT a lens for arterial blood, a crescent for venous, sulci for aneurysmal, and upstream ventricles for a block.

Where the sources disagree

Sources differ: the values below are the ones to give on the exam, with the source each comes from in brackets.
QuestionWhat to answer
Prevalence of schizophrenia0.5% (lecture); 0.5 to 1% (quiz key); "1 in 10" (patient panel) is psychotic experiences, not a disorder
Male peak onset23 (slide); 22 was also said, and means the same early twenties
Dopamine tractsFour pathways: nigrostriatal for EPS, tuberoinfundibular for prolactin, mesolimbic for feeling bad, mesocortical for the therapeutic effect
Antipsychotic dosesHaloperidol 2 to 5, clozapine 300 to 600, quetiapine 600 to 900 (slide) for the digit rule; the licensed ranges (AFP review) when a stem quotes them
Schizophrenia criteriaDSM-IV-TR (slide); DSM-5 needs one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech, and dropped the bizarre-delusion carve-out and the subtypes
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome mechanismDecreased dopamine from D2 blockade; a stray statement of increased dopamine is wrong
Validation levelsSix ways (slide); five levels (workshop), the fifth the most validating
ADHD symptom countsNine per domain; 6 of 9, or 5 at age 17 and older; both decks print only eight inattention items
Generalised anxiety in youthOne of six associated symptoms; adults need three
Lobes of the brainSix on a lab question including insula and limbic; five on a lecture question, with the limbic lobe not discrete
Epidural shapeBiconvex, lens-shaped; the imaging deck's "biconcave" names the same lesion
Fourth-ventricle outletsMedian aperture (Magendie) plus paired lateral apertures (Luschka); the flowchart omits the median
Tentorium's anterior attachmentThe petrous ridge; the clinoids are endpoints

The formative quiz, walked through

Eleven single-best-answer questions, all psychiatry, none neuroanatomy; two are written in the second person as a resident, which is the applied style to expect.

  1. Evidence-based treatment of schizophrenia. Assertive community treatment teams reduce hospitalisations. They do not raise employment (that is supported employment); CBT reduces distress attached to hallucinations but does not stop them; family psychoeducation reduces relapse, not substance use.
  2. The pathway behind neurological side effects. Nigrostriatal. Tuberoinfundibular is prolactin, mesolimbic reward, mesocortical the antipsychotic effect.
  3. A negative symptom. Low motivation, avolition. Hallucinations, paranoid delusions and thought insertion are positive.
  4. Epidemiology. Prevalence 0.5 to 1%. Incidence is about 15 to 20 per 100,000 person-years, an order of magnitude below 1 per 1,000; most cases begin before 30; men are affected more, not less.
  5. A 35-year-old with lupus, hypertension and old depression, one week into prednisone 50 mg, with pressured speech, irritability and voices for days. Steroid-induced psychosis: the timeline names the drug. Lupus psychosis needs a flare; schizophreniform needs no substance cause and one to six months; a depressive recurrence does not present manic.
  6. An 88-year-old with Alzheimer's disease on the medical ward wants to leave because he dislikes the food and Western medicine, and the team asks for a Form 1. He should be assessed by the treating team for capacity: does he understand and appreciate the risks and benefits of refusing antibiotics. Refusing treatment is not grounds for a Form 1, dementia is a mental disorder under the Mental Health Act, and an incapable patient's decisions pass to a substitute decision-maker, still without a Form 1.
  7. Why quetiapine sedates. Significant affinity for histamine receptors: a three-digit, low-D2-affinity drug whose excess binds off-target receptors. Its D2 affinity is lower than haloperidol's, muscarinic blockade gives dry mouth and constipation, and there is no low-dose mesocortical effect.
  8. A 19-year-old who cannot sit still, with muscle contractions, tremor, stiffness and facial movements after a new antipsychotic in its usual dose range. Haloperidol: single-digit, highest affinity, most EPS. Loxapine and olanzapine are two-digit; clozapine is three-digit with no EPS.
  9. Delusional disorder against schizophrenia. Delusional disorder does not include hallucinations. There is no prodromal decline, the course is chronic rather than self-limiting, and antipsychotics treat both.
  10. A 45-year-old construction worker, angry that there is nothing wrong with him. The finding that warrants an antipsychotic is a nine-month belief that the FBI hired him to protect the prime minister: fixed, implausible, past both duration thresholds. Noises after a concert are tinnitus with a real stimulus; two months of low mood after a job loss is a mood symptom with a precipitant; fear of criminals three weeks after a mugging is a plausible, reality-based worry. "Nothing wrong with me" is impaired insight.
  11. A 70-year-old with Alzheimer's disease, new visual hallucinations of a fairy, worse in the evenings, sleepy and inattentive. The least appropriate action is to prescribe an antipsychotic and see him in a month. Acute visual hallucinations with sundowning and inattention in dementia are delirium until proven otherwise: examine chest, abdomen and nervous system, order urinalysis, blood count and electrolytes, and consider the emergency department. Antipsychotics also carry the boxed warning for mortality in dementia-related psychosis.
Four of the eleven items are answerable from lectures alone, five need the assigned review as well, and two test content none of the week's material carries: assertive community treatment, and the Mental Health Act's Form 1 criteria. Both are answered above.

The patient-educator panel

Hallucinations and delusions are common human experiences, not specific to schizophrenia, and at population level are often not distressing; voices vary in valence and some people do not want theirs removed. The clinical task is dual: elicit the symptoms and signs, and understand the meaning the person and their family make of them, in frameworks of religion, spirituality, culture and trauma. Partner by listening deeply, understanding their perspective on the crisis, and avoiding coercion whenever possible, because coercion damages the future relationship with the illness, its treatment and its providers; manage the short-term crisis safely while building a safe, meaningful, dignified, self-determined life. When giving a diagnosis, explain what you mean and what you do not mean; stigma comes as self-stigma, structural stigma and discrimination in work, housing and social life. Antipsychotics block D2 in the mesolimbic pathway and their four adverse-effect domains are weight and insulin resistance, sedation, sexual dysfunction and neuromotor effects; the four non-pharmacological supports named are peer support, CBT, alternative medicine and the Hearing Voices movement. Validate without insisting: connect to the emotion, not the content. A patient may withhold symptoms because disclosure has a cost, such as a dose increase. Most people with schizophrenia are victims, not perpetrators. Clinicians facilitate healing by holding and instilling hope.

Applied cases across the week

  • A young man in the emergency department with agitation and psychosis: de-escalate ("you're not in trouble, we're here to help"; do not argue with or agree with the delusion), then haloperidol or loxapine with lorazepam; screen for substances and the cause, since a found cause is no longer schizophrenia.
  • A woman hours after her first SSRI dose, on St. John's Wort and tryptophan, at 39 °C with hyperreflexia: serotonin syndrome, a severe Type A pharmacodynamic interaction; stop all three; the hospital reports, the practitioner does not.
  • A man four days after an antipsychotic dose increase, confused then rigid and febrile: neuroleptic malignant syndrome; check creatine kinase, stop the drug, fluids, cooling, dantrolene and bromocriptine.
  • A 14-year-old who discloses abuse and begs for secrecy: report to the Children's Aid Society yourself, now; the safety of a child under 16 is a stated limit of confidentiality.
  • A 15-year-old who has stopped attending school: school avoidance is not a diagnosis; find the separation anxiety, social anxiety or depression beneath it; CBT first, SSRI off-label if impaired, observe for suicidality to 24.
  • A medical student with excellent grades who cannot start tasks since leaving home: intelligence and structure compensated; a transition unmasked; screen with the self-report scale, confirm with the checklist rated for childhood and now.
  • An 85-year-old with blood from the ear after a fall: temporal bone fracture; if the collection on CT is a lens against a suture, the middle meningeal artery; if a crescent across sutures three days later, the bridging veins.
  • A CT with lateral and third ventricles dilated and a normal fourth: aqueductal stenosis, obstructive; all four dilated after a subarachnoid bleed, blocked granulations, non-obstructive.
  • A ring-enhancing mass with oedema: metastasis, abscess or glioblastoma; imaging may not tell them apart.
Find the cause before calling it schizophrenia, count the digits before predicting the side effect, clear confusion before diagnosing psychosis, validate before you assess, report on suspicion under 16, and read every scan by the mass effect it threatens. The formative quiz rewards exactly those reflexes: pathway to side effect, dose to side effect, delusion to duration, drug to timeline, refusal to capacity, and hallucination in dementia to delirium.

guides.title: Week 42 · 19 Cram Sheet
guides.html:
Night-Before High-Yield

Psych III — Psychosis, Personality Disorders, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I

Week 42 · Psych III — Psychosis, PD, ADHD & Neuroanatomy I
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite
★ Do-not-miss · first-step reflexes
Acute psychosis with agitation in the ED → de-escalate first (casual, respectful; “you're not in trouble, we're here to help”; do not argue with or agree with the delusion), then antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine: haloperidol or loxapine with lorazepam, oral or IM. Screen for a cause: a found cause is no longer schizophrenia; methamphetamine is the commonest.
Hyperthermic, hyperreflexic, clonus, dilated pupils, hyperactive bowels, hours after a serotonergic agent → serotonin syndrome. Clinical diagnosis; serum serotonin is useless. Stop every serotonergic drug, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine if moderate to severe; no antipyretics, no restraints.
Confusion, then lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, fever, over 1 to 3 days on a dopamine antagonist → neuroleptic malignant syndrome (6 to 10% fatal untreated; 30% rhabdomyolysis). Creatine kinase, stop the drug, aggressive fluids, cooling, benzodiazepines, dantrolene, bromocriptine.
Fever and neck stiffness on clozapine, or any infection → check the neutrophils: agranulocytosis. CBC weekly for 6 months, fortnightly for 6, then monthly; myocarditis in the first weeks; seizures dose-related.
New visual hallucinations, sundowning, drowsiness and inattention in dementia → delirium until proven otherwise. Examine, urinalysis, CBC, electrolytes, consider the ED. Do not start an antipsychotic and wait a month.
Pressured speech, irritability and voices days after starting prednisone → steroid-induced psychosis, not schizophreniform or lupus psychosis.
Child under 16 discloses abuse or neglect → reasonable grounds to suspect is enough: report immediately and directly to the Children's Aid Society yourself, and again on new grounds. At 16 or 17, permitted but not required.
Suicidal thoughts disclosed → ideation, then ways, then means acquired, then intent, then past attempts; acute vs chronic, active (plans) vs passive (thoughts of death); end on reasons for living. Six risk domains, not one.
Thunderclap headache, new deficit, fever with neck stiffness, head trauma, immunosuppression, or new severe headache over 50 → emergent head CT.
Trauma to the temple, brief loss of consciousness, lucid interval, then decline → epidural haematoma: pterion, middle meningeal artery, lens on CT that stops at sutures, expands fast. Neurosurgery.
Elderly fall, days of worsening headache, confusion, contralateral weakness → subdural haematoma: bridging veins, crescent that crosses sutures.
Depressed skull fracture → raises pressure, emergent repair; intracranial gas means an open fracture and infection risk. CSF from the nose or ear → dural tear, pressure falls, brain sags. Otorrhagia after trauma is a temporal bone fracture.
Posterior fossa bleed → small compartment, brainstem at the outlet, tonsillar herniation; and any supratentorial mass with a blown pupil → uncal herniation through the tentorial notch onto the midbrain and third nerve.

Schizophrenia in numbers Wong L1–L2 · AFP 2014

Prevalence 0.5% (lecture); 0.5–1% (quiz key)
Peak onset Men 23 (slide), women 40 as a late second peak; 80% before 30; M:F 2:1
Heritability · familial risk About 80% · MZ twin or both parents 40–50%, first degree 10–15%, second 3%, third 2%, baseline 0.5%
Risk factors Maternal influenza RR 7 (first trimester); urbanicity RR 2, attributable risk 34%; season of birth RR 1.11; smoking-lung cancer RR 30 for scale
Violence 85% of forensic patients psychotic; ~40/40/15 early, late, late-late starters; ~40% of first episodes could have been charged; targeted persecutory delusion most dangerous; strangers rarely
Suicide · mortality Suicide 13×, lifetime ~5% (higher with hallucinations, delusions, substance use, past attempts); mortality 2–3×, cardiovascular and respiratory
Criteria Two of five for a month, six months total, functional decline; DSM-5 needs one of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech
Schizophreniform · brief psychotic · delusional 1–6 months · 1 day–1 month · delusions without hallucinations
Negative symptoms Affective flattening, alogia, avolition (low motivation, social withdrawal)
Mood congruence Depressed: nihilistic, somatic, guilty; manic: grandiose → mood disorder with psychotic features
Hallucination modality Schizophrenia auditory (voices, meaningful, in a known language); delirium visual; hallucinogens visual distortion; temporal lobe seizures olfactory
Abi-Dargham Baseline D2 availability equal; amphetamine-induced release 13.8% vs 7.1%
Histology Bigger ventricles, smaller cortex; hippocampus smaller but not specific; pyramidal cells shifted deep; fewer interneuron markers and spines

Antipsychotics Wong L2 · AFP 2014 · WFQ

Pathways Nigrostriatal EPS; tuberoinfundibular prolactin; mesolimbic feeling bad; mesocortical the antipsychotic effect
Digit rule Single digits (haloperidol 2–5, risperidone 6–9, paliperidone 6–12, fluphenazine 5–10) high affinity: EPS, prolactin. Tens (olanzapine 20–30, loxapine 50–100) mixed. Hundreds (chlorpromazine 300–800, clozapine 300–600, quetiapine 600–900) low affinity: sedation H1, hypotension α, constipation and no EPS muscarinic
Why quetiapine sedates · most EPS Histamine affinity · haloperidol
EPS treatment Benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, procyclidine (anticholinergic); propranolol for akathisia; lorazepam, amantadine, diphenhydramine. TD: irreversible; VMAT2 inhibitors
Receptors D1–D5 all GPCRs; D1-like raise cAMP, D2-like lower it; benzodiazepines act at GABA-A
Generations Equal efficacy; typicals EPS, atypicals metabolic; clozapine the only truly atypical; boxed warning for mortality in dementia
Algorithm 4 weeks no improvement → switch 4–6 weeks → clozapine → ECT. No combinations, no loading dose (NICE)
Best at keeping out of hospital LAI paliperidone 0.51, LAI zuclopenthixol 0.53, oral clozapine 0.53; depots work because the drug is in the body; ~1/3 take pills as prescribed
Efficacy · weight Clozapine −0.89, amisulpride −0.73 · ziprasidone −0.16 kg, aripiprazole +0.48, risperidone +1.44, clozapine +1.89, quetiapine +1.94, olanzapine +2.78, zotepine +3.21
